Sports.title: Featured Comment: Has F1 failed to promote quality racing? | Brief
Sports.content:
Those in charge of Formula 1 have allowed its new rules to turn racing into a ‘battle of the bots’, says @RedPill:

I felt there was going to be some trust and proper direction within FIA and Liberty Media who owns the rights to F1 to make sure the quality of (human) racing was going to remain high quality. Boy, we were wrong. The whole debacle and agreed verbiage in contacts allowed the power unit manufacturers and investors to pretty much be the ones to dictate what was going to be allowed in F1, while retaining huge powers in the wording to prevent changes.

Fans, drivers, teams, FIA and Liberty Media are now stuck with it. I hate how the drivers are more passengers in their own cars while racing. Yes, there’s too much going in the cars, that the drivers can’t possibly manage everything and race in full anger, but this is no secret or anything new. The powers that be needed to craft specifications that used the latest tech, but still retain the drivers’ ability to fully race the car, the way a race car driver is suppose to race. That is why we watch the races.

We come and watch these F1 races because there’s humans in control of brilliant machinery, racing them to the ninth degree, but there’s a limit. If I wanted to watch automated machinery duke it out and see battle of bots I would instead go to robot contests, not F1.

Red Pill (@RedPill)

Sports.title: Which of Antonelli’s rivals is his biggest threat for the championship this year? | Debates and Polls
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s strong position in the lead of the championship standings at the summer break is remarkable enough already for a driver in his second season in Formula 1.

But what makes his position all the more impressive is that, arguably, no single driver has yet emerged as his clear rival. Antonelli has won six of the 11 rounds so far, more than the rest put together, and only his team mate George Russell has taken multiple wins.

Despite that, Russell is not Antonelli’s closest rival in the standings: Lewis Hamilton is leading a resurgent Ferrari. Plus, the final round before the summer break saw McLaren claim their first victory of the season. Three of the last five grands prix were won by teams other than Mercedes – could Antonelli biggest threat come from one of them?

Lewis Hamilton

50 points behind

The possibility of Hamilton fighting for the championship against the driver who took the Mercedes seat he vacated last year is a compelling narrative. But is it a likely outcome? Hamilton is Antonelli’s closest rival in the points but has missed opportunities due to penalties in recent races.

George Russell

59 points behind

Russell should be Antonelli’s closest rival for the championship but various factors have left him well behind including unreliability (not that Antonelli has been immune), some misfortune and his risky first-lap lunge at Spa. He’s also on course to incur a power unit change penalty before his team mate. Still, Russell should have the equipment and the experience to put Antonelli under pressure.

Charles Leclerc

81 points behind

Hamilton may be closer to Antonelli in the standings but Charles Leclerc has arguably looked more competitive. Providing he avoids a repeat of the dip he fell into around Spain and Monaco, he could emerge as Antonelli’s biggest threat.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Lando Norris

91 points behind

Like Mercedes, unreliability has dogged McLaren this year. They often haven’t been quick enough either, though Norris has now won both a grand prix and a sprint race. The MCL40’s Hungaroring upgrade clearly paid off, and may prove enough to bring the McLarens into regular contention. The reigning world champion is a long way behind, though.

Max Verstappen

110 points behind

If last year demonstrated anything, it is unwise to write off Max Verstappen if he is not mathematically out of contention. Having been 104 points off the lead with 249 remaining, he eventually lost by the narrowest margin in F1 history (relatively). But lying 110 points behind in a car which hasn’t won a grand prix yet may be too much even for him.

Oscar Piastri

127 points behind

Oscar Piastri has proved a close match on pace for his team mate as usual but he’s even further behind in the standings. He went into the final round of last season with a shot at the championship but that doesn’t look likely to happen this year.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Isack Hadjar

151 points behind

Isack Hadjar has impressed with the quality of his performances alongside Verstappen and may yet recover the points he dropped after losing his podium finish in Monaco. But his points deficit to Antonelli is surely too large and the Red Bull not competitive enough yet for him to be a realistic title contender.

I say

Hamilton may be closest in the points but Russell surely has the better combination of opportunity and equipment at the moment. If he can stop the rot in the second half of the season I would back him to put Antonelli under pressure for the title.

Sports.title: Domenicali resists Briatore’s call for sprint races at every round | Brief
Sports.content:
Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali will not move to add sprint races at every round next season, but still plans to hold more than the current six.

Alpine consultant Flavio Briatore recently argued for F1 to hold sprint races every week and, as is done in Moto GP.

Speaking in Liberty Media’s latest earnings update call for investors, Domenicali said limiting the number of sprint rounds gives them scarcity value.

“Sprint races is an opportunity that, first of all, started because we wanted to produce something that could create action on the track, creating leverage for the promoter and ourselves to create action on the tracks starting for the weekend,” he said. “We’re going to have more sprint races next year, yes. We’ll inform when we will announce the calendar, how many.

“The principle is very simple. This is also an opportunity to increment the revenue stream, for sure. This is an opportunity for us to have new deals, as we have already seen, and moving in this direction will be our future. We want to do in the right way because, of course, this will allow us also to make sure that the scarcity is a value.”

Formula 1

Sports.title: Antonelli says he ‘let pressure destroy me’ in mid-season slump last year | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli admitted he succumbed to pressure when he suffered a slump in form during the middle of his debut season last year.

The Mercedes driver went through a seven-round spell when he finished in the points just once – albeit on the podium. His dip in form coincided with changes to Mercedes’ car which he struggled to get to grips with.

“I had a good start to the season, then I had a difficult period,” said Antonelli in a recent interview. “In the European season I really struggled and in that moment I let the pressure kind of destroy me as well during that period.

“I felt like I was letting down so many people who had believed in me. Of course especially Toto [Wolff, Mercedes team principal], because he was the main one who took the decision [to promote him].

“Obviously I didn’t feel good in that period. I wasn’t doing well. But then I had a big meeting with the team after the European season and it kind of allowed me to reset and just start again.

“Then I slowly found my way back. I had a good second half of the season and that gave me confidence, being able to overcome those difficult moments and gave me the confidence ahead of this year. It also made me learn a lot about myself, not only as a driver, but as a person as well.”

Antonelli said the experience taught him useful lessons about coping with adversity. “Obviously [during] that European season, I think probably most of the things I did, didn’t help me at all,” he said.

“But also I learned about how my body responds to those moments, how my brain responds, what helps me to get back into the right focus, the right mindset, what helps me to stay 100% in terms of energy during the whole weekend. So how to manage myself with events, obviously the driving and everything. So I’ve learned a lot about myself and how as well to respond to difficult moments.”

Mercedes promoted Antonelli directly to their top team, in the seat formerly occupied by Lewis Hamilton, at the age of 18. Antonelli said making his F1 debut with a front-running team left him feeling depleted by the end of the 24-round championship.

“I was so drained at the end of the year,” he said. “Obviously the team did an incredible job in trying to protect me. But the learning curve – I think I’ve learned much more than if I would have done in a smaller team.

“The learning curve was incredible, it was like doing three years at once. It was overwhelming, physically, mentally, because I’ve made so many new experiences as well.

“Also, doing a full F1 season for the first time, you don’t really know where you’re going, what you’re about to face. Obviously the year prior to F1, I’ve been doing race shadowing and everything, but it’s not the same.

“When I was doing shadowing, I was watching, I wasn’t there on track doing the job. So I felt very overwhelmed at the end of the year. And it was good to have a bit of a break to just have a little bit of time to analyse and reflect on the year and understand what were the good things and why and why some things went not in the right way.”

Having become the youngest driver to lead the world championship, Antonelli says he is trying to enjoy the position and the attention which comes with it, particularly in his home country.

“It’s like in any sport at the highest level, there’s always pressure and of course, being Italian, Italy has been missing an Italian driver for quite a long time and obviously also knowing myself because I’m Italian.

“We know how as Italians we can get very excited about things and how expectations can get over the moon. But obviously that comes with a bit of a extra pressure. But I’ve been enjoying, I have been enjoying. I think what I’ve been trying to do as well is to embrace the pressure and trying to actually shine under pressure.”

Sports.title: Norris vs Piastri: 2026 F1 team mates’ head-to-head scores at summer break | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The super-close contest between the McLaren team mates last year would have made for a thrilling world championship fight even if Max Verstappen hadn’t got involved.

Now in their fourth season as team mates, with a completely different type of McLaren to get used to, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have been fairly well-matched on the whole. However in individual races their relative performance has varied, most notably in Hungary last weekend, where Norris was clearly much quicker.

Norris has been on a strong run lately, out-qualifying his team mate for the last five rounds in a row. Though it bears pointing out that Piastri missed first practice at the last round and was badly baulked by Lewis Hamilton when he began his final run.

It took Piastri until the third round of the season merely to start a grand prix, suffering a mortifying pre-race crash at home, then retiring before the start along with Norris in Shanghai. He rebounded magnificently at Suzuka and might have won had it not been for the timing of a Safety Car period.

McLaren have had further technical trouble since then: Norris had back-to-back failures while Piastri’s retirement in Hungary capped a frustrating race where a wayward backmarker had already cost him the lead. Piastri had a rough race in Canada as well, where both McLaren drivers paid the price for a tactical gamble which backfired.

It was therefore fitting that Norris delivered the team’s first win as F1 headed into the summer break. His 36-point lead over Piastri looks like a fair reflection of their relative performances given the various setbacks both drivers have suffered. The world champion holds the upper hand so far but Piastri is keeping him honest as always.

Sports.title: Terence Crawford Exposed Canelo Alvarez’s Carefully Managed Career
Sports.content:
Gennadiy Golovkin spent years pursuing Canelo before finally getting him in the ring at 35. Their first fight ended in a controversial draw, with many observers believing Golovkin deserved the decision.

Canelo’s 2019 move to light heavyweight provided another example. He challenged 36-year-old Sergey Kovalev for the WBO title rather than Artur Beterbiev, who held the WBC and IBF belts after stopping Oleksandr Gvozdyk.

The same criticism followed Canelo at 168. Jaime Munguia, Edgar Berlanga and William Scull received fights while more dangerous younger contenders remained outside his schedule.

That history provides some perspective on Crawford’s accomplishment. Canelo had spent much of his career operating from a position where his team could choose the opponent and timing. Crawford stepped into that environment. He took away the advantages careful matchmaking had helped preserve.

McIntyre had seen through the aura years earlier. Once Crawford finally got the opportunity, Canelo proved to be the fighter BoMac had always believed his pupil could solve.

Sports.title: Abdullah Mason vs William Zepeda Is The Fight TNT Needs
Sports.content:
“Not sure if ‘The Fight’ can generate the same impact that ‘Boxing After Dark’ had during its prime, but this fight would go a very long way to further validating the series. Both winning big on its first two shows, a head-on collision is the natural next course of action,” said Donovan on X.

There are no negotiations for Mason-Zepeda at this stage, but Mason has already made it clear that he likes the matchup. The 22-year-old recently described Zepeda as the type of opponent who can give him a career-defining fight. Zepeda brings relentless pressure and an enormous punch output, presenting Mason with a much tougher physical test than Bell did.

The first two broadcasts introduced Mason and Zepeda separately. Putting them together next would give viewers a reason to follow the series from one card to another rather than treating each event as an unrelated main event.

Boxing After Dark developed its reputation by giving fighters difficult fights and bringing successful performers back against increasingly dangerous opposition. The Fight doesn’t need to duplicate HBO’s old formula, but Mason against Zepeda would be a strong place to start building its own.

Sports.title: Frazer Clarke: Moses Itauma’s Speed Too Much For Hrgovic
Sports.content:
“Just a phenomenon, honestly. So much respect for him. The way he conducts himself, the things he’s doing, really good fighter,” Clarke told Andrew McCart of iFL TV. “A big test, they’re saying, against Hrgovic. I think he beats him well. I really do. The speed’s too much. Speed with the power, the ability, the mindset.”

Hand quickness may be the most interesting part of Clarke’s prediction. Hrgovic has dealt with strong heavyweights, but Itauma presents a different problem because of how quickly he can close distance and deliver his left hand.

Hrgovic cannot afford to spend long periods waiting for Itauma to initiate. If he gives the younger heavyweight room to attack first, he may find himself reacting to punches rather than establishing his own offense.

The Croatian does have something Itauma has yet to prove against this level of opposition: experience in difficult fights. Hrgovic went 12 rounds with Zhilei Zhang and Daniel Dubois before losing to Dubois in 2024.

That makes August 29 considerably different from Itauma’s previous bouts. He has looked destructive against fighters who gave him little resistance, but Hrgovic should force him to show more.

Clarke expects Itauma to pass that test convincingly. If he’s correct, Hrgovic may become the first opponent to demonstrate just how far the young heavyweight has already progressed.

Sports.title: Kell Brook Hints At Chris Eubank Jr. Comeback Fight
Sports.content:
“There’s some massive news about to drop. Yeah, I’m coming back,” Brook said to talkSPORT Boxing. “Back in the professional ring. Boxing Board of Control. Me in there again.”

Brook says the fight is nearly finalized and will happen before the end of 2026. When Eubank’s name was put to him, he initially responded, “Who knows, brother? Who knows?” before conceding, “It could be.” He said an announcement will come soon.

A Brook-Eubank fight would be built heavily around nostalgia. The former champion hasn’t competed since stopping Amir Khan in six rounds in February 2022, another all-British fight that arrived many years after fans originally wanted it.

Brook has also been largely a part-time fighter since challenging Gennadiy Golovkin at middleweight in September 2016. He moved up two divisions after negotiations for Golovkin to fight Eubank fell apart, subsequently suffering a fractured right orbital bone in a fifth-round stoppage loss.

Nine months later, a fractured left orbital bone accompanied his 11th-round knockout loss to Errol Spence Jr. Only five appearances followed over the next five years, including a four-round loss to Terence Crawford in 2020 before his victory over Khan.

That inactivity creates a commercial question. Brook was a major British name during his peak, but a younger generation of fans has seen very little of him as an active fighter.

It will be interesting to see if Turki Alalshikh has any interest in financing Brook-Eubank. Putting money behind Eubank’s fights with Conor Benn made sense because Benn is younger and remains a major attraction in Britain. A 40-year-old coming out of another lengthy retirement presents a different proposition entirely.

Eubank and Brook have flirted with the matchup before, including after Eubank’s 2023 rematch victory over Liam Smith. If this is the “massive fight” being teased, Brook and Eubank will be selling nostalgia for a matchup that would have meant considerably more years ago.

Sports.title: Errol Spence’s Decline Started Years Before Crawford
Sports.content:
“It was quite sad watching Errol Spence in that fight, to be honest with you,” Hearn said to Jai McAllister Boxing. “Having promoted him in his prime in the Kell Brook fight, like how good he was. He was a shell of himself, and I think he has been for years.”

Spence had been putting considerable strain on his body well before his October 2019 car crash. He allowed his weight to climb substantially between fights and acknowledged having to spend portions of training camp taking it back off. After his grueling win over Shawn Porter in September 2019, Spence admitted there was nothing good about gaining more than 25 pounds and then using camp to lose it. The crash came less than two weeks later and kept him out of the ring for more than a year.

Spence returned against Danny Garcia in December 2020 and won comfortably, but the destructive version that finished Brook wasn’t there. Garcia was 32 and already had losses to Porter and Keith Thurman.

The difficulties continued against Yordenis Ugas in 2022. Ugas badly hurt Spence in the sixth round before Spence recovered, took control, and ended the fight in the tenth.

Crawford then produced the most one-sided defeat of Spence’s career in July 2023, dropping him three times before the ninth-round stoppage.

The performance deserves full credit. But it also created the impression that Crawford alone was responsible for making Spence look so ordinary.

Years of difficult weight management, punishing fights, inactivity, and the physical consequences of the car crash had already taken something from Spence before Crawford got him.

Hearn saw Spence near his best against Brook. His belief that Spence had been a shell for years supports what the previous fights were already showing: Crawford didn’t destroy the prime version of Errol Spence.

Sports.title: Car Salesman Hearn Over-Sells Teremoana’s Heavyweight Future
Sports.content:
“I don’t think you guys have seen anything like this before in Australia,” Hearn said. “I think legitimately a chance for you to have a long-reigning heavyweight world champion. Got the size, got the power, got the personality.”

The physical tools are obvious. Teremoana is 11-0 with 11 knockouts, has enormous size and power, and reached the quarterfinals at the 2024 Olympics. What he doesn’t have is a professional win that supports Hearn’s enormous expectations.

Calling DeAndre Savage a “big step up” only inflates Wednesday’s fight. Savage is 35 with a 10-1 record, and Brandon Moore beat him over 10 rounds last year. He’s a reasonable opponent, but beating him tells us little about Teremoana’s ability to compete with the best heavyweights.

Hearn went further, saying he sees “something different” in Teremoana and believes he can bring heavyweight world titles to Australia.

Harrison couldn’t resist.

“You made Teremoana sound like he’s fighting Hercules,” Harrison told Hearn during an exchange in which he joked about the promoter’s ability to sell fighters.

That’s the issue. Teremoana may eventually justify Hearn’s praise, but blasting through lower-level heavyweights doesn’t establish that he’s destined for a long championship reign.

We still need to see him fight beyond the early rounds, deal with a skilled heavyweight who can neutralize his pressure and make adjustments when raw power doesn’t immediately solve the problem.

If Hearn really has Australia’s next elite heavyweight champion, give Teremoana opposition that lets him prove it.

Sports.title: How Wealth and Fame Changed Jack Dempsey
Sports.content:
Everything changed after Dempsey destroyed Jess Willard on July 4, 1919. The heavyweight championship turned Dempsey into one of America’s biggest sports celebrities. His fights generated enormous gates. Movies and endorsements brought him even more money. He also became part of Hollywood’s social world.

The fighter who once struggled financially could now afford mansions and a lifestyle that would have been unimaginable during his early years. Boxing gradually occupied less of his time.

After defeating Georges Carpentier in July 1921, Dempsey went nearly two years without defending his championship. He returned to beat Tommy Gibbons in July 1923 before surviving a wild fight with Luis Ángel Firpo two months later.

Dempsey was only 28 after stopping Firpo, an age when a heavyweight champion might normally be approaching his best years. Instead, he didn’t have another official fight for nearly three years.

During that period, Dempsey’s celebrity continued growing. Hollywood remained part of his life; he participated in exhibitions, and in 1925 he married actress Estelle Taylor. His relationship with longtime manager Jack “Doc” Kearns also ended bitterly.

The contrast with the hungry fighter who had pursued Willard was striking. Dempsey no longer needed to fight regularly to make money or establish his name. Boxing had already given him financial security and national fame.

When Dempsey finally returned to defend against Gene Tunney on September 23, 1926, he was 31 and hadn’t competed in an official bout since Firpo.

Tunney took advantage, outboxing Dempsey over 10 rounds to win a unanimous decision and the heavyweight championship. The inactivity shouldn’t be used to diminish Tunney’s accomplishment. Tunney was an exceptional fighter who defeated Dempsey again in their famous 1927 “Long Count” rematch.

But the larger question remains: what might Dempsey’s career have looked like if wealth and celebrity hadn’t pulled him so far from regular competition? Dempsey became champion at 24. By his late twenties, he had money, mansions, movie work, and access to a world far removed from the one that created the Manassa Mauler.

Success didn’t destroy Jack Dempsey. It gave him the life he had fought to obtain. The price was that boxing no longer demanded everything from him.

Sports.title: Tamm Thibeault Can’t Afford To Wait For Claressa Shields
Sports.content:
She captured the IBF and WBO middleweight titles Saturday night with a 10-round shutout of Desley Robinson, winning 100-90 on all three scorecards. It was her first time going 10 rounds, and she had to deal with a cut caused by an accidental head clash.

Gaining extra ring time would help, but there comes a point where waiting becomes counterproductive. If Thibeault spends another two or three years building her record against lower-tier middleweights, she will be 31 or 32 before getting Shields.

Who is she supposed to fight in that period that prepares her for Claressa?

There isn’t another Shields available at middleweight. Thibeault can collect defenses and complete rounds, but opponents at levels below Shields aren’t going to duplicate her hand speed, reflexes, or ability to make adjustments.

Shields hasn’t exactly been sharpening herself against elite opposition, either. Savannah Marshall in 2022 was the last opponent who presented her with the kind of threat Thibeault potentially brings. Shields has continued collecting titles since then without facing someone capable of seriously testing her.

That doesn’t make Thibeault the favorite. Shields remains the more accomplished professional and has dominated everyone put in front of her.

Thibeault’s best opportunity may come sooner rather than later. She possesses the amateur schooling, size, southpaw stance, and physical strength to make the fight interesting.

Waiting years for preparation that lesser opposition cannot provide may leave Thibeault older without making her any more ready for Shields.

Ghana News.title: Luv FM Kel-Charcoal Debate kicks off with thrilling wins for Wesley Girls and CHRISSEC
Ghana News.content:
The 8th edition of the Luv FM Kel-Charcoal High School Debate has officially commenced, with the first preliminary round held at the Christian Service University in Kumasi on Monday, August 10, 2026.

The opening contest featured Kumasi Wesley Girls’ SHS against Mancell Girls’ SHS, debating the motion: “Ghana Education Service Should Reintroduce Corporal Punishment.”

Kumasi Wesley Girls’ SHS argued in favor of the motion, while Mancell Girls’ SHS opposed it in what turned out to be a closely contested battle of arguments, rebuttals, and counterarguments.

The principal speaker for Kumasi Wesley Girls’ SHS argued that the absence of corporal punishment has contributed to increasing indiscipline in some senior high schools.

She cited instances of student unrest and violence to support the school’s position.

Mancell Girls’ SHS, however, mounted a strong opposition, challenging the arguments presented by their opponents and making a case against the reintroduction of corporal punishment in Ghana’s educational system.

At the end of the contest, Kumasi Wesley Girls’ SHS emerged victorious with 200 points, narrowly defeating Mancell Girls’ SHS, who scored 194 points.

The second contest of the day saw Otumfuo Osei Tutu II College face Christ the King SHS (CHRISSEC) on the motion: “Equality before the Law Is a Mirage in Ghana.”

Otumfuo Osei Tutu II College argued in favor of the motion, while Christ the King SHS opposed it.

The contest produced another engaging display of logical reasoning, confidence and persuasive speaking, with both schools putting forward strong arguments in their bid to progress to the next stage of the competition.

However, Christ the King SHS emerged the clear winners with 214 points, beating Otumfuo Osei Tutu II College, which recorded 173 points.

The result brings the campaign of Otumfuo Osei Tutu II College in this year’s competition to an end, while Christ the King SHS advances to the next phase.

The two contests marked the opening day of the 8th edition of the Luv FM Kel-Charcoal High School Debate, with participating schools expected to continue battling for a place in the subsequent rounds.

The competition continues to provide a platform for students to demonstrate their public

speaking, critical thinking, research and debating skills.

Tomorrow’s contests are also expected to be exciting and fiercely competitive, with Mankranso SHS taking on Ibadur Rahman SHS in the first debate of the day.

The second contest will feature a highly anticipated clash between inaugural champions T.I. Amass and Okomfo Anokye SHS, as the schools battle for a place in the next stage of the competition.

Ghana News.title: No Roof, no future: Ghana’s rent crisis is turning survival into a luxury
Ghana News.content:
Imagine working for an entire month and, before you have even received your salary, knowing that a large part of it already belongs to your landlord.

Imagine spending years in school, earning a qualification, finally securing a job and discovering that independence comes with a price you cannot afford.

Imagine being a parent forced to choose between paying rent, buying food for your children and paying their school expenses.

For many Ghanaians, these are not imaginary situations. They are everyday realities.

The search for accommodation in Ghana has become more than a search for a place to sleep. For an increasing number of people, it is a struggle for dignity, stability and the right to build a normal life.

The question is no longer simply, “Where can I find a room?” It is, “How much of my life must I sacrifice to afford one?”

That is the painful reality of Ghana's housing and rent crisis.

Across the country, particularly in rapidly growing urban and educational communities, the cost of accommodation continues to place enormous pressure on households. As populations increase and people move towards areas where jobs, schools and businesses are concentrated, the demand for housing continues to rise.

But for the ordinary Ghanaian, income has not necessarily risen at the same pace.

The result is a painful imbalance: expensive accommodation on one side and limited incomes on the other.

And somewhere in the middle is the Ghanaian trying desperately to survive.

A young graduate may spend years listening to parents say, “Just finish school and get a job. Things will become better.”

Then graduation comes.

The certificate is framed. The job application is submitted. Eventually, employment arrives.

But instead of the freedom that was imagined, another problem appears.

Rent.

The young worker begins searching for a room and discovers that securing one requires money that could take months or even years to accumulate. If the room is affordable, it may be far from work. If it is close to work, it may be too expensive.

The choice becomes painful: live far away and spend heavily on transportation, or live closer and surrender a significant portion of the salary to rent.

For some young people, this is where the dream of independence begins to collapse.

They return to their parents' homes.

Not because they are lazy.

Not because they do not want to become independent.

But because the mathematics simply does not work.

This is one of the quiet frustrations of being young in Ghana today.

Young people are told to work hard, acquire skills, become independent and build their future. But what happens when the first step toward independence—a decent place to live—is financially out of reach?

The advance-rent burden

Then there is the issue of advance rent.

For many tenants, paying monthly rent is difficult enough. Having to produce a large amount of money upfront makes the situation even more challenging.

A person may have a monthly income but still be unable to secure accommodation because their savings cannot cover the required advance payment.

This creates a cruel situation.

You can have a job and still struggle to find a home.

You can earn a salary and still be unable to move out of your parents' house.

You can work every day and still remain financially trapped.

Some people borrow from relatives. Some take loans. Others spend their entire savings.

By the time they finally get the keys to the room, they may already be carrying a financial burden that follows them for years.

A home is supposed to provide security.

But for many tenants, the journey into a home begins with debt.

Students are not spared

The accommodation crisis is equally painful for students.

For a student who has travelled from another region to attend university, gaining admission should be a moment of celebration. Parents should be thinking about tuition, books and academic needs.

Instead, accommodation can become one of the first and most frightening financial challenges.

Rooms close to campuses can be expensive. Affordable options may be located far away. Some students share rooms with several people simply because that is what their families can afford.

Others spend hours travelling to lectures.

And every day spent travelling is another day in which time, energy and money are lost.

A student who should be preparing for an examination may instead be worrying about where to sleep next semester.

A parent who has struggled to pay school fees may suddenly be confronted with another demand for accommodation.

Education is supposed to create opportunities and break cycles of poverty.

It should not create a new cycle of accommodation insecurity.

When cheaper accommodation comes with another price

But even finding cheaper accommodation does not necessarily mean the problem is solved.

Sometimes the cheaper room comes with poor sanitation, unreliable water, inadequate ventilation, overcrowding, leaking roofs or unsafe surroundings.

For families with children, the consequences can be particularly serious.

Imagine raising children in a room where several people share limited space, where proper ventilation is lacking and where basic sanitation is inadequate.

Imagine a child trying to study in a crowded room because the family cannot afford anything better.

We must ask ourselves: At what point does affordable housing become too expensive if the price is human dignity?

Being poor should not mean being forced to live in unsafe conditions.

Rent is eating more than salaries

The cost of accommodation also affects what happens outside the home.

When people cannot afford to live close to their workplaces, they move farther away.

Then comes transportation.

The worker wakes up before dawn, joins an overcrowded vehicle, spends hours on the road and arrives at work already exhausted.

At the end of the day, the journey begins again.

The money saved on rent may then disappear into transportation costs.

This creates a vicious cycle.

Cheap accommodation can mean expensive transportation.

Expensive accommodation can mean financial hardship.

And somewhere between the two, the ordinary worker is struggling to breathe.

The cost is not only financial.

It is emotional.

It is the stress of constantly calculating whether the salary will last.

It is the fear of receiving a notice that the rent is due.

It is the embarrassment of repeatedly asking family members for help.

It is the frustration of working hard and still feeling as though one is standing in the same place.

It is the exhaustion of spending hours commuting because home is too expensive and work is too far away.

These are the hidden costs of Ghana's housing crisis.

The family is also paying the price

Housing insecurity does not affect individuals alone.

It affects families.

A young couple may postpone marriage because they cannot afford accommodation.

Parents may delay having another child because they are struggling to provide adequate space for the children they already have.

Families may remain in overcrowded houses because moving into a better apartment would consume too much of their income.

Some young adults remain dependent on their parents well into adulthood because the cost of independent living is simply too high.

The housing crisis is therefore influencing personal decisions that should ideally be based on choice rather than financial desperation.

And this should concern us as a nation.

What kind of development are we building?

Ghana often speaks about development in terms of roads, buildings, economic growth, investment and urban expansion.

But development must ultimately be about people.

What does economic growth mean to the worker who cannot afford rent?

What does urban development mean to the family living in an overcrowded room?

What does employment mean to the graduate whose entire income disappears into accommodation and transportation?

What does progress mean to the student who cannot find a safe place to live?

These questions deserve honest answers.

A country cannot call itself successful simply because it is building more houses.

The important question is: Who can afford to live in them?

If the average worker cannot afford the homes being constructed, then the country is building houses without solving the housing problem.

Government cannot look away

Government has a major responsibility in addressing this crisis.

Affordable housing must become a long-term national priority rather than a political slogan that appears during election campaigns and disappears afterwards.

Ghana needs stronger partnerships between the public and private sectors to increase the supply of genuinely affordable homes.

Housing finance must become more accessible.

Land administration must improve.

Urban planning must be strengthened.

Local authorities must ensure that expanding communities have adequate roads, drainage, water, sanitation, electricity, schools and healthcare facilities.

And tenancy laws must be properly enforced.

Tenants also need greater awareness of their rights and responsibilities.

Landlords have legitimate costs and responsibilities, and not every landlord is responsible for the housing crisis. But where exploitative practices occur, tenants must have effective avenues for protection and redress.

The solution must be balanced, practical and long-term.

A house is not just a building

Perhaps the biggest mistake we make when discussing housing is treating it as merely a construction issue.

A house is where a child does homework.

It is where a mother prepares food after a long day at work.

It is where a father rests after spending hours earning a living.

It is where students prepare for examinations.

It is where couples build families.

It is where people recover from the pressures of the outside world.

A home provides psychological and emotional security.

When that security becomes uncertain, the effects can reach every aspect of life.

That is why the rent crisis should not be treated as a private inconvenience.

It is a national development issue.

The market woman deserves a safe home.

The teacher deserves a decent home.

The nurse deserves a decent home.

The driver deserves a decent home.

The farmer deserves a decent home.

The graduate deserves a decent home.

The student deserves a safe place to study and sleep.

The ordinary Ghanaian deserves more than simply surviving from one rent deadline to another.

Ghana must act before the crisis becomes normal

The greatest danger is that we may become accustomed to the crisis.

We may begin to believe that expensive rent is simply part of life.

We may accept overcrowding as normal.

We may accept young adults remaining permanently dependent on their parents.

We may accept workers spending hours commuting every day.

We may accept families sacrificing food and education to pay rent.

We may accept the idea that owning or even comfortably renting a home is only for the wealthy.

We must not.

A decent home should not be a privilege reserved for people with high incomes or powerful connections.

Housing is fundamental to human dignity.

If Ghana wants productive workers, we need stable homes.

If Ghana wants successful students, we need safe accommodation.

If Ghana wants strong families, we need affordable housing.

If Ghana wants young people to build their future here, we must make it possible for them to actually live here with dignity.

The housing crisis is therefore not simply about landlords and tenants.

It is about the kind of country we want to become.

Do we want a country where people work simply to pay rent?

Do we want a country where young people postpone their dreams because they cannot afford a room?

Do we want a country where families remain trapped in overcrowded homes because decent accommodation is beyond their reach?

Or do we want a Ghana where working hard provides a genuine path to stability?

The answer should be obvious.

No roof, no stability. No stability, no meaningful progress.

Ghana cannot continue to demand productivity from people whose basic living conditions remain insecure.

We must build more affordable homes, strengthen the rental system, enforce existing protections and plan our cities around the people who actually live and work in them.

Because at the heart of this crisis is a simple truth:

The Ghanaian is not asking for a mansion. They are asking for somewhere safe to call home.

And in a country blessed with human resources, land and enormous potential, that should never be too much to ask.

Ghana News.title: Domestic violence in Ghana: The crisis behind close doors
Ghana News.content:
Home is supposed to be the place where fear ends.

It is where a person should be able to close the door behind them, breathe freely and know that they are safe. It is where children should learn what love looks like, where couples should find companionship, and where families should find comfort after the pressures of the outside world.

But for too many people in Ghana, closing the door does not bring safety.

It brings fear.

Behind the walls of ordinary homes, some people are living with threats, insults, intimidation, beatings, sexual abuse, financial control and psychological torment. Some wake up every morning wondering what will trigger the next outburst. Others have become so accustomed to abuse that they have stopped recognising their own suffering as something that deserves attention.

From the outside, everything may look normal.

A family may attend church together.

They may appear together at social gatherings.

They may post smiling photographs online.

Neighbours may describe them as a “good family.”

Yet behind the door, someone may be crying.

This is the uncomfortable reality of domestic violence in Ghana.

It is a crisis that does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it hides behind makeup, long sleeves, excuses, silence and carefully constructed smiles.

And because much of it happens away from public view, society can underestimate its scale and seriousness.

Domestic violence must therefore be understood as more than physical assault.

It can take the form of emotional and psychological abuse, sexual violence, economic abuse, threats, intimidation, stalking, humiliation, isolation, controlling behaviour and destruction of property.

A person does not have to walk into a hospital with a broken bone before society takes their suffering seriously.

A woman who is constantly told that she is useless is being harmed.

A man whose movements, friendships and finances are controlled through threats is being harmed.

A child who watches one parent violently abuse another is being harmed.

An elderly relative who is threatened, neglected or financially exploited within a household is being harmed.

The wounds may not always be visible, but the damage is real.

The first challenge Ghana must confront is the culture of silence surrounding domestic violence.

For generations, many families have been taught to protect the reputation of the household at almost any cost.

When a woman reports that her husband is abusing her, relatives may tell her to be patient.

When a husband reports abuse, he may be laughed at.

When a young person complains about violence at home, they may be told not to expose family matters.

When neighbours hear repeated arguments, they may decide that it is not their business.

When religious leaders become involved, the emphasis may sometimes be placed so heavily on preserving the relationship that the safety of the victim becomes secondary.

This must change.

There is nothing honourable about protecting the reputation of a family while a member of that family is being destroyed.

There is no peace in a home where one person is afraid of another.

And there is no strength in a family that survives by forcing its most vulnerable member to suffer in silence.

The phrase “it is a family matter” must no longer be used as an excuse to look away.

Domestic violence becomes a national issue the moment it threatens the safety, health and dignity of citizens.

It becomes a national issue when children are traumatised.

It becomes a national issue when victims require medical care.

It becomes a national issue when workers lose productivity because of physical and psychological injuries.

It becomes a national issue when families are destroyed.

And it becomes an even greater national tragedy when violence ends in death.

The country cannot wait for the worst possible outcome before taking the problem seriously.

Another reason victims remain trapped is economic dependence.

For a person who has no stable income, leaving an abusive home can appear almost impossible.

A mother may know that her partner is dangerous, but she may also know that she cannot immediately afford rent.

She may wonder where her children will sleep.

She may worry about school fees.

She may fear losing access to food, healthcare and other basic necessities.

A victim may therefore remain in a dangerous relationship not because they approve of the abuse, but because they are calculating the consequences of leaving.

This is why economic empowerment must be part of the domestic violence conversation.

Skills training, employment opportunities, access to financial services, safe accommodation and social support can give victims options.

A person should never have to choose between physical safety and economic survival.

But financial dependence is not the only chain.

Fear is another.

Some victims have been threatened with death.

Some are told that their children will be taken away.

Some are threatened with public shame.

Some are warned that their families will be attacked.

Others have been abused for so long that their confidence has been systematically destroyed.

An abuser may repeatedly tell a victim that nobody else will love them.

They may say that the victim is worthless.

They may convince the victim that the abuse is their fault.

Over time, the victim may begin to believe it.

This is why psychological abuse deserves the same seriousness as physical violence.

A wound on the body may heal.

The belief that you are worthless can remain for years.

Children also carry a heavy burden in homes where violence occurs.

A child does not need to be directly beaten to become a victim of domestic violence.

Hearing threats, witnessing assaults and living in an atmosphere of fear can profoundly affect a child's emotional and psychological development.

A child who should be thinking about school may instead be listening for the sound of an angry parent approaching.

A child who should be sleeping peacefully may be wondering whether another argument will begin during the night.

Some children become withdrawn.

Some become aggressive.

Some struggle academically.

Some develop anxiety.

Others may grow up believing that violence is simply part of family life.

This is where the crisis becomes generational.

Children learn what relationships look like by observing adults.

If violence is repeatedly presented as normal, some may eventually reproduce the same behaviour in their own relationships.

The cycle continues.

That is why breaking domestic violence is not only about protecting today's victims.

It is about protecting tomorrow's generation.

Ghana must also be careful not to reduce the conversation to women alone.

Women and girls face significant risks of domestic and gender-based violence, and their protection must remain a priority. However, men can also experience abuse, and male victims often face a different kind of silence.

A man who reports that his partner is physically or emotionally abusing him may be mocked.

He may be told to defend himself.

He may be accused of being weak.

He may fear that nobody will believe him.

This culture of ridicule can prevent male victims from seeking help.

The message must be clear: violence is wrong regardless of who commits it and regardless of who suffers it.

Protecting victims should never become a gender competition.

The goal is safety, justice and prevention.

There is also a group that is frequently forgotten in conversations about domestic violence: older people.

Elderly parents and relatives can experience neglect, intimidation, physical abuse and financial exploitation from people within their own households.

Some are too dependent on their caregivers to report what is happening.

Some fear being abandoned.

Others remain silent because they do not want to see their own children punished.

Their vulnerability makes their protection particularly important.

A society that values family must also protect those who become dependent on family members in old age.

The legal framework is another important part of the conversation.

Ghana has the Domestic Violence Act, 2007 (Act 732), which provides a legal framework for addressing domestic violence.

But laws are meaningful only when victims can actually access protection and justice.

A victim should not have to navigate a confusing system alone.

Police officers, healthcare workers, social workers, lawyers and other professionals involved in domestic violence cases need appropriate training and resources.

Reporting mechanisms must be accessible.

Victims must be treated with dignity.

Cases must be handled seriously.

And where protection orders or other legal remedies are available, they must be meaningful in practice.

The fear that “nothing will happen” can be enough to prevent a victim from reporting abuse.

That fear must be defeated by a justice system that people can trust.

However, the responsibility does not end with the police or courts.

Healthcare facilities are often among the first places where victims appear.

A person may arrive with injuries without openly saying what happened.

Healthcare workers must therefore be equipped to recognise possible signs of abuse and respond sensitively.

Social workers and support organisations also need adequate resources to help survivors rebuild their lives.

It is not enough to help someone leave an abusive environment.

We must ask what happens afterwards.

Where will the survivor live?

How will they earn an income?

How will they care for their children?

How will they recover psychologically?

How will they rebuild their confidence?

Leaving may be the beginning of the journey, not the end.

Religious and traditional leaders also have enormous influence.

Many Ghanaians turn to churches, mosques, traditional authorities and family elders during moments of crisis.

This influence can be used positively.

Leaders can educate their communities about healthy relationships, challenge harmful beliefs and encourage victims to seek appropriate help.

But one message must be made clear: reconciliation should never come before safety.

Telling an abused person to return to the same environment without addressing the danger is not necessarily reconciliation.

Sometimes the most responsible intervention is to create distance, protect the victim and ensure that professional assistance is available.

Marriage preservation must never become more important than human life.

The media, too, must do more.

Domestic violence stories often attract public attention when they involve severe injuries or death. But reporting should not begin only when tragedy occurs.

Journalists should examine patterns.

What happened before the violence escalated?

Did the victim seek help?

Were there previous complaints?

Did relatives know?

Were warning signs ignored?

Were there institutional failures?

What could have prevented the situation from becoming fatal?

These are the questions that can turn reporting into public service.

The media must also avoid victim-blaming.

Instead of asking, “Why did she stay?”, society should ask why the perpetrator believed violence was acceptable.

Instead of asking why a victim did not report earlier, we should ask whether the environment made reporting safe and accessible.

Instead of turning survivors into objects of pity, we should give them dignity.

Social media has created another dimension to the problem.

Online platforms can help expose abuse and give victims a voice, but they can also encourage public shaming, misinformation and the circulation of sensitive images.

A serious domestic violence case should not become entertainment for social media users.

Behind every viral video may be a traumatised human being.

Ghanaians must learn to respond with compassion rather than curiosity.

Prevention must also begin before relationships become violent.

Schools can play an important role by teaching children about respect, boundaries, emotional intelligence and healthy relationships.

Young people need to understand that jealousy is not love.

Possessiveness is not love.

Control is not love.

Threats are not love.

And violence is certainly not love.

Boys should be taught that masculinity does not require domination.

Girls should be taught that they do not owe anyone their silence.

Young people of all genders should learn that disagreement can exist without abuse.

Families must also create environments where children feel safe enough to speak when something is wrong.

The fight against domestic violence must become preventive rather than reactive.

We cannot continue waiting until someone is seriously injured before we become concerned.

We cannot wait until a child is traumatised before we ask questions.

We cannot wait until another life is lost before the nation expresses outrage.

Every violent incident that is ignored sends a message.

Every victim who is dismissed sends a message.

Every perpetrator who escapes accountability sends a message.

And that message can encourage the next act of violence.

Domestic violence also has economic consequences that deserve greater attention.

When victims are injured, they may be unable to work.

When children are traumatised, their education can suffer.

When families break down, financial pressures increase.

Healthcare costs rise.

Legal processes consume resources.

Productivity is lost.

The consequences therefore extend far beyond the walls of the home.

Domestic violence weakens families, communities and, ultimately, national development.

A country cannot build a productive population while allowing large numbers of people to live in environments of fear and abuse.

The fight against domestic violence therefore belongs in Ghana's national development conversation.

It belongs in discussions about healthcare.

It belongs in education.

It belongs in economic empowerment.

It belongs in justice.

It belongs in social protection.

It belongs in community development.

And it belongs in the national conversation about human rights and dignity.

Ghana needs a coordinated response.

Government agencies must work together.

Law enforcement must be strengthened.

Support services must be accessible.

Shelters and safe spaces must be adequately supported.

Public education must move beyond occasional campaigns.

Schools must teach healthy relationships.

Employers should understand how domestic violence can affect workers.

Communities must stop protecting perpetrators through silence.

Families must learn to support victims rather than shame them.

Religious and traditional leaders must prioritise safety.

And citizens must learn that noticing abuse and doing nothing is not neutrality.

At the same time, prevention must include rehabilitation and behaviour-change programmes for perpetrators where appropriate.

Punishment is necessary where the law requires it, but Ghana must also confront the beliefs and behaviours that produce violence.

If a person leaves one abusive relationship and repeats the same behaviour with another partner, society has not solved the underlying problem.

We need accountability, but we also need prevention.

Ultimately, the question Ghana must answer is simple:

What kind of society do we want to become?

A society where families protect their image while victims suffer?

A society where children grow up believing violence is normal?

A society where victims are blamed for the actions of their abusers?

Or a society where safety, dignity and respect are considered non-negotiable?

The answer should not be difficult.

Home must be safe.

Marriage must be safe.

Childhood must be safe.

Old age must be safe.

Relationships must be built on respect rather than fear.

We must stop calling control love.

We must stop calling violence discipline.

We must stop calling silence peace.

And we must stop treating domestic violence as a private matter that outsiders should never discuss.

Because the truth is that there is nothing private about a national crisis that destroys lives, traumatises children, weakens families and places pressure on the country's health, justice and social systems.

Behind every statistic is a person.

Behind every police report is a story.

Behind every injury is pain.

Behind every silent victim is a voice that may be waiting for someone to say, “You do not deserve this.”

Ghana cannot afford to wait for another tragedy before acting.

We must make it easier for victims to speak, safer for them to leave, harder for perpetrators to escape accountability and less acceptable for communities to look away.

The battle against domestic violence will not be won by government alone.

It will be won when parents teach their children respect, when communities refuse to protect abusers, when institutions respond with seriousness, when the media reports responsibly, when victims are supported rather than blamed, and when every Ghanaian understands that violence has no place in a healthy home.

A home should be the first place where a child learns love.

It should be the first place where an adult experiences security.

It should be the place where people can remove their fears, not where new fears are created.

Home should not be where violence begins.

Home should be where safety begins.

And until every Ghanaian can say that with confidence, the work of confronting domestic violence is far from over.

Ghana News.title: AKSA Energy case: Ghana has evidence to trigger own accountability process – Osae-Kwapong
Ghana News.content:
Democracy and Development Fellow at the Centre for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana), John Osae-Kwapong, says Ghanaian law enforcement agencies already possess information that could form the basis for domestic investigations into the AKSA Energy-related bribery allegations.

His comments follow disclosures that Ghanaian institutions, including the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) and the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), collaborated with US authorities in investigations that contributed to the conviction of an individual over a bribery scheme linked to a power plant deal involving Ghana.

According to Mr Osae-Kwapong, the collaboration demonstrates that Ghanaian law enforcement agencies have the capacity to investigate complex corruption cases and gather evidence capable of supporting criminal accountability.

“For me, it says to me that these are agencies capable of conducting investigations and coming up with evidence needed to support holding persons accountable for allegedly having committed certain crimes,” he said.

He, however, believes the collaboration with US authorities raises a further question about what Ghanaian institutions intend to do with the information they have gathered.

Mr Osae-Kwapong said the disclosures by the OSP suggest that Ghana may already have preliminary information that could be used to initiate its own accountability processes.

“If you look at the OSP statement, then it also says to me that these critical institutions are in possession of at least some information that can be the basis of triggering our own accountability processes within, you know, in Ghana,” he explained.

He argued that Ghana should not simply rely on the outcome of the US proceedings but should use the information obtained through the collaboration to examine whether any Ghanaian individuals or institutions may have been involved in wrongdoing.

“At least that's my take on it, that if EOCO and other agencies, they help in terms of collaborating with the U.S. in pursuing this case against the said gentleman who has been convicted in the U.S., then it tells me that we do have some preliminary information that we can use as the first step towards also triggering our own accountability processes in Ghana,” he said.

It follows the US conviction of former Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) Managing Director, Asante Kwaku Berko, in the high-profile international bribery case.

The OSP said on Monday, August 10, that it assisted the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) with investigative and evidentiary material through Ghana’s established mutual legal assistance framework.

According to the anti-corruption agency, the support provided by Ghana was specifically recognised by the United States Department of Justice (DoJ) as having played a significant role in the prosecution.

Ghana News.title: TUSAAG backs GAUA strike over unresolved pay disparities
Ghana News.content:
The Technical Universities Senior Administrators Association of Ghana (TUSAAG) has declared its support for the ongoing strike action by the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA), saying the two groups face similar concerns over pay disparities and conditions of service.

In a statement dated August 9, TUSAAG said it “associates itself fully” with the industrial action and considers GAUA’s demands inseparable from its own concerns.

The two associations jointly submitted a conditions of service proposal for negotiation, but according to TUSAAG, the proposal was rejected on grounds of transitional limitations on the part of the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission.

An interim allowance was subsequently negotiated in place of the conditions of service agreement.

TUSAAG said it and GAUA have since observed what it described as concerning pay disparities arising from the negotiations.

“The unequal treatment and unresolved grievances that GAUA is contesting mirror the very concerns TUSAAG has raised through the same negotiations, and we recognize in GAUA's decision to strike a struggle that is, in every practical sense, our own,” the statement said.

The association said strike action was not taken lightly, arguing that it follows persistent concerns, stalled negotiations and the inability to safeguard members’ interests through dialogue alone.

“Having sat at the same negotiating table and faced the same pay disparities, TUSAAG fully appreciates why GAUA has been left with no option but to withdraw its services,” it said.

TUSAAG has consequently pledged to stand with GAUA, its leadership and members throughout the industrial action.

It also said it regards GAUA’s demands as inseparable from its own and will not distance itself from the dispute.

The association is calling on the relevant authorities and stakeholders to engage GAUA “in good faith, with urgency and sincerity” to resolve the pay disparities and other issues at the centre of the dispute.

TUSAAG further said it would continue monitoring developments and remain ready to provide additional support towards what it described as a just resolution.

The association also commended GAUA’s leadership for its resolve in defending the interests of its members and urged stakeholders in the tertiary education sector to support a swift and equitable resolution.

Ghana News.title: BoG and SEC roll out Ashanti NaVALI initiative to drive responsible virtual asset adoption
Ghana News.content:
The Ashanti Regional phase of the National Virtual Asset Literacy Initiative (NaVALI) has been launched to protect financial stability in Ghana’s fast-growing digital finance sector.

The initiative follows the enactment of the Virtual Asset Service Providers Act 2025 (Act 1154) and is aimed at ensuring that innovation in virtual assets progresses responsibly, with a strong emphasis on consumer protection and market integrity.

The NaVALI is a collaborative initiative led by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) in partnership with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), academia and key industry stakeholders.

It is anchored on two key objectives: strengthening institutional capacity in virtual assets and enabling technologies such as blockchain to ensure effective regulation and supervision, and driving nationwide awareness of the risks and implications of virtual assets to prevent uninformed and risky adoption as the sector evolves.

The launch, held at University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development (USTED) under the theme: “Understand before you undertake,” was attended by regulators, market players, consumer advocates, and members of the media.

On the sidelines of the event, the Head of the Fintech and Innovation Department at the Bank of Ghana (BoG), Elhanan Owureku Asare, said regulators are establishing the necessary structures, systems, and processes to ensure the timely and orderly operationalisation of the new Act.

He explained that NaVALI is designed to place education and awareness at the centre of the country’s digital finance regulatory framework.

The goal, he noted, is to equip consumers, industry players, and public institutions with the knowledge needed to make informed decisions and avoid risky or uninformed participation in the virtual asset space.

Owureku Asare stressed that a well-informed ecosystem is critical to safeguarding consumer protection, market integrity, and financial stability.

“Effective regulation and enforcement cannot be achieved by regulators alone without a clear understanding of how virtual assets work and the risks they carry,” he said.

He added that the initiative reflected a proactive and collaborative approach to ensuring that innovation in virtual assets progressed responsibly in the country.

"NaVALI is a collaborative initiative being implemented by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to intensify awareness around crypto and digital asset operations. Given that this is the new financial system in the modern world, we cannot do away with it. This strategic plan is therefore necessary to prevent operators from taking advantage of and defrauding Ghanaians," Owureku Asare stated.

Investing in Crypto

The Deputy Director-General for Finance at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Mensah Thompson, cautioned Ghanaians interested in crypto and digital financial asset operations to be vigilant when investing.

According to him, investors must verify the legitimacy of service providers before committing any funds.

“Individuals interested in investing in crypto or digital assets must be vigilant. You must ensure that any Virtual Asset Service Provider you deal with is licensed by the appropriate regulatory authorities,” he said.

He noted that licensing is key to protecting consumers from fraud and ensuring market integrity in the growing digital asset space.

“We don’t want a situation where unlicensed operators take advantage of Ghanaians. That is why it is important for the public to check and confirm that any platform they use has approval from the Bank of Ghana or the SEC,” he added.

Mr. Thompson stressed that regulation and public education must go hand in hand to build a safe and well-informed digital finance ecosystem.

He also stressed that the Virtual Asset Service Providers Act represents a defining milestone that will reshape the country’s financial ecosystem, spanning banking, capital markets, and emerging digital finance activities.

He said the legislation signalled a fundamental shift in how financial services would be delivered and regulated, with virtual assets and blockchain technology increasingly influencing traditional systems.

Mr. Thompson expressed the commitment of the SEC to forge close collaboration with the BoG to support industry players and market operators as they adjusted to the new regulatory landscape.

He said that the launch of the National Virtual Asset Literacy Initiative was critical to carrying the public along in this transition, stressing that education was indispensable to responsible innovation.

“This initiative marks a significant step in our national journey to deepen understanding of virtual assets and their role within the broader financial system,” he said.

Prospects for financial inclusion

The Deputy Director-General explained that while virtual assets and new financial rails offered strong prospects for financial inclusion, efficiency and economic growth, they also carried risks to investor protection, market integrity and financial stability.

For that reason, he said a comprehensive and well-coordinated national approach was required to balance innovation with effective safeguards.

Prof. Joseph Antwi Baafi, Lead Knowledge Partner for NaVALI and Head of the Department of Economics at USTED, said the awareness drive will be decentralized to ensure that Ghanaians across the country are reached, regardless of location.

"We will be carrying out this exercise in our various schools, marketplaces, churches, and other gathering places,” he said. “The idea is to take the conversation directly to the people, because digital finance is no longer limited to offices and banks,” he noted.

Prof. Antwi Baafi added that “we cannot ignore digital assets. They are part of the new financial world. Our job is to make sure Ghanaians are not left behind, and that they are protected as they engage”.

He also urged citizens to actively participate in the awareness programs, stressing that knowledge is the first line of defense against fraud.

“This, I believe, will help them to understand digital money, virtual assets, the opportunities available, the risks involved, and the safety practices they need to adopt,” he explained.

He said NaVALI’s role is to bridge that knowledge gap so people can make informed decisions and participate safely in the evolving financial system.

Prof. Baafi, who co-authored the National Virtual Assets Education Manual, said the manual will be used as the primary resource for trainers and facilitators during the outreach.

Dean of the School of Graduate Studies at USTEC, Prof. Humphrey Danso, added that the National Virtual Assets Education Manual, introduced under NaVALI, would serve as a structured tool for public education, policy engagement, and stakeholder dialogue.

He cautioned against the damage caused by fraudulent investment schemes, adding that education, not fear, remains the best defense.

“Many of us still recall the damage done by fraudulent investment schemes that impacted thousands of Ghanaian households. Today's fraudster does not necessarily knock on your front door. They enter your mobile phone, appear on your social media timeline, create convincing websites, and impersonate respected institutions. They lure you with promises of huge returns, exploit trust, manipulate fear, and prey on your hope,” he observed.

"The greatest weapon against such deception is not fear. It is education," he concluded

Ghana News.title: Corporate Ghana, international community present relief donations to government following June 29 disaster
Ghana News.content:
Corporate organisations and institutions have donated cash, food, medical supplies and other essential items to support victims of the June 29, 2026 flood disaster.

The donations were presented to the Office of the President as part of ongoing efforts to provide relief to communities affected by the torrential rains and flooding, particularly in Accra.

Senior government officials, including Deputy Chief of Staff (Administration), Nana Oye Bampoe Addo; Legal Advisor to the President, Marietta Brew; and Presidential Adviser and Special Aide, Joyce Bawa Mogtari, received the donations on behalf of the government.

Two organisations also presented cash contributions towards the relief effort.

SoftCare FM Manufacturing Company Limited donated GH¢200,000, while the Ghana Institute of Surveyors contributed GH¢50,000.

Among the largest donations was a package from the Ghana Association of Chinese Societies and Companies, which provided a wide range of food, medical and household supplies.

The donation included 1,112 bags of rice, 4,000 bags of sachet water, 500 cartons of sunflower oil, 490 cartons of Frytol oil, 490 cartons of canned mackerel, 646 cartons of gari and 501 cartons of spaghetti.

The association also donated 295 cartons of sardines, 235 cartons of biscuits, 208 cartons of tomato paste, 50 cartons of shito and other provisions.

Its medical and sanitation supplies included 2,000 malaria rapid test kits, 800 HPV test kits, anti-malaria medication, hand sanitiser and disinfectant.

The relief package further included 3,000 sleeping mats, 400 school bags, 3,200 T-shirts, 3,100 plastic buckets, 3,000 plastic basins and five 2,000-litre stainless steel water tanks.

The association also supplied chest freezers, electric cookers, electric fans, shovels, mosquito coils and temporary shelter and bedding materials.

Other major donations

Scancom Plc (MTN Ghana), supported by the Multimedia Group's flood relief campaign, donated 1,400 student mattresses, 1,192 blankets and 998 relief boxes containing food items, blankets, mosquito repellents, mosquito nets and detergents.

Sentuo Group Limited contributed 4,000 bags of 25kg rice, 600 bags of 50kg sugar and 387 boxes of granular maize.

Ecobank Ghana donated medicines and other medical supplies, alongside 1,000 bags of sachet water, 195 mattresses, 250 blankets and bales of used clothing for men, women and children.

Softcare FM Manufacturing Company Limited also donated 100 bags of washing powder, 100 boxes of soap, 100 boxes of sanitary pads and 50 boxes of baby diapers.

B5 Plus Limited contributed 70 bags of 50kg rice, 100 bags of 50kg maize, 50 cartons of Cerelac, 75 jerrycans of cooking oil, sardines, bottled water and other relief items.

Its donation also included 200 blankets, 200 two-litre jerrycans, 150 mosquito nets, 100 pairs of Wellington boots and 100 raincoats.

Eezzy Group donated rice, spaghetti, canned beef, sardines, tomato paste, cooking oil, seasoning powders and baking supplies.

Tobinco Group provided 100 boxes of Omal antiseptic, 5,000 gallons of Omal liquid soap and 400 gallons of Omazone bleach.

Kam Trading & Farms Limited also contributed 445 bags of 25kg rice.

The donations form part of a wider response to the devastating flooding of June 29, which left several communities in Accra and other parts of the country severely affected.

The government has since been coordinating relief and recovery efforts, while corporate organisations, civil society groups and other institutions have mobilised resources to support affected households.

The latest contributions are expected to help provide immediate necessities, including food, clean water, medicines, bedding, sanitation products and other household items, as affected communities work towards recovery.

Ghana News.title: AKSA Energy deal: Ghana must conduct own investigations despite US conviction – Osae-Kwapong
Ghana News.content:
Democracy and Development Fellow at the Ghana Centre for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana), John Osae-Kwapong, says Ghana must conduct its own investigations into the circumstances surrounding the AKSA Energy deal despite action already taken by authorities in the United States.

According to him, the developments surrounding the case raise serious concerns about the integrity of public office and Ghana’s public procurement processes.

Speaking on Joy FM's Top Story, Mr Osae-Kwapong acknowledged that authorities in the United States have taken action against the individual at the centre of the case, but argued that this should not end Ghana’s responsibility to examine what happened on its side of the transaction.

“Of course we would have to get to, I know on the U.S. side they have dealt with the issue and the individual involved. But I believe that it is also incumbent upon us, as part of our fight against corruption and to ensure integrity in government, that it is incumbent upon us to also further look into this matter," he said on Monday, August 10.

He noted that Ghana has, over the years, committed to strengthening integrity in public office and intensifying the fight against corruption.

“So when you read stories like this that allege that the integrity of public office or the integrity of the public procurement process was somehow compromised, then it becomes very worrying,” he explained.

Mr Osae-Kwapong said the allegations bring renewed attention to the need for stronger measures to prevent corruption within government and ensure that public procurement processes are conducted transparently.

His comments come amid growing calls from civil society organisations and anti-corruption campaigners for Ghanaian authorities to investigate possible local involvement in the alleged bribery scheme.

The renewed scrutiny follows the conviction of a former Tema Oil Refinery Managing Director in the United States over bribery-related offences connected to a power plant deal involving Ghana.

The development has also raised questions about the circumstances surrounding the renewal of the AKSA Energy agreement with the Ghanaian government in October 2022.

Mr Osae-Kwapong stressed that a domestic investigation would be important in establishing whether Ghanaian public officials or institutions breached procurement rules or compromised the integrity of the transaction.

He said such an investigation would also demonstrate Ghana’s commitment to accountability and the fight against corruption in public office.
