After the service, the Catholicos addressed those gathered outside the cathedral. He said the authorities were taking steps to undermine the Church’s authority, restrict its autonomy and bring it under their control.

“The authorities are persecuting the Church and the clergy. They have arrested and restricted the freedom of a number of clergymen, benefactors and other patriotic individuals through unlawful and fabricated criminal cases,” he said.

The Catholicos dismissed the charges against himself and the six clergymen as groundless.

“We remain steadfast in our faith and determination to defend our rights, which are guaranteed both by our country’s Constitution and by the fundamental principles of international law.”

Opposition declares a “day of shame”

Marianna Gakhramanyan, an MP from the opposition I Have Honour Alliance, said:

“Today is a day of shame. The Catholicos of All Armenians, our spiritual father and the head of our Church, is standing trial in Etchmiadzin. It is shameful and unprecedented. This is an attack not only on the independence of the Armenian Apostolic Church but also on Armenia’s Constitution, which clearly states that the political authorities have no right to interfere in the affairs of the Church and that the Church is separate from the state.”

“Who is defending the Church – us or you?” asks ruling party MP

Commenting on opposition lawmakers who came to support the Catholicos, Civil Contract MP Artur Hovhannisyan said:

“The Church has begun interfering in Armenia’s domestic and foreign policy.”

He also referred to the allegations that the Catholicos had violated his vow of celibacy:

“We are the ones standing with the Church. We are the ones defending the Church. You are defending clergymen who broke their vow of celibacy, who engage in politics and use religion and the Church to protect themselves from the consequences of breaking that vow and taking part in politics. Anyone who has broken the vow of celibacy should leave the Church.”

The ruling Civil Contract party’s election manifesto also outlines plans to reform the Church. Under the proposal, the “de facto head of the Church”, as Pashinyan’s team refers to the Catholicos, should leave office. The plan calls for the election of a locum tenens, the adoption of a new Church charter containing “mechanisms to preserve centuries-old traditions”, and, ultimately, the election of a new Catholicos.

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan told Reuters:

“Pashinyan has come to see the Church as a political threat and as an institution capable of supporting the opposition and various political parties in their efforts to gain power.

“The case against the clergy fits into a broader pattern of selective justice pursued by Pashinyan’s government, under which leading opposition figures have been arrested and some of their property has been confiscated by the state.”

Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

World.title: Azerbaijan FM in Kyiv: gas for Ukraine, visit to Irpin, Ukrainian drones
World.content:
Azerbaijani FM visits Ukraine

Azerbaijan‘s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov paid an official visit to Ukraine on 6 August.

It was the first visit by an Azerbaijani foreign minister to Kyiv since the start of Russia‘s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Bayramov began his visit with a trip to Irpin, where he viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones and laid a wreath at a memorial to fallen defenders at Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry.

He also held meetings with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, President Volodymyr Zelensky, Head of the Presidential Office Andriy Yermak, Defence Intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov and National Security and Defence Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

One of the most notable announcements was Azerbaijan’s stated willingness to supply Ukraine with natural gas if needed.

The two sides also discussed the possible use of Ukraine’s underground gas storage facilities to strengthen regional energy security.

These developments are significant both regionally and internationally, particularly in the context of Azerbaijan’s relations with Russia.

In mid-July, Bayramov met Sergei Lavrov in Moscow and said the “difficult period” in bilateral relations was over and that ties had been fully normalised. A few weeks later, in Kyiv, he reaffirmed Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, while also signalling Baku’s interest in expanding energy cooperation.

The visit illustrates Baku’s multi-vector foreign policy. While maintaining dialogue with Russia, Azerbaijan has continued to provide humanitarian assistance to Ukraine and has expressed its readiness to support the country in the energy sector if required.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

Symbolic and practical significance of the Irpin visit

Irpin was one of the towns where the Russian advance on Kyiv was halted in 2022. Hundreds of civilians were killed during the fighting, and more than 70% of the town’s housing stock was destroyed.

Azerbaijan has contributed to Irpin’s reconstruction.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

The minister laid flowers at the bust of academician Zarifa Aliyeva in the park named after her, and visited the Zarifa Aliyeva Linguistic Lyceum and Irpin Central City Polyclinic, both rebuilt with Azerbaijan’s support. He was also briefed on future reconstruction projects, including plans to restore the town’s House of Culture.

In his statement, Zelensky said Bayramov had visited a school, a hospital and a rehabilitation centre supported by Azerbaijan. The visit to Irpin was seen as a demonstration of humanitarian solidarity with Ukraine, as well as Azerbaijan’s willingness to share its experience in rebuilding territories recovered from occupation.

I received Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, @Bayramov_Jeyhun. This is the Minister’s first visit to Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. He began his visit in Irpin, where he visited a school, a hospital, and a rehabilitation center supported by… pic.twitter.com/7HTLIaz3EF — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) August 6, 2026

The visit to a town devastated by Russian forces, together with Bayramov’s review of reconstruction efforts and Azerbaijan’s continued support, was seen as underscoring Baku’s intention to reaffirm its longstanding position despite the “normalisation” of relations with Moscow, particularly its commitment to the principle of territorial integrity.

Following the official welcoming ceremony at the Foreign Ministry, Bayramov and Sybiha viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones. They then laid a wreath at the Memorial to the Fallen Defenders of Ukraine and observed a moment of silence in their honour.

Meetings and gas supply pledge

During expanded talks with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, the two sides discussed their strategic partnership, trade, energy, transport, humanitarian cooperation and regional security. Bayramov reiterated the need for an early end to the fighting and a diplomatic settlement based on international law, while reaffirming Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

He said Azerbaijan’s total humanitarian assistance to Ukraine had exceeded 50 million US dollars. Bayramov also highlighted reconstruction projects in Irpin and rehabilitation programmes for children.

During his meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the discussions focused on Russian attacks, the situation in the Black Sea, the disruption of grain export routes, defence cooperation, and cooperation in the energy, oil and gas, and agricultural sectors.

Zelensky thanked Azerbaijan for its energy and humanitarian assistance, as well as for maintaining constructive dialogue. Bayramov, in turn, spoke about the post-conflict situation in the South Caucasus and reconstruction efforts in the territories regained by Azerbaijan.

As part of his official visit to Ukraine 🇺🇦, FM of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 @Bayramov_Jeyhun visited the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Kyiv.



The Minister met with the Embassy staff and received a comprehensive briefing on the Mission’s activities. pic.twitter.com/UPqN5Hn9rx — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

At a joint press conference, particular attention was drawn to Bayramov’s remarks on possible gas supplies: “If the need arises, we will be ready to supply gas to our friendly Ukraine.”

He highlighted SOCAR’s long-standing presence on the Ukrainian market, as well as the importance of Ukraine’s underground gas storage system – the largest in Europe – for regional energy security.

The statement can be seen as signalling Azerbaijan’s willingness to contribute to the diversification of Ukraine’s energy supplies, while also supporting alternative routes for Caspian gas exports to Europe. Against the backdrop of Russia’s strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Ukraine, Baku’s offer also underscores the importance of competition and diversification in the energy sector.

During meetings with Kyrylo Budanov and Ihor Klymenko, the sides also discussed regional and international security, as well as prospects for energy cooperation. They reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of state sovereignty, territorial integrity and the inviolability of internationally recognised borders.

Expert: “Azerbaijan will continue to provide Ukraine with political, economic and humanitarian support”

lkhan Shahinoglu, head of the Atlas Research Centre and a political commentator considered close to the Azerbaijani authorities, wrote that the visit is being closely watched by Russia:

The Kremlin will closely monitor Jeyhun Bayramov’s meetings in Kyiv. Azerbaijan’s partnership with any country is an exclusive sovereign right, and no other state has the right to interfere in that process.

At the same time, Russia, which is waging a war of conquest against Ukraine, closely watches those who cooperate with Kyiv. President Ilham Aliyev‘s response to the same question from Ukrainian journalist Gordon, asked at the Shusha Global Media Forum two years in a row – that ‘Ukraine should not reconcile itself to occupation’ – angered chauvinistic circles in Russia. They believe Azerbaijan should accept the annexation of Crimea and the occupation of Ukrainian territories.

Just as Jeyhun Bayramov visited Moscow some time ago, he has now travelled to Kyiv. Ukraine is Azerbaijan’s partner, and Baku will continue to provide it with political, economic and humanitarian support.”

World.title: Giga Avaliani case: Two more arrested 10 months after Georgian teacher’s murder
World.content:
Two more arrested in Giga Avaliani murder case

Two more suspects have been identified in the high-profile murder case of a 28-year-old teacher in Georgia. On 5 August 2026, two teenage girls – Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili – were arrested.

Giga Avaliani, a mathematics teacher, was killed in October 2025. Five people have already been convicted over his murder, while the trial of a sixth defendant is still under way. With the arrest of the two girls, the total number of suspects in the case has risen to eight – all of them minors.

The arrests of Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili, after several convictions had already been secured, mark an unexpected and significant development in the Giga Avaliani case.

Nia Imnadze was one of Giga Avaliani’s former students and the girlfriend of the principal defendant, Aleksandre Gabashvili. Prosecutors accuse her of incitement to commit the crime.

According to local media, Anastasia Beruashvili is a friend of both Nia Imnadze and another convicted defendant, Giorgi Rikadze. She has been charged with failing to report the crime.

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics tutor, was returning home late on 1 October 2025 when he was attacked outside his apartment building. He fell into a coma following the assault and died on 24 October without regaining consciousness. Investigators say the attack was motivated by jealousy and what they describe as “unwanted communication with a girl”. The defendants have given a similar account. According to their version of events, Avaliani sent sexually explicit messages to his student Nia Imnadze, who told her boyfriend, prompting him to confront the teacher. Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, rejects that account. She says Nia had been skipping lessons and that Avaliani informed the girl’s mother, angering the student. According to Kupatadze, the attack was planned afterwards.

The Giga Avaliani case has become one of Georgia’s most high-profile criminal cases in recent years. Much of the public attention surrounding it has been driven by Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, who campaigned for what she said should be a thorough and impartial investigation. Her efforts also helped generate significant public pressure over the handling of the case.

From the outset, Kupatadze maintained that Nia Imnadze bore primary responsibility for what had happened and repeatedly called for her arrest. The recent detention of the two girls has therefore raised new questions.

But the key question remains: if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, why were the two girls not arrested earlier? Was their detention the result of new evidence, or did it come only after sustained public pressure and Eka Kupatadze’s campaign?

Detention of two girls

Both girls were arrested late on the night of 5 August, in what appeared to be coordinated operations. News of the arrests first emerged through a video of Nia Imnadze’s detention, which was released by her lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili.

The footage is deeply distressing. It shows a large number of police officers arriving at Nia’s home. Her mother, visibly distressed, pounds on the front door, shouting: “Come in, all of you!”, “Maniacs!”, “Murderers!”, “Do you know that Niako is innocent?!”

The girl’s father, meanwhile, tells the police: “You are going to make me do something the whole of Georgia will be talking about. If you treat my child so unjustly, I will do it.”

Police officers try to calm the distraught parents.

“Why are you taking my child? On what grounds? What does the court order say?!” the mother asks.

“The lawyer has reviewed the court order,” one of the officers replies.

“Giorgi, on what grounds are they arresting her?” the mother asks the lawyer.

“On the basis of a court order containing only formal wording, nothing specific,” the lawyer replies.

Nia sits in the hallway on a sofa, curled up with her face buried in her hands. The video is being filmed by her lawyer, who occasionally strokes her hair.

Shortly after the video was released, reports began circulating on social media that the second girl, Anastasia Beruashvili, had also been detained. No footage of her arrest was made public, but the Ministry of Internal Affairs later confirmed that she had been taken into custody.

During her arrest, Nia Imnadze became unwell and was taken to hospital, where she spent the night. On 6 August, she was transferred to a pre-trial detention centre. Anastasia Beruashvili was also taken there.

Minors charged in Giga Avaliani's murder case in Georgia – read more Five people have already been convicted in connection with Giga Avaliani’s murder: Aleksandre Gabashvili – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. He was the principal defendant in the case and was found guilty of organising a group assault and intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm as part of a group, resulting in the victim’s death. Giorgi Rikadze – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. A friend of Aleksandre Gabashvili, he was convicted on the same charges. Demetere Chikovani – sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was convicted of attempted intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm in the Avaliani case, as well as organising group violence in connection with the case and four other incidents. Ani Naskidashvili – sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. She was found guilty of failing to report a particularly serious crime. Another minor – sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He was convicted of giving false testimony. The nature of the false statements has not been disclosed. His case was heard behind closed doors, lawyers involved in the proceedings are bound by a non-disclosure order, and the teenager’s parents have declined to speak to the media. According to TV Pirveli, the boy is named Luka Klatkin. Giorgi Malania – arrested in July 2026 and charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. Malania is the son of a former senior Interior Ministry official, who served as deputy interior minister between 2016 and 2019. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered.

Eka Kupatadze’s reaction

“Georgia has won another battle against the killers of a healthy, innocent and talented young man – Giga Avaliani!” Eka Kupatadze said in response to the girls’ arrests.

Giga Avaliani’s family has always maintained that those who carried out the attack were not the only people involved. They have consistently called on investigators to identify and prosecute all those who may have played a role in the crime.

The family has paid particular attention to the alleged role of the two girls. Eka Kupatadze has repeatedly said that they knew the attack was being planned.

Until recently, however, prosecutors had taken no apparent action against additional suspects, prompting repeated criticism of the investigation from Avaliani’s family.

Kupatadze even appealed for help to Ekaterine Khvedelidze, the wife of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling party and widely regarded as Georgia’s “informal ruler”. Khvedelidze replied to her letter, expressing sympathy and support for the mother who had lost her son.

“As far as I am aware, the investigation has not yet been completed. I am confident that the relevant state authorities will see it through to the end and that all the circumstances will be thoroughly examined, so that no question surrounding the terrible tragedy that has befallen you remains unanswered,” Ekaterine Khvedelidze wrote in her reply.

Formal charges

On the evening of 6 August, both girls were formally charged.

Nia Imnadze at the time of her arrest

Nia Imnadze has been charged with incitement to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm committed by a group. The offence carries a maximum sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment.

Anastasia Beruashvili has been charged with failing to report a particularly serious crime, an offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

Under Georgian law, sentences imposed on minors are reduced by one quarter.

“The investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs under the supervision of the Prosecutor’s Office established that, in September 2025, Nia Imnadze began taking mathematics lessons with Giga Avaliani. The accused, Nia Imnadze, told her friends Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Malania that her teacher, Giga Avaliani, had allegedly shown her excessive attention. By doing so, the accused incited Aleksandre Gabashvili to attack Giga Avaliani together with his accomplices,” the Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

According to the statement, Aleksandre Gabashvili, together with Giorgi Rikadze, Giorgi Malania and Demetere Chikovani, “decided to act on that incitement.”

What defence says

The defence has denied all the charges.

According to Nia Imnadze’s lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili, there is no evidence in the case to support the allegation that she incited the attack.

The lawyer also rejected reports that prosecutors had obtained data and messages from Meta, and that the arrests followed an examination of those materials.

“Criminal proceedings cannot be based on suspicion. They must be based on lawfully obtained evidence, and no other standard can override that principle,” Lekishvili told reporters.

Ketevan Vardanashvili, the lawyer representing Anastasia Beruashvili, made similar arguments. She said Anastasia had not witnessed any crime and that she and Nia Imnadze had seen each other only once, for a few minutes.

“They had no friendship and no contact,” the lawyer said.

As for Anastasia’s relationship with the convicted defendant Giorgi Rikadze, Vardanashvili said that “even if she was his girlfriend, that does not mean she had any knowledge of the crime.”

Complaint or incitement?

The arrests of the two girls have sparked intense debate on social media. Many commentators agree that everyone responsible for Giga Avaliani’s death should be held accountable and that justice should be served. Many have also expressed sympathy for Eka Kupatadze.

At the same time, some have questioned the actions of the law enforcement authorities. They have asked whether prosecutors have sufficiently strong evidence against the two girls, particularly Nia Imnadze, who faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.

The Prosecutor’s Office statement says only that Nia Imnadze told her friends that Giga Avaliani had allegedly shown her excessive attention. It does not explain whether she knew an attack was being planned or whether she urged her boyfriend to take any specific action.

“Does complaining to friends amount to incitement?” some social media users have asked.

Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: What causes those electric-blue flashes at the local boat ramp?
World.content:
Don't panic if you see an electric-blue flash next time you're dipping your toes at the local swimming spot, it's just bioluminescence.

Videos showing the phenomenon, which appears as a blue glow in the water when it's disturbed, were posted over the weekend, taken at boat ramps around Brisbane.

Queensland doesn't see bioluminescence as much as New South Wales, or Tasmania in recent years, but when conditions are right it can be spectacular.

Loading...

Bioluminescence refers to a glow released by chemical reactions taking place within a tiny marine species of dinoflagellates, Noctiluca scintillans.

These minute unicellular creatures — also known as sea sparkles — feed on diatoms, algae even more microscopic than they are, and use photosynthesis.

'A little bit unusual'

Griffith University Australian Rivers Institute Professor Michele Burford said while bioluminescence is a trait of many marine species, the blooms seen in Brisbane were caused by species of dinoflagellates.

"They produce this bioluminescence in response to some sort of threat or movement of water that causes them to do this chemical stimulation of a light pulse," she said.

"They're tiny little things, but because they can gather together in blooms or form concentrations near the water's edge, that's when you see that luminescence, which looks like one thing but is actually a whole lot of tiny little organisms all lighting up at the same time."

The unicellular Noctiluca scintillans — also known as sea sparkles — are responsible for creating blooms of bioluminescence. (Wikimedia Commons: Nadine Neaud-Masson)

The dinoflagellates, like most plants, absorb nutrients from their environment and photosynthesise energy from sunlight, but Professor Burford said it was slightly more complicated.

"The thing about dinoflagellates, they're a little bit unusual. They're kind of halfway between an animal and a plant in the way that they work in the natural environment," she said.

Glow-in-the-dark wombats Australian scientists are surprised to learn that many animals glow under UV light, though more research is required to discover why.

Bioluminescence is not uncommon in the natural world, according to marine ecology expert and senior lecturer at Griffith University, Vincent Raoult.

"They go from really small organisms like the phytoplankton to slightly larger ones like little marine zooplankton, like copepods which are a tiny crustacean, all the way up to very large organisms such as squid, and even some shark species bioluminesce."

Dr Raoult said it wasn't clear yet why the organisms flash their lights, and there were a lot of potential explanations.

"One of them is communication, and that can be communication with other organisms … in the form of a warning, or it can be in the form of telling other organisms to be aware that they're there," he said.

Bioluminescence has been increasing in Tasmania, which experts say could be due to climate change. (Supplied: Robbie Moles)

He said it was also common as an attractant among animals living in the dark depths.

"In really deep sea environments … it's in fact one of the only sources of light, and as a result it's used both as a warning cue and also as an attractant to lure food."

Glow hunters

For those on the hunt for bioluminescence, there are some steps you can take to maximise your chances.

While it's present in the daytime as well, it's much more obvious at night.

South-east Queensland gets its share of bioluminescence, such as in waters off Queens Beach in Moreton Bay, near Brisbane. (Supplied: Hayley Cox)

Try to pick a particularly dark night, as a bright moon can really take the edge off that neon-blue glow, and get to the location a couple of hours after sunset.

"In Brisbane at least, we tend to see it in the winter months," Professor Burford said.

There are some known hotspots in south-east Queensland with potential for the phenomenon.

Professor Burford said the lower Brisbane River especially can have blooms in the winter months, "so it isn't a bad place to go on a calm winter's night".

"But to a degree, there's an element of luck. Sometimes you get lucky and sometimes you don't," she said.

Bioluminescence is generally not an indicator of an unhealthy waterway, Professor Burford said, and Dr Raoult agreed.

"In general, it's perfectly safe. I would just be wary of warnings that might have been put out by councils and so on for water quality more generally," Dr Raoult said.

"But I would certainly not link a nice bioluminescing ocean with an unhealthy habitat that might be dangerous."

Professor Burford said citizen science was a "great vehicle" for learning more about bioluminescence.

"Certainly people posting where they're seeing it and when is a valuable resource because you can't be out monitoring everything all the time and typically people don't monitor at night when they're looking at water quality.

"So, it's good to have that information from the public."

World.title: Prisoners break down barriers by teaching each other to read
World.content:
John* worked in construction for decades, but there was something stopping him from moving up in his career — reading and writing.

"Most people I started out with are supervisors or project managers, and I've never been able to do that," he said.

John is among a group of prisoners learning to read through a peer-led model at Loddon Prison in central Victoria.

His teachers are fellow prisoners, and there is no classroom or timetable.

"It's quite an embarrassing thing to realise you can't read and write," John said.

"If it wasn't for H and Simon* doing the one-on-one, I probably wouldn't go to education.

"It doesn't suit me in a classroom where everyone's at a different stage. It's just uncomfortable."

Prisoners John and H* with a rigging licence workbook. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Confidence boost

Loddon Prison is believed to be the first in Australia to introduce a phonics-based program from the United Kingdom called Turning Pages.

The program, developed by charity Shannon Trust, is being delivered in the vast majority of prisons across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

John started out with the Turning Pages books, but now he and his mentors are tackling the coursework for a rigging certificate.

"We're working on stuff that's actually going to change my future when I get released," he said.

"Hopefully ... get off the tools and be able to read the computer instead of just asking someone else to read it."

Another learner, Dane*, said his confidence had grown through the program.

"I can actually write my own letters and cards now. It's amazing," he said.

"I'm also doing my forklift ticket as well. It'd be great. Once I get released, I can maybe go out and get a job in a store."

Literacy struggles are common among the prison population.

A third of people entering prison have only completed schooling to year 9 or below, according to a 2023 report by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

More than half never completed formal education beyond school.

Peter Foti and Gavin Blair have seen the success of the program inside Loddon Prison. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

For Simon*, one of the mentors, he realised how much people could take reading for granted, even in prison.

"It's debilitating for them. Filling in a canteen slip or just reading an officer's name tag," he said.

"There are a lot more prisoners than we thought who do not know how to read. There's so many who fall through the cracks."

Before the program, Simon said he would not have known where to start in teaching someone to read.

"When I get out, my daughter's going to be six years old. I'm going to teach her how to read," he said.

The prisoners who volunteer their time can attain a unit of competency called mentoring in the workplace.

They run an open weekly session and then identify those who need one-on-one support.

The individual sessions are informal, taking place anywhere from someone's cell to the yard if there is some time to spare.

Generational change

Peter Foti is the vocational services manager at Loddon Prison and said the program helped those with low literacy levels take a step towards formal education, resulting in generational change.

He said it was one of the "most rewarding" things he had been involved with.

"The beauty of this program is it's the men helping each other and lifting each other up, and then they're feeling confident enough to engage in formal education," he said.

"Someone who may be the first person in their family for many, many years to complete formal education ... their children will have a different idea of what education can bring to their lives."

Vlad* is a mentor and said it also gave a sense of purpose to those serving longer sentences.

"I've been here for seven years, and I've done countless parole letters for guys," he said.

"The gratitude they have, it's almost a little bit overwhelming sometimes. I just find it really rewarding."

*Names have been changed to protect prisoners' privacy.

World.title: 'Ah, sorry guys': Pilot's reaction after Antarctic mishap damages plane
World.content:
An accident that damaged an Australian-contracted aircraft in Antarctica has triggered new safety protocols on the icy continent, internal government documents show.

The incident, which occurred on January 3 this year, involved an airborne BK-117 helicopter and a stationary Twin Otter ski plane.

The chopper, operated by Helicopter Resources, was conducting "sling load operations" at a site known as Nunatak 1.5, about 318 kilometres north-east of the Australian-run Davis Station.

Images from the report into an incident in Antarctica, in which a helicopter lifting fuel barrels struck a plane's wing. (Supplied)

At the time of the incident, the chopper was carrying four old fuel drums attached to a hook at the end of a 100-foot cable.

The plan was to offload the fuel drums near the side of the Twin Otter, which would then transport the drums to a landing site near Davis Station known as Whoop Whoop.

But an investigation report by the Australian Antarctic Division (AAD) says the cable's hook made "inadvertent contact" with a key section of the Twin Otter's wing.

"The remote hook, attached to a sling load of four fuel drums, struck the trailing edge [of the] Twin Otter's wing, causing damage to the aileron trim tab and associated actuator mechanism," the report stated.

The incident occured at a site known as Nunatak 1.5, about 318 kilometres north-east of the Australian-run Davis Station. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

The pilot and the ground crew were not injured.

"However, the accident rendered the Twin Otter unserviceable, and all personnel in the field were returned to Davis Station via helicopter as a priority," the report stated.

As a result, the Twin Otter, operated by Canada's Kenn Borek Air (KBA), was out of action for more than two weeks during the height of summer operations.

'Sorry guys': Radio transcript reveals moment of impact

Details of the incident were revealed in documents released to the ABC following a Freedom of Information request.

The documents include an incident report that categorised the accident as having a "moderate" actual severity and a "major" potential severity.

They also include a transcript of radio communications between the helicopter's pilot-in-command and a member of the ground crew.

The AAD investigation found the chopper's cable hook made "inadvertent contact" with a key section of the Twin Otter's wing. (Supplied)

"How close do you reckon you can get?" the ground crew member asks the pilot as the chopper approaches. "I'll see what it's like once I get my head out the door here, but maybe like 4 or 5 metres," the pilot responds.

The ground crew member then calls out the height of the fuel drums as they slowly descend towards the ground.

"Righto, 50 metres there," they tell the pilot. "Twenty-five … 10 … yeah that's down," they say over the next 43 seconds.

Two seconds later, the pilot responds: "Ah, sorry guys".

Helicopter pilot's view during fuel barrel lift operation in Antarctica. (Supplied)

Plane spare parts flown to Antarctica

The investigation report said the pilot had intended to hover with the fuel drums a metre above the ground at a location 10 metres away from the Twin Otter's wing, before slowly moving the load to within 4–5 metres of the plane.

"The pilot stated they misjudged the height of the load off the ground and was higher than intended as the load approached the ground," the report stated.

"This resulted in the load overshooting [its] intended target point and coming to rest under the wing of the Twin Otter with the remote hook contacting the trailing edge of the wing."

The incident was reported to Davis Station within minutes.

A BK117 helicopter was conducting "sling load operations" when its cable hook made contact with the plane's wing. (Australian Antarctic Program: Pete Harmsen)

Helicopter Resources also submitted notification of the event to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau as an "immediately reportable matter".

The documents show those involved returned negative results to drug and alcohol tests.

The Twin Otter was initially secured in place at Nunatak 1.5 before it was given a special flight permit by Canadian and Australian authorities to be flown to Whoop Whoop four days later.

Parts to repair the wing were then flown to Antarctica with the assistance of the US Antarctic Program, before the Twin Otter was given the all-clear to return to service on January 19.

Protocols introduced to reduce risk

The AAD's investigation report identified several key issues relating to the incident, including:

No specific procedure or risk assessment was in place for the type of external load operations that were taking place;

A pre-task briefing between the pilot and ground crew did not include discussion about approach and departure paths or site-specific hazards;

The pilot misjudged the height of the sling load, resulting in an overshoot;

The pilot's decision to place the fuel drums close to the Twin Otter "did not display a risk management mindset appropriate to the Antarctic context";

There were no height call-outs from the ground crew below 10 metres, which "may have affected the pilot's situational awareness".

Helicopter Resources has subsequently put in place a number of corrective actions.

These include an amendment to the company's operating manual, which mandates a minimum 10-metre separation for sling loads near aircraft, unless approved otherwise.

The aviation company will also implement enhanced pilot and ground-crew training relating to risk awareness and communication protocols.

In a statement, the AAD said it operates a number of aviation assets with experienced contractors in Antarctica.

It reiterated the incident had resulted in no injuries to personnel and only minor damage to the plane.

"A thorough incident investigation identified improvement opportunities that have been debriefed, shared and implemented to avoid any similar incidents in the future," it said.

World.title: Greyhound badly injured in race supporting Tasmanian industry
World.content:
On a Sunday night in the regional New South Wales town of Temora, tragedy struck on the greyhound track.

It was race two, August 9, a 330-metre dash to the finish for seven greyhounds.

The race was named "We Stand With Tasmania Pathways".

WARNING: This story contains images that may cause distress for some readers.

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby bolts from the box and collides with another dog at the first turn.

She's flung into the side metal barrier and struggled to get back up.

A stewards' report from the night said it was likely she broke her shoulder blade and injured her "tricep".

The greyhound has been stood down from racing for 60 days and the race replay video has been deleted from the state's racing website.

On a prominent betting site, the race replay has also been edited to exclude the fall.

It is one of several races called "We Stand With Tasmania" that have resulted in falls and injuries.

Loading...

On December 22, 2025, during race three at Maitland in NSW, Hey Pat fell and sustained a serious foreleg fracture.

The greyhound is now listed as deceased.

Two greyhounds fell on October 20 last year during race one in Nowra, NSW.

And during race five in Warragul, Victoria, on October 23, Collinda Blinder falls and tumbles after the first turn.

Printed caps in support of Tasmania's greyhound industry have been spotted track-side. (Supplied)

The race where Manila Shelby was injured has been uploaded to Greyhound Racing South Australia's website.

In Tasmania, when a dog is injured on the track, a video of the race is never uploaded.

The Tasmanian industry's peak body Tasracing said this decision is made out of respect to the industry, as well as the greyhound trainer and animal involved.

Tasmanian Greens animal rights spokesperson Cassy O'Connor said the race was "horrible viewing" and "characteristic of the dangerous conditions greyhounds are forced to race in".

"This is happening in our name as Tasmanians," Ms O'Connor said.

"Manila Shelby isn't the first greyhound to be injured in mainland races under the 'Stand With Tasmania' banner, and sadly, she won't be the last.

"But we have the power to stop greyhounds being put in harm's way in this state."

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby sustained injuries during a race in Temora, New South Wales, on August 9, 2026. (Supplied: Greyhound Racing NSW)

The greyhound races authorities don't want you to see If you watched greyhound race videos on Tasracing's website, you would likely never know that dozens of dogs were injured or killed during events last year.

The state government has committed to cutting funding to the industry from 2029, which coincides with the end of the current funding deal for the code.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said in August last year "it was time to make a call on the future of the sport", and he "continues to be concerned about animal welfare".

"It's time to draw a line in the sand and ensure an orderly exit from greyhound racing in Tasmania," Mr Rockliff said at the time.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with a greyhound (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

Legislation to phase out the industry passed Tasmanian parliament's lower house in December 2025, but was pulled from the upper house after the state government feared it didn't have the numbers to pass.

"Greyhound racing is out of step with community expectations. It does not prioritise animal welfare," Tasmanian Liberal MP Marcus Vermey said.

Tasmanian Labor continues to support the industry.

Greyhound Racing NSW has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Quitting dream job over climate fears a 'no-brainer' for former pilot
World.content:
Snow-capped mountains, striking thunderstorms, fairy floss clouds and vivid sunsets stretching as far as the eye can see.

These magical views were a common occurrence during Geoff Collis's 40 year career in the aviation industry.

Mr Collis first became enamoured with planes at the young age of 10.

"I started making model aeroplane kits and getting into the history of aviation and just everything to do with planes," he said.

" Instead of rock and roll band posters on my walls when I was a teenager, I had pictures of planes. "

Views like this were common during Geoff Collis's flying career. (Supplied: Geoff Collis)

A logical progression from there, he said, was to train to become a pilot.

He began that process towards the end of high school and spent the next four decades soaring high into the sky.

"Even to this day, after like 42 years and 25,000 hours in the logbook, there's still an incomparable buzz from taking off," he said.

Despite this passion, Mr Collis started to struggle with his role amidst a warming climate.

"I was just looking at the amount of fuel I was ordering for each flight … and I thought, 'How can I justify continuing in this sort of role?'

" It was a 2.4 million litres a year jet fuel habit. "

Mr Collis would often see snow-capped mountains on route to Queenstown, New Zealand. (Supplied: Geoff Collis)

From pilot to baker

A surprising reprieve came in the midst of worldwide lockdowns.

At the age of 55, he was partially stood down during the COVID-19 pandemic, like many aviation workers.

In an attempt to find a fulfilling pastime, he enquired about apprenticeships at his local bakery in Melbourne's north-east.

Geoff Collis now spends his days baking pastries. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

He began upskilling in the craft of baking breads and patisseries within a matter of months.

The Eltham bakery became his second home during the pandemic years, but he was expected to return to work full-time once the aviation industry returned to pre-COVID levels.

Mr Collis always had a passion for baking, which helped pave the way for a new career. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

In 2023, he paused his baking apprenticeship and took to the skies once more. But before long, he decided it was time to permanently leave his life as a pilot behind.

He returned to baking this time a year ago, all for the sake of the planet.

"I started to realise that most of what [the industry] appeared to be doing [for climate change] was really just tokenism, spin and greenwashing," the former Jetstar pilot said.

"I got to the point where I just thought … I don't think I can, in clear conscience amidst the climate situation we're facing, be part of the industry anymore.

" Eventually, it was a no-brainer. I had really no option but to to to walk away from it. "

After four decades in the aviation industry, Mr Collis decided to become a baker. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

Aviation emissions taking off

While aviation is responsible for a relatively small percentage of greenhouse gas emissions globally — between two and three per cent annually, on average — many people acknowledge it is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonise.

The federal government said aviation emissions were continuing to grow, bucking the trend as "total emissions have started to decline across the economy".

Its 2023 Aviation Green Paper stated that emissions were "likely to continue to grow as other sectors continue to decarbonise with mature technologies".

According to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) 2025 environmental report, global aviation emissions were "expected to increase through 2070 by two to five times 2018 levels".

Geoff Collis often flew in and out of Melbourne, enjoying the cityscape from above. (Supplied: Geoff Collis)

Mr Collis' former employer, the Qantas Group, also acknowledged it was operating on a growth model.

In a statement, it said: "We know that Australians love air travel and we expect to keep growing to meet that demand, but we are also focused on reducing the impact of our operations where we can."

"We’re doing that by investing in new aircraft, improving flight planning and procedures and increasing our procurement of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

"We're also working with government and industry to help build a SAF industry here in Australia, which will be critical to our long-term decarbonisation goals and has the potential to create thousands of jobs in regional Australia."

The number of flights taking off in Australia has surpassed pre-pandemic levels. (ABC News)

Dr Ya-Yen Sun from the University of Queensland's business school said the sector's forecast growth would likely undermine much of the work being done to decarbonise, which included introducing more energy efficient planes and sustainable aviation fuels.

"The energy efficiency has improved, but the demand outweighs the energy improvement," the associate professor says.

"So as a result, I think it's quite challenging to reduce flying emissions."

Despite these challenges, Qantas remained committed to reducing net emissions by 25 per cent by 2025, and achieving net zero by 2050.

The one per cent

Those working in the sustainable tourism sector argue that reducing the overall number of planes in the air would help reduce emissions, but it is a complex picture for countries as large as Australia.

Roughly one per cent of the world's population accounted for more than half of the total emissions from passenger air travel.

The top one per cent of the world's population are responsible for the majority of air travel emissions. (Reuters)

"Personally, I think travel is a privilege, but it's also something that we need to provide to people," Dr Sun said.

"And if we say no, you cannot fly anymore just due to the environmental concern, I think it's too harsh on people. So for Australia, I think probably we need to put more pressures on the airlines."

Dr Sun said a carbon tax or emissions trading scheme could be possible solutions in Australia.

"Essentially, if you emit more emissions, you need to pay more financial cost. If you reduce your emissions, you will be awarded financially," Dr Sun said.

Geoff Collis was working as a Jetstar pilot when he decided to leave the industry. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Connecting with other pilots

While coming to terms with his decision to quit flying, Mr Collis came across a group of former and current aviation workers in the UK who established an organisation called Safe Landing to help pilots struggling with climate concerns.

"Knowing there are other people out there who came to the same conclusion as myself was reassuring and reaffirming," he said.

" There was a huge sense of like, 'Wow I'm not the only oddball who's feeling this way.' "

He said before meeting this group, the usual response from people he spoke to was, "What difference is one person not [flying] going to make?"

"But I think it's about leading by example … or showing people alternatives to the automatic response to air travel," he said.

"If air travel was priced properly to reflect its impact on the planet, then we might find that people actually start questioning their need for travel."

Geoff Collis is enjoying life at his Eltham bakery, in Melbourne's north-east. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

Although the former pilot is no longer spending his days high in the sky, he admits that he'll always have a soft spot for the metal flying machines.

"If a plane goes overhead, you can't help it, it's just almost like an automatic response [to look up].

" But I don't really miss it for a moment, I don't miss it for a day. "

World.title: Debut memoir reveals what it's really like to be a woman in her 30s today
World.content:
Sheree Joseph always assumed the first book she wrote would be fiction.

"We all have this idea of writing the Great Australian Novel," she says, laughing.

First books, she'd always figured, were supposed to be ambitious and invented.

Memoir was what came decades later, once you'd lived enough life to justify looking back.

Joseph worked towards fulfilling her literary ambitions throughout her 20s, joining Western Sydney's Sweatshop Literacy Movement, workshopping a novel manuscript with Wild author Cheryl Strayed in 2017 and publishing semi-autobiographical short stories.

But life had other plans.

Her father died. A six-year relationship ended. The pandemic left her isolated in Sydney. An unsuccessful fertility journey offered "no reprieve from any of the pain", she says bluntly.

By 33, Joseph was standing in the ruins of a life that was supposed to look a certain way by now. She had no partner, no kids and had achieved none of the milestones we often measure ourselves against, subconsciously or otherwise.

While she drew on these life-altering moments in her writing, she hid behind fictionalised versions of the truth.

But after a trip to Europe with friends turned into an exhilarating three-month extended stay, when she returned to Sydney and sat down to write again, Joseph found there was only one story left.

"There was actually no other story but this one to write," she tells ABC Arts.

That story is Juicy: How to Live a Life in the Wreckage of Expectations, a funny yet devastating memoir that, gratifyingly, isn't just a document of falling apart.

"I had never read or heard about anyone experiencing my story the way I was living it," Joseph writes. (Supplied: Hardie Grant Publishing)

It chronicles a woman rebuilding herself in real time. Friendship, kinship, sex, grief and joy collide somewhere between the locales of Sydney and the sun-bleached Mediterranean, or, as she affectionately calls it, "Tomato Europe".

To give shape to her story, Joseph looked to an unlikely guide: Inanna, an ancient Sumerian goddess who descends to the underworld, relinquishing a piece of royal apparel at each of its seven gates before she can be reborn.

Funnily enough, Joseph had always compared her recent string of adversities to being in hell, like Dante's Inferno.

"The death and rebirth cycle really stuck with me as not only a way to structure the memoir but also to see more of the meaning behind the suffering," she says.

A new type of memoir

Joseph found few examples in Australian publishing of the type of memoir she wanted to write.

The stories she came across were "usually by someone with a big following, a celebrity, or their stories were very much a tragedy, but an obvious tragedy".

Instead, she looked overseas, where she encountered a different style of life writing that resonated more closely with her own experience.

Writers such as Dolly Alderton, author of Everything I Know About Love, and Elizabeth Gilbert, of Eat Pray Love fame, had built memoirs from moments of uncertainty, writing about adulthood in their 20s and 30s while still living through it.

Joseph recently re-read Gilbert's bestselling 2006 memoir. "It was, for its generation, [a story showing that if] something is wrong, we need to do something about it. And then we go on a journey," she says.

"Someone always has to be the first to go to the really difficult places and read the room where the culture is shifting."

Loading Instagram content

Joseph's fresh take on the genre follows in Gilbert's footsteps.

It's not easy, though, notes Joseph. "I can see why people don't do it — it's vulnerable and hard, especially when you're present in it, but I wanted to write my story to help people and show that our stories are varied and have so many elements. They don't just have to be grief-filled; they can also be filled with joy."

Juicy sits deliberately in the mess of right now: fertility anxiety, dating-app fatigue, egg-freezing and women in their 30s navigating identity without the road map previous generations relied on.

Rather than waiting for neat resolutions, Joseph writes from inside that uncertainty.

During her research, one statistic stuck with her: "Apparently [by] around 2030, 45 per cent of working-age women in the US will be single and child-free, and a lot of it will be by choice," she says.

"Yet, we don't have enough context for why this is."

As younger generations carve out different paths from their predecessors, they need new narratives to reflect these changing realities.

'The Great Egg Shortage'

One of the memoir's most powerful chapters recounts Joseph's fertility journey and the misconceptions and silence that surround infertility.

Joseph underwent two rounds of egg-freezing during the COVID-19 lockdown. She lived alone at the time, which only exacerbated her sense of isolation.

She details the experience, from initially feeling judged when meeting with a fertility specialist to having to inject herself daily and receiving updates from her doctor via Zoom, in her book.

"I really needed just one person who could say, 'You know what? I've had the same experience exactly as you have. And here's what I did, and here's how I got through it, and you'll be OK,'" she says.

Siri Hustvedt felt her husband's ghost. She wrote a book about it The author of What I Loved has published a moving memoir drawing on letters and journals documenting the last days of Paul Auster, her partner in life and writing.

She searched for stories by people who'd had similar experiences but came up empty-handed.

Instead, she turned to grief memoirs, but they failed to provide the comfort she was looking for.

"I really needed to see that specific intersection," she says. "And then I realised — I'm going to have to create it."

The resulting chapter is both brutally honest and unexpectedly funny.

She writes: "Here I am, robed up like Jesus in a fluffy, baby-blue bathrobe, quite literally being emotionally crucified … A whole fifteen years of possible reproductive age evaporated into thin air."

Being Lebanese, on her own terms

Joseph is also acutely aware of the narrow lane Lebanese Australian stories are usually afforded.

"A lot of them are either family-oriented or tragedy because that's what's allowed or accepted," she says.

Juicy refuses to be put in a box. Culture runs through the memoir without being translated or explained for an imagined outsider.

"It's telling these stories but also talking about everyday life as it exists for me, without having to qualify it as a Lebanese story," Joseph says.

"This book is unusual," she admits. "A woman having fun and partying and being Lebanese is, like, what? Unheard of? There are so many taboos you're breaking."

Nor does she romanticise contemporary single life.

Despite the joyous moments of freedom, fun, lust and friendship that permeate the book, when asked how she would describe the modern single Australian woman, her answer arrives fast, and it's a little unglamorous.

"She's suffering and in crisis," caught between settling for something sub-par or having given up entirely, Joseph says.

She sees this attitude across genders, too, "especially in heterosexual relationships. The masculinity crisis and lack of apathy, romance, joy and fun — it's all connected."

July's best books This month's best new books include an erotic novel set in a Tasmanian lighthouse, a 'wonderfully weird debut' about a woman's obsession with a cat and a Harlem heist novel.

Taking place over several years, the memoir eventually brings Joseph back to Sydney, humbled and with a new, refreshing outlook.

"I hope the main thing [people] feel after reading this is endless possibilities for their life, and that they have the power to make the choices to live that better life," she says.

For now, Joseph is letting herself enjoy this moment: the launch, the conversations, the tour.

But she's already thinking about her next book, which will be fiction.

Her Great Australian Novel, it seems, might still be coming.

Juicy is published by Pantera Press.

World.title: Where does your superannuation go when you die?
World.content:
Where your superannuation savings go when you die is not always straightforward, but there are ways to increase the chance the money will go where you want it to with minimal delays.

As ABC News reported on Monday, it is estimated 15.5 million Australians may not have made a binding death benefit nomination, so it is worth exploring how to set up one to ensure your super money (and any insurance payout) goes to whom you wish to receive it.

A binding nomination means the fund will pay to one or more of your dependants and/or your legal personal representative (executor of your estate).

If you have made a non-binding nomination or did not make a nomination, the trustee of the fund may use their discretion to decide which dependant or dependants is paid the death benefit.

Super inheritance pitfalls Most Australians have not made a legally binding death benefit nomination to ensure their superannuation goes to who they want it to when they die.

According to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), a dependent can include:

their spouse or de facto spouse

a child of the deceased (any age)

a person in an interdependency relationship with the deceased

a person substantially financially dependent on the deceased

An interdependency relationship exists between two people if all the following conditions are met:

they have a close personal relationship

they live together

one or both provides the other with financial support

one or both provides the other with domestic support and personal care

What happens if you don't have a dependent? How can you nominate who gets your super?

Superannuation does not automatically form part of your estate or get distributed by your will because it is held in a trust by your super fund.

Scott Forster, special counsel at Queensland Estate Lawyers, says a member cannot simply nominate anyone they choose.

"For example, a neighbour, grandchild or sibling cannot generally be nominated unless they meet the definition of dependent for super purposes," he said.

"Because the definition of a dependant can be complex, it's important to seek legal advice if you are uncertain if someone qualifies."

If you want to leave your super to someone who does not qualify as a legal dependant under superannuation law (such as adult children, siblings or friends), it must go through your estate via your will.

Loading...

To leave your superannuation as part of your estate, you must formally nominate your legal personal representative (the executor of your will) as the beneficiary with your super fund. That will ensure the super money, and any insurance, is paid out according to the instructions in your will.

You can log in to your member online portal or request a death benefit nomination form. Then on the nomination form, name your legal personal representative.

Some super funds do not allow binding nominations to be made digitally and require it on paper with two wet signatures. Check with your super fund what the process is.

You will also need to update your will to ensure it outlines how you want the super fund money distributed once it is paid into your estate.

Bear in mind that depending on what super fund you are with, binding nominations typically lapse after three years, so it would be worth checking with your fund about renewing them regularly to keep them valid.

Different super funds have different rules on death benefit nominations, so check with your fund. (Supplied: Pexels)

Louise du Pre-Alba, a consultant to the super industry, says the reason super funds are required to pay out to dependents over others is simple.

"If someone has to go on a government age pension while $2 million is going into an estate to be distributed in a different way, as a taxpayer, I would say, why am I subsidising that system?" she said.

"Of course, if someone is single, if someone doesn't have children and doesn't have financial dependents, things should be made easier and more straightforward for them so that they can leave money in accordance with their wishes and their will."

Loading...

What are the tax implications on super death benefit payouts?

Most people do not realise that super death benefits can be taxed. That is because super is concessionally taxed on the way in.

You pay a discounted tax rate on super contributions on the way in, as well as on super earnings.

The rationale behind the top-up taxes on super passed on through inheritance is that the previous tax discounts were intended to help fund one's retirement, not to subsidise an inheritance for someone else.

Who can inherit your superannuation? Consumers are being urged to make 'binding' death benefit nominations to avoid lengthy legal disputes between family members and loved ones.

How payouts get taxed depends on who receives the money and whether it is paid as a lump sum or a regular income stream.

Tax dependents — for example, a spouse or a child aged under 18 — pay zero tax.

Non-dependents — for example, independent adult children — can face up to 32 per cent tax on the taxable parts of the payout.

Mr Forster says whether a superannuation death benefit is taxed depends on tax law rather than superannuation law.

The tax treatment will depend largely on who receives the benefit and the components of the superannuation account.

There are circumstances where a child aged over 18 is still studying and financially dependent on their parents can qualify as a dependant, Mr Forster says.

"A child with certain disabilities may also qualify.

"These tax rules apply whether the superannuation benefit is paid directly from the super fund or it is paid to the deceased's estate."

For someone who is not a tax dependant, such as adult children who do not meet the tax criteria of dependency, tax will be payable on the benefit paid.

"What tax is payable will depend on the tax components of the benefit being paid," Mr Forster said.

" A superannuation death benefit can contain tax-free, taxed and untaxed components. "

The tax-free component is not subject to tax.

The taxed component consists of amounts that have already been taxed within the superannuation system and will usually attract further tax "in the order of 15 per cent" (17 per cent including Medicare).

The untaxed component is where no tax has yet been paid on this part of your superannuation, and the tax payable on this will be in the order of 32 per cent including the Medicare levy.

The exact tax outcome varies depending on the recipient, their dependency status and the components of the superannuation benefit being paid.

KPMG partner and superannuation expert Ross Stephens says the tax rates for death benefits also depend on whether the amounts are being paid as lump sums or income streams (pensions), and whether the benefit includes an insured component, and if so, whether the fund had claimed a deduction for the insurance premiums on the policy.

Proposed levy could cost self-managed super funds The assistant treasurer is looking to revamp funding for the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, saying that large super funds, as well as people with self-managed super funds (SMSFs), could be asked to chip in.

Some people gift super before they die

Mr Stephens notes that many industry commentators believe the tax settings discriminate between members who have dependants and those who don't.

"For example, a person that knows they are dying may be able to withdraw all of the monies in their superannuation fund prior to death and, say, gift these monies to their adult children, and the taxes and death benefits would not be payable," he said.

"Whereas if the same person dies unexpectedly and has no dependants at the time of death, death benefits paid to non-dependants would be subject to these taxes."

While in many cases death is unexpected, Scott Girdlestone, a partner at Wealth Advisory, says for people who do have time to get their affairs in order, "it may be appropriate to consider a lump sum payout" to an intended recipient before a person's passing.

"This is only available if the individual satisfies a condition of release, but two relevant conditions are terminal illness and total and permanent disablement, which can be used where it is beneficial to do so.

"Under these circumstances, the tax treatment is often more favourable and can reduce the tax that beneficiaries of an estate may pay."

This is not intended as legal or financial advice and people should speak to a lawyer and or tax adviser about their individual circumstances.

World.title: What happens if you do not complete your census form?
World.content:
Have you checked your mail recently?

You might have received an envelope with census written on it.

It's not junk mail or a scam letter; it contains important details to help you complete the census tonight.

What is the census?

It's something the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) does every five years to count every person and every household in Australia.

Technically called the Census of Population and Housing, it gives the ABS a snapshot of Australia on a particular night.

This year, census night is Tuesday, August 11.

The ABS is our official national statistical agency tasked with gathering information about the people and economy of Australia.

Outside the census, the ABS is responsible for data about things like inflation, unemployment and how many people got married last year.

Information collected via the census helps the government make decisions about things like health care, transport, schools and infrastructure.

You're allowed to complete your census early. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

How safe is it?

The ABS is an independent statutory authority and an official organisation trusted by 90 per cent of the general community, according to an ABS survey last year.

And the personal information you give on your census form is confidential and protected by law.

It is not shared with anyone else.

This means government agencies like the Department of Home Affairs, the Australian Taxation Office and Centrelink cannot see what you have written on your census form.

"We have a range of processes and protections that make sure information on census forms stays confidential," an ABS spokesperson said.

"For example, we use the strongest encryption technology available to make sure information from the online census form is secure.

"People should be reassured that organisations [other government departments and marketing companies] can't access any personal information you include on your census form."

The legislation around the census also imposes strict secrecy obligations on all ABS employees.

How does it work?

You have to participate in the census wherever you are staying on census night.

Each household has to fill out a census form.

Typically, there will only be one form per household.

However, people can complete their census separately from their household if they want.

They will need to call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227 to get a special number to complete their census online or request a paper form to be sent by mail.

Can I do the census online?

Yes.

You can either fill out a paper form or complete it on the ABS Census website.

The online census portal looks like this. (Supplied: Australian Bureau of Statistics)

Your home should have received a letter from the ABS containing a census number and a temporary password; you will need to enter these details on the website to complete the census online.

If you don't have a census number, you can go to this website, where you'll be prompted to enter your mobile phone number so the ABS can text you a one-time PIN and your census number.

For help over the phone, you can call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.

Where do I get my census form?

You'll be able to find the form online at the ABS website.

The ABS may have sent you a paper form.

The paper form has enough spaces for six people, but you can request an extra form or complete the census online if there will be more than six people at your place tonight.

If you want a paper form and haven't received one, you can request one via this online portal or by calling the 24/7 automated paper form request service on 1800 130 250.

An additional paper form may take up to 10 days to arrive, but the ABS says you will still have time to complete it.

You can complete the census online, but you can also fill out a paper form instead. (Supplied: Australian Bureau of Statistics)

Do I have to do the census?

Yes.

Participating in the census is compulsory.

Even if I'm not a citizen?

Yes, non-citizens must complete the census.

Almost everyone in Australia on census night needs to be counted.

That includes people on visas, international students and people visiting from overseas.

However, foreign diplomats and their families living in Australia are not included.

What if I'm not at home on Tuesday night?

Here are some of the most common reasons for being away:

If you're spending the night at someone else's place , you should be included on the form for the household you're staying at.

, you should be included on the form for the household you're staying at. If you're doing shiftwork on census night and will return the following day, you should ask someone else in the household to count you on the household form.

and will return the following day, you should ask someone else in the household to count you on the household form. If you end up staying at work because of multiple shifts , the ABS says you should complete a census form at your workplace.

, the ABS says you should complete a census form at your workplace. If you're spending the night in accommodation like a hotel, hospital or staff quarters, you'll need to fill out a personal form (as opposed to a household form) or complete the census online. The same goes if you'll be in transit within Australia on census night.

If no-one will be at your household on census night, you should let the ABS know by either filling out this online form or calling the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.

If you're not sure what to do in your specific situation, you can call the Census Contact Centre for advice.

Data collected during the census helps the government plan for the future. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

What if I'm out of the country?

You do not have to complete a census form if you're out of the country on census night.

What about children?

Children and babies must be counted.

If your child is staying at someone else's place on census night, they should be included on the census form for the household they're staying at.

If they're away at a school camp , the ABS says you should include your child on the census form as if they were at home.

, the ABS says you should include your child on the census form as if they were at home. If they're at boarding school and they live there less than six months of the year , include them in your household census form.

, include them in your household census form. If they're at boarding school and live there for more than six months of the year, they'll be counted at their boarding school, and you should mark them as "away" on your form.

If you have shared custody of your child, they should be included on the form for whatever household they're staying at on census night.

Put down the address they spend most of their time at under the "usual address" question.

Does every person have to fill out a form?

No, not if someone else they live with or are staying with has included them and their details on the household form.

Some households might elect one person to fill out the form on everyone else's behalf.

Others might pass the census around and complete their own details.

It's up to you and your household to decide.

Can you do the census early?

Yes.

You're able to complete the census as soon as you get your letter, as long as you know where you'll be on Tuesday night.

As of the morning of Thursday, August 6, more than 1.2 million forms had already been completed.

At the last census, more than 3 million households completed their forms early.

There are laws protecting the information provided in census forms. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

What happens if I forget?

You are able to submit your form late, the ABS spokesperson said.

"There is still time to complete your form after census night," they said.

But make sure you fill it out.

"While we aim to get everyone to participate in the census voluntarily, penalties can apply if someone refuses to complete the census," the spokesperson said.

However, the ABS website says it will contact people to encourage participation as a first port of call.

But if they don't respond to this, the ABS will send a formal legal instruction to complete the census.

Failing to comply with this direction could lead to prosecution.

Is there a fine for not completing the census?

Yes.

"If a person does not complete the census, they could be fined up to $364 a day," the spokesperson said.

"It is also an offence to knowingly provide false or misleading statements or information."

People found to have lied on their census form could face a fine of up to $3,640.

Wait, when is census night again?

Census night is August 11.

That's tonight.

World.title: Meta releases new AI model as Zuckerberg writes 6500-word essay on the future
World.content:
TechnologyAI Meta releases new AI model as Zuckerberg writes 6500-word essay on the future Vlad Savov August 11, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A
