Meta Platforms introduced a new, downloadable AI model that can run on a personal computer, adding fuel to a US debate over whether the increasingly powerful technology should be freely available or kept under tighter control. Users will be able to download and customise the new Muse Glimmer, a distilled version of the company’s Muse Spark 1.2 model designed with a focus on efficiency to minimise system requirements, Meta said. “Rather than centralising superintelligence, we should distribute it widely and give every person the ability to direct it”: Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg. AP At 30 billion parameters, the Muse Glimmer is “small enough” to need only one graphics card to power its work, which will primarily involve agent-like AI tasks such as schedule management and file organisation, according to Meta. The release, along with a 6500-word essay penned by Meta chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg, challenge a vision of AI championed by startups like OpenAI and Anthropic, which largely favour keeping the technology under tight control. Google offers its Gemma family of open-weight models that can be run on local devices, while low-cost open models from Chinese companies including DeepSeek, Moonshot and Alibaba Group have intensified pressure on US rivals who charge for access.



The weights, or values that help the AI system make decisions, for Muse Glimmer will be available via the Hugging Face collaboration platform. Meta intends to make the weights for a version of the more powerful Muse Spark available as well. There is no fee for download, though users would bear their own computing costs. Related Article AI Moon landing: Why this Chinese AI model rattled global sharemarkets Shares of Meta were up about 1 per cent in New York trading on Monday. “Rather than centralising superintelligence, we should distribute it widely and give every person the ability to direct it,” Zuckerberg wrote in the essay. “This has the potential to begin a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential.”



Zuckerberg didn’t name specific companies but criticised rivals that are “focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions.” OpenAI and Anthropic have raised concerns about the safety of open models after a series of reported breaches that saw AI models escape testing environments. Zuckerberg said Meta is creating “personal superintelligence for everyone.” Zuckerberg’s missive puts Meta at centre stage in the intensifying debate in Washington and Silicon Valley over how to respond to a wave of open-weight AI models from Chinese startups like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 that pose a new challenge to the proprietary products from leading American labs. View post on X Some policymakers have considered imposing restrictions on open-weight models from China, and the prospect of government curbs has drawn objections from tech industry leaders, including Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang. They insist that open-weight models are good for the long-term development of AI and help bolster its security, and in his essay, Zuckerberg concurred. “I do not believe restricting access to foreign open-source models is an effective solution,” the Meta chief wrote. “Our goal should be for American open-source models to be the best globally.” Zuckerberg has spent years promoting the idea of open-weight technology, and the company previously released several open-weight AI models known as Llama, which received mixed reviews.



Trump administration officials have held back on any steps to rein in open systems, and last week told top US tech companies that open-weight models wouldn’t be subject to government testing for now under a new AI safety framework that was completed earlier this month. Under the program, companies would have 30 days to voluntarily submit cutting-edge models for safety reviews before their release. In his essay, Zuckerberg cautioned against relying on what he called a “rigid process and review timeline,” arguing instead for closer collaboration between the government and the private sector that speeds the release of American models to preserve the US advantage in AI. “This has the potential to begin a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential.” Mark Zuckerberg US technology firms are pouring money into AI development, with companies including Meta, Amazon.com, Alphabet and Microsoft committing more than $US2 trillion for expansion. The huge sums being spent have triggered investor concerns that the lavish spending will ever pay off. Meta began charging for developer access for its Muse Spark 1.1 model for the first time last month.



Meta is also developing plans for a cloud infrastructure business that will sell access to AI computing power and models, along the lines of Amazon Web Services, though the lack of detail on the plan from Zuckerberg has frustrated investors who worry about the company achieving a return on investment. Related Article Updated

AI Anthropic’s Claude AI hacked three real companies during testing The company said on Monday that it intends to set up a $US1 billion fund to invest in US communities where it owns and operates data centres. Major infrastructure projects proposed by companies like Meta and Google have been met with resistance in many locations across the US as detractors protest against data centres’ use of land, energy and water. World.title: FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaMental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence Grant McArthur August 11, 2026 — 5:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victoria’s flagship new youth mental health service is being led by a fly-in, fly-out boss from Queensland, as reports mount of violence, drug use and patient deaths in its first year of operation. The Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service has been beset by staff claims of deteriorating patient care and frustration with senior management – including chief executive Dr Leanne Geppert, who they say only attends the service for a handful of days a month from her interstate base. Dr Leanne Geppert has been reappointed as the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service’s CEO despite living in Queensland. At least six senior youth mental health clinicians, leading specialty programs at the service, have quit, the deaths of two patients last month have been referred to the coroner and WorkSafe is looking into complaints of ongoing security concerns. Earlier this month, four thugs forced their way into the reception area at the service’s Sunshine campus and assaulted two people and fled before police arrived.



News of the troubled program comes after The Age yesterday revealed a landmark report into Victoria’s progress following the mental health royal commission had been significantly altered to remove remarks critical of the state government’s progress. Queensland-based Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service CEO Dr Leanne Geppert’s LinkedIn post from Easter 2026. The youth service was billed as a major response to Victoria’s mental health royal commission when it opened in June 2025, operating as the state’s first dedicated public youth mental health service for people aged 12-25. Six workers at the service – including psychiatrists, psychologists and nurses – spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, to detail the senior medical staff exodus, a rise in violent incidents, widespread drug use in secure wards, and claims that the hospital’s management is more focused on its brand than patient care. One of their most significant concerns is so-called “absentee management”, led by Brisbane-based Geppert who was recently awarded a three-year contract extension.



“The chief executive lives in Queensland. We don’t see her often at all and, when we do, she is dealing with the board,” a senior clinician said. Geppert was initially appointed as interim chief executive to transition Orygen’s world-renowned clinical service from the Royal Melbourne Hospital’s management into a new standalone state government youth mental health service. A Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service spokesperson said Geppert was appointed based on “her deep expertise in youth mental health, system reform and clinical service leadership”, and recently reappointed due to her strong performance. But the government-funded health service refused to provide information about how frequently its chief executive is on site. “Dr Geppert maintains a regular presence across PYMHWS sites and meets with staff, consumers and stakeholders as part of her leadership responsibilities,” the spokesperson said.



Geppert has a strong background in mental health having previously been the chief of clinical services at Orygen in Brisbane, the Deputy Commissioner for the Queensland Family and Child Commission, and in her continuing role as an adjunct senior lecturer at Griffith University. But some of Victoria’s most experienced youth mental health experts say they have grave concerns about the flagging performance of the service. Orygen executive director Professor Pat McGorry has become so troubled by issues within his partner organisation that he last month presented Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt with a six-page briefing outlining his concerns. Patrick McGorry has raised his concerns about the youth mental health service with the Mental Health Minister. Luis Enrique Ascui As well as its Parkville hospital, the service also operates in Sunshine, Footscray and Werribee, where it is co-located and works in partnership with Orygen-run headspace services.



McGorry’s briefing, seen by The Age, claims the organisation is not delivering safe, high-quality or sustainable care, and has failed to spend its budget treating desperate young people due to a lack of staff. A former Australian of the Year for his pioneering work in youth mental health, McGorry said the “absentee model of management” may have contributed to a wider crisis at the service which undermined vital post-royal commission reforms. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress “There are serious concerns that clinical care is being affected and that an escalation in serious incidents involving PYMHWS clients is creating significant risk for PYMHWS patients and staff, for the young people and families attending co-located headspace services and for Orygen’s headspace staff,” McGorry said. “There are also concerns that clinical practice guidelines are no longer being consistently followed. Patients are being discharged earlier than guidelines mandate and fidelity to evidence-based treatment is declining.”



McGorry told this masthead he had not heard back from Stitt regarding the claims set out in his briefing, and that he remained highly concerned about the situation. A PYMHWS spokesperson said the service was committed to providing safe, high-quality care. “PYMHWS continues to perform strongly against the vast majority of measures used to assess our performance,” they said in a statement. “In its first year, PYMHWS has maintained a strong focus on recruitment and retention as the service has grown. Workforce availability continues to be a challenge across the broader system.” Australian Medical Association Victorian president Dr Simon Judkins said he was worried the once world-renowned service would not recover if it was not immediately turned around.



“We are concerned that an exemplar service is being ruined by poor management decisions,” Judkins said. “Huge concerns that if the senior, experienced clinicians continue to leave, this valuable service will not recover.” A nurse working in the service’s inpatient ward said they were distraught by the recent death of a patient with complex and long-term issues. After months as an inpatient, the young man was discharged to a hotel room and found dead six days later. “We did harm here. We were the cause of this harm, and that hurts,” the nurse said.



“We’ve been a health service for all of a year.” The service said it would be inappropriate to comment on “individuals, specific incidents or potential coronial matters”. Staff said the patient’s death came amid wider concerns at the levels of drugs being used on wards and the lack of integrated drug and alcohol counselling. “PYMHWS is not here as a health organisation, PYMHWS is here for the brand,” the nurse said.



“It is about keeping up this image. It is messed up – these are human beings.” Health and Community Services Union Victorian branch secretary, Paul Healey, said mental health staffing and bed shortages meant young consumers were falling through the cracks. “The Victorian state government must urgently intervene to fund staff, implement ratios and deliver on the royal commission in the way in which it was intended,” he said. A senior psychiatrist still working at the service said many of the managers and new clinicians had little or no expertise or interest in youth mental health and the service had abandoned its internationally recognised model that has achieved positive patient outcomes. “The whole point of the royal commission was that the mental health system was broken, and yet they are dedicated to making it [PYMHWS] look like every other mediocre service,” the senior psychiatrist said.



“There has been a complete takeover by bureaucrats whose sole focus is corporate structure and values, and activity targets with no real purpose, certainly not good patient outcomes. “There has been an exodus of expertise, including many senior leaders in the field. They have left in despair because their decades of painstaking work and progress is being destroyed.” PYMHWS told The Age its workforce had grown by 42 per cent in its first year, with five new people hired for every one who departed, while transitioning the 500-strong workforce from Royal Melbourne Hospital into the standalone youth service.



Another psychiatrist, working in a different area of the service, said care for complex patients was being displaced in favour of lower acuity patients that look better on a reporting spreadsheet. “It’s like Peter Mac saying: ‘We’re now going to treat ingrown toenails’,” the doctor said. The psychiatrist said well-documented and researched long-care options were being pushed aside. “That is being absolutely run into the ground by people that are either not competent enough to know what it involves, or are wilfully destroying it. “So we seem to be moving back to a model of episodic care, which is everything that we really kind of pushed against 30 years ago, knowing that it didn’t work.



“And management doesn’t listen. None of them have ever attended our clinical reviews, they don’t really know what we do.” WorkSafe confirmed it was now monitoring the service over the ongoing incidents. “WorkSafe is monitoring the workplace to ensure health and safety obligations are being met and health and safety risks are being adequately addressed,” a WorkSafe spokesperson said. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. World.title: Thomas Keneally told Matt Nable to keep writing, so he quit his job
World.content:
CultureBooksTake 7 Thomas Keneally told Matt Nable to keep writing, so he quit his job Kylie Northover August 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Nable is quite the Renaissance man, having begun his career as a professional NRL player for Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles and South Sydney Rabbitohs, before becoming a national amateur boxing champion. After retiring from sport in his 20s, he began writing a novel about the sporting world, and sought the advice of playwright and author Thomas Keneally, who mentored him. The Final Winter eventually became a screenplay for his debut film, in which he also starred – launching him as both writer and actor. These days he’s also a director and a bestselling author. With the recent release of his latest novel, Mire, Nable says if it wasn’t for Keneally, he wouldn’t be enjoying the multifaceted career he has today. “That conversation,” he says, “changed my life.” Renaissance man: Matt Nable’s career spans professional sports, acting, directing and writing. Sally Flegg Worst habit?

I have a few. But probably being a noisy eater. At least that’s what my wife and daughter tell me. It really annoys them. And an internal habit that drives me crazy is that I can fixate on something, and it plays on a loop in my head – really frustrating when you’re trying to move forward and be productive. Over the years, I have gotten better at shutting down that noise and letting go. But every now and then, it still bites me. Greatest fear?

Losing one of my children. Beyond that, I can’t see anything to be afraid of that matters. There’s fear around certain things that I would consider irrational fears; I don’t like spiders or snakes, sharks I have a healthy fear of, but none of those keep me up at night. Losing a child does. I think all parents feel that way. I used to fear death. That’s completely gone. I don’t quite know why that it is, but I’m not afraid of dying. I was a horribly affected Catholic boy, to a point I was in some constant manner of guilt. It was exhausting. I was going to hell for everything. When I turned, and I turned hard, I had no fear of where I’d go when I died. So maybe that’s how I got to where I am now.



Nable (right) with his brother Aaron, who died from MND in 2024. The line that has stayed with you? “The people that matter, are the people that believe you matter … and tomorrow is never promised.” My brother passed away with MND in March 2024. And when he was diagnosed, and because there is no cure, he had that quote tattooed on his arm. It was a stark reminder that we are all just here without any idea of what’s coming and how long we have left. I now have the same tattoo. In February last year I did a psilocybin retreat, which for me was profound – confronting but enlightening. One of the great understandings I got from the experience was the people who matter are the people who believe you matter. And that’s where my attention, my time and my love need to be directed. Biggest regret?



Not being more present when my kids were smaller. I’m envious of parents when I see them with their small kids. It just went so fast. I yearn for those moments now, I cherish the memories. I look at photos all the time … I was far too self-involved back then. If I could run into my younger self, I’d give him a good clip behind the ear, and tell him to pay attention to what’s going on right before him. Nable’s latest novel, Mire is out now. Tell us about your turning point I had written a manuscript and had given it to Thomas Keneally. He’s a mad Manly fan, and somehow remembered me when I’d played there. He read it, and told me that I should continue writing. I did. And 12 months later he read my next effort. It took a while for him to get back to me, but he called one day, and he said, “Son, this is what you should be doing, and I wouldn’t say that if I didn’t believe it because it would be immoral of me.” I literally quit the job I was doing a week later. If not for Tommy and what he’d said, I’m not doing any of this. Not writing, not acting … I don’t know where I’d be. The artwork or song you wish was yours?



I have great respect and a love of songwriters who are able to tell vivid stories in short pieces of language. John Mellencamp, Billy Joel – they have the ability to give enormous texture through words mixed with the music. You can taste and smell where they’re talking about, and you can feel the people in the centre of the composition. I’d love to be able to do that. I started playing guitar in 2002, and I really am not very good. I got to a level and just kind of stayed there. So, I tried to write a few songs – and it was just awful. I quickly packed that up and got back in my own lane. Related Article Take 7 ‘My opinion didn’t count’: Tina Arena discusses ill-fated marriage to Ralph Carr in new documentary If you could time travel, where would you choose to go? The future is kind of scary to me. I’m not technological, so I fear I’d be redundant somewhere in the not-too-distant future. Perhaps to when I was a young boy, with my family bouncing around army barracks. As I said, I lost my youngest brother in 2024. We were all together back then. They were much simpler times, and we were all so happy. I’ve written about those memories to some degree in every novel that’s been published. There are moments while writing that are of real joy, and sometimes sadness. And then [I’d go] to a time when all my children were younger. Mire (Hachette) by Matt Nable is out now.

World.title: ASX set to dip on RBA day, Wall Street drifts; Oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip on RBA day, Wall Street drifts; Oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty Stan Choe August 11, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is drifting near its all-time high, while oil prices rise on uncertainty about when the Strait of Hormuz could reopen and get the global flow of crude going again. The S&P 500 fell 0.1 per cent after flipping between small gains and losses, coming off its record set on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 133 points, or 0.3 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.4 per cent lower. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a steady session. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent at the open. The ASX slid 0.3 per cent on Monday. The Reserve Bank announces its interest rates decision at 2.30pm AEST, with money markets and economists in near-unanimous agreement that the central bank’s monetary policy board will hold the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent when it wraps up its latest two-day meeting. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.56¢. Reporting season is starting to heat up, with Southern Cross Media Group and Life360 among companies due up today.



Momentum is slowing for US stocks following a rally powered by soaring profits for big US companies. Reports are on track to show earnings per share for companies in the S&P 500 were 50 per cent higher in the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That would be the best growth since five years ago, when the economy was roaring out of the chasm created by COVID. Related Article Opinion

Retail How one David Jones supplier got paid when the others didn’t Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Berkshire Hathaway is one of the latest companies to deliver a stronger profit for the last quarter than analysts expected, and the company built by legendary investor Warren Buffett said over the weekend that it’s also invested some of its massive pile of cash into stocks under its new CEO, Greg Abel. Berkshire Hathaway has been famous for buying stocks at what it considers low prices, and criticism has been high that US stocks generally look too expensive. But when they report strong profits, it helps them look less pricey. Berkshire Hathaway’s stock rose 1.4 per cent, and its immense size made it one of the strongest forces pushing upward on the S&P 500 index.



MarineMax jumped 45.8 per cent after the retailer, marina operator and superyacht services provider said it agreed to sell itself for about $US1.5 billion ($2.1 billion) in cash to a portfolio company of Blackstone. Varex Imaging leaped 48.7 per cent after Teledyne Technologies said it would buy the maker of X-ray imaging components for $US18.90 per share in cash. Technology stocks were the biggest weights on the market. Nvidia fell 2.5 per cent and Apple fell 2 per cent. Intel fell 3.4 per cent after saying it may sell $US15 billion of its stock. Such a move would dilute the ownership stakes of existing investors, and Intel said it would likely use the cash for investments to take advantage of the huge spending underway on artificial-intelligence technology. In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 4.7 per cent to $US87.50. It had swung between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach an agreement that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Middle East again to deliver crude worldwide.



But hopes are turning toward caution again, and the price of Brent is back to where it was earlier this month, as well as in mid-July, mid-June and in the first week of the war in March. Higher oil prices push inflation upward, and the main event for Wall Street this week will likely be Wednesday’s update on how bad inflation was last month. Economists expect it to show inflation slowed to 3.4 per cent from 3.5 per cent in June. Related Article Opinion

Japan Why fears of a Japanese implosion have the world on edge Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist A slowdown would mean less pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they would also slow the economy by making it more expensive for US households and companies to borrow money. They would also undercut prices for stocks and other investments. A report on Friday showing unexpectedly weak hiring across the United States lowered Wall Street’s expectations for an upcoming hike to interest rates. But traders still see a 50 per cent chance the Fed will raise its main interest rate at its next meeting in September, according to data from CME Group.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.70 per cent from 4.65 per cent late Friday. That’s up from 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran, and it’s already sent rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe after rising in much of Asia. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 2.1 per cent for one of the world’s bigger moves. World.title: First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCity life First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square Megan Gorrey August 11, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The City of Sydney is forging ahead with plans to bulldoze seven buildings opposite Town Hall to create a $150 million civic square featuring native trees and water fountains, new designs reveal, despite a backlash over the project’s cost and scale. Lord Mayor Clover Moore’s council in February voted to accelerate demolition of the buildings, including Woolworths supermarket, to make way for the long-promised public plaza at the corner of George, Park and Pitt streets in the heart of the central business district in about six years. An artist’s impression of the proposed civic square opposite Town Hall in Sydney’s CBD. Choi Render The designs include a curved grove of native trees and water fountains to cool the square. Choi Render Moore said the designs for the square, prepared by Sydney design practice JPW and landscape architects ASPECT Studios and to be published today, would mitigate rising urban heat.



“The trees and the water element will create a cooling environment for people to meet and greet or come to celebrations we might hold there,” Moore said. “I’m really thrilled that it’s very Sydney. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Clover’s vision: Town Hall Square will be George Street on steroids Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “It’s another change that will be fantastic for the city, and I think when people see it they will fall in love with it.” Moore said the 4200-square-metre plaza would feature eucalypts, moving water, seating and circular paving patterns to provide an outdoor venue for large events and celebrations including markets, festivals, concerts and sporting event live-sites. The square will have an Aboriginal name. “We’ve reached a point where we’ve acquired the buildings, we’ve saved the money, we’re ready to go.”



JPW director Matthew Morel said the “uniquely Sydney” square would “provide generous, flexible civic space found in the world’s great cities”. ASPECT Studios global design director Sacha Coles said night lighting would boost safety, and the square would be “a stage for Sydney’s civic life”. The City of Sydney has been planning for more than 40 years to demolish the Woolworths block and six other buildings to create a new public domain. The tree canopy would be lit up at night to improve safety. Choi Render The council hopes the square will provide a live-site for sporting matches. Choi Render In February, Moore signalled her ambition to start demolition work for the square – which had previously been delayed for another decade – before the council term ends in 2028.



Between 1985 and 2019, the council acquired six of the seven properties required for the project, starting with the Woolworths building on the corner of George and Park streets. Negotiations are under way for the council to compulsorily acquire the final building, home to a Foot Locker shoe store, on George Street. Related Article Opinion

City life Sydneysiders must shape their new Town Hall Square before it shapes them Carlo Ratti Architect and engineer Councillors endorsed the proposed scope of works for the project, allowing it to proceed to the next stage of concept design, planning approvals and construction. When the development application is submitted next month, there will be an opportunity for public comment on the draft designs. The Central Sydney Planning Committee will decide the application. The square is due to be completed in 2031. Labor councillor Yvonne Weldon has opposed the project due to its steep cost, telling a council meeting earlier this year the project was putting the organisation under “serious financial stress”, and the public plaza would “come at the cost of other projects and programs”.



“I’m all about improving and expanding our public spaces, but to me, this just doesn’t stack up.” Business Sydney executive director Paul Nicolaou, a staunch critic, has also warned the project would weaken the city’s economic core when it needed more investment and jobs. The Woolworths building is among seven blocks that will be bulldozed for the square. Edwina Pickles “The proposal would require the demolition of an active commercial building at significant cost, followed by the further expense of constructing and maintaining a new civic plaza. At a time when governments and cities face competing infrastructure, transport, housing and safety priorities, it is difficult to justify such expenditure, particularly when the city already has substantial public open space,” Nicolaou has said. The council says it has allocated $150 million for design, demolition and construction. All costs for the square, including those associated with the termination of existing leases and funds to acquire the final property, have been factored into long-term financial plans.



Moore said the council would need to invest more than $200 million to upgrade the existing buildings to modern office standards so they could be rented – a spend she said would be “crazy”. Related Article Climate crisis Dark roofs, no trees and black roads: The Sydney suburbs designed to get even hotter “It was the same when we pedestrianised George Street – [critics said] it was too costly, it shouldn’t happen,” she said. “Private investment in George Street [since then] has been $8 billion; we anticipate this square will be an enhancement for people wanting to visit, work and invest.” Woolworths has said the Town Hall outlet is its most visited supermarket nationally, drawing 6.5 million customers a year.



Tourism and Transport Forum chief executive Margy Osmond said the council’s “once-in-a-generation” project would create a landmark, attracting investment and visitors and potentially changing “the way people experience this part of the city”. World.title: If space is the true measure of cruising luxury, this is a winner
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceShip reviews If space is the true measure of cruising luxury, this is a winner Kate Armstrong August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Silversea Silver Moon Built 2020

2020 The cruise Busan to Tokyo (seven days of a 14-day itinerary) via Kanazawa, Aomori and Hakodate

Busan to Tokyo (seven days of a 14-day itinerary) via Kanazawa, Aomori and Hakodate Passengers 596

596 Crew 411

411 Decks eight passenger decks

eight passenger decks Length 212.8 metres Silver Moon is one of Silversea’s Classic ships. The Ship Mirroring her sister ship Silver Muse, Silver Moon is one of Silversea’s eight Classic ships. An additional four in the fleet are Expedition ships. Owned since 2018 by the Royal Caribbean Group, the brand has maintained a loyal following, as reflected by the many repeat clients on this trip.



Boarding 



The spaces The Panorama Lounge serves morning tea and coffee and later morphs into a cocktail venue. Silver Moon’s true strength is its spaces. There are many, and these distinct and welcoming areas ensure there’s no pressure for room. It’s easy to find your patch. The Dolce Vita, the heart of the ship, is home to both reception and the shore excursion desk (I love its pale turquoise velvet accents). The elegant Panorama Lounge serves morning tea and coffee before morphing into a cocktail venue, while the Observation Library has books and games tables. True to its name, the cosy Arts Cafe serves up an arty theme along with a decent cappuccino, specialty teas and pastries. A pool deck, jogging track and fitness centre cater to the active. Evening restaurants range from the 220-seater Atlantide to the delightfully intimate 32-seat venue Kaiseki. The Venetian Lounge is an inviting entertainment venue. The stateroom A curtain divides the bed and the sitting room in the neutral-hued Veranda Suite.



Our Deluxe Veranda Suite is very comfortable. The palette is neutral and the layout is perfect. A curtain divides the bed from the lounge area where there’s a decent-sized sofa with cushions and a throw blanket, plus a coffee table and a generous-sized desk with adjacent shelving. Floor-to-ceiling glass windows let in plenty of sun; heavy curtains block out nocturnal lights. The verandah has deck chairs and a table. The bathroom’s full-length bathtub is a bonus, and perfect for winding down after the busy day on shore. A walk-in robe’s ample storage helps you keep things shipshape. The food S.A.L.T. Kitchen restaurant on Silver Moon. With eight restaurants, Silver Moon offers everything from French dishes at La Dame, to pizza at Spaccanapoli, to Asian fare and an omakase menu at Kaiseki. The quality between venues can vary, however. The “classic” restaurant, Atlantide, is the most reliable in terms of consistency, even though it’s the largest option. Our standout favourite, and to our surprise the least frequented, is S.A.L.T. Kitchen. During this cruise, it prepares superb Japanese and Asian fusion dishes. (S.A.L.T. is Silversea’s “Sea And Land Taste” program that offers locally inspired menus and land-based culinary excursions). For sweet lovers, the gelati, made on board, are consistently excellent. The S.A.L.T. Bar’s cocktail staff shake up the scene, with martinis to gimlets and any challenge thrown their way. Don’t miss the Silver Moon cocktail. Wellness



With a full program, I don’t have time to try the Zagara Spa, but it offers a hair salon, a thermal suite, massage and medi-spa treatments (including Botox and fillers), plus several seaweed-based therapies. For an extra fee you can access a compact outdoor relaxation space with a small hydrotherapy pool (the area is “private”, but shared with others who’ve upgraded). The well-equipped fitness centre has plenty of room, light and ocean vistas. Entertainment S.A.L.T. Lab is the venue for hands-on cooking classes. Here, it’s less about the “cruisical” and more about a variety of performances, held in the Venetian Lounge where club chairs are arranged around small tables, or you can sit in tiered banquettes. The program ranges from traditional South Korean music to the final evening’s Motown-style production. Themed dances, such as the 1970s-focused Boogie Fever, light up the Panorama Lounge. A jazz duo channel Ella Fitzgerald and other melodies at Silver Note, an intimate New York-style jazz bar that also serves cocktails, while pianists perform at various locations around the ship. The insightful presentations about each port by on-board lecturer Evelyn Evans are a hit. Daily classes range from bridge to origami, but my choice is the class at S.A.L.T. Lab, a fabulous hands-on cooking session, where I learn to whip up grated turnip miso soup and daikon leaf rice. The crew



Although all suites have an assigned butler in addition to a room attendant, we have no requirements beyond the regular suite service and generally, the crew are pleasant and respectful. Service standards fluctuate in the restaurants, especially at breakfast, where there’s both a buffet and hot dish menu in La Terrazza. In smaller venues, it’s another matter; our server in S.A.L.T. Kitchen, Kai, describes each dish so evocatively that his enthusiasm alone makes it worth dining there. The verdict Subtle elegance, fascinating port stops and informative talks. The details Silversea’s 14-day (12-night) Japan itinerary sails from Tokyo to Tokyo. Fares from $19,100 a person. See silversea.com

Not so swell Standards: not Silversea’s fault (they consistently stress the dress code in communications), but some passengers insist on wearing inappropriately casual clothing in formal settings. And, as a non-smoker, I don’t appreciate how the designated smokers’ lounge (Connoisseur’s Corner) is located so close to the delightful Panorama Lounge. The writer was a guest of Silversea.

World.title: What happened to all the sex in The Odyssey?
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCinema What happened to all the sex in The Odyssey? Kerrie O'Brien August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Christopher Nolan’s interpretation of The Odyssey – the film that’s drawn millions to cinemas around the world since its release in July – is missing some of the poem’s really interesting women, and its sexiness, according to Classicist Mary Beard. “It’s de-feminised it,” she says. “And turned it into a kind of battle scene.” The UK-based writer, podcaster and former professor of Classics at Cambridge University is concerned people will walk away from the movie thinking that what Homer wrote in around the eighth century BC was an aggressive, tough story. “Actually, The Odyssey is one of the least macho works of ancient Greek literature,” she says. Calypso, played by Charlize Theron, appears in Christopher Nolan’s version of The Odyssey. But where’s all the sex? Alamy Stock Photo “I feel pretty strongly that this is an Odyssey rewritten for contemporary 21st-century American, slightly masculinist culture.” For Beard, one of the key themes of Odysseus’ homecoming to his wife is the rival sexual encounters on the way. “So there is Calypso, who keeps him as a kind of sex toy for about seven years and that is featured in the movie. But also you have Circe, this enticing witch, who – at least in the poem of The Odyssey – turns his men into pigs,” she says. “Now, the point of Circe in the poem is that she too is keeping Odysseus there to be her lover. Now, she’s not doing that in Nolan[’s film]; she’s a rather wonderful character ... but she’s not the same.”



Mary Beard says Circe (played by Samantha Morton) is “a rather wonderful character”, but she’s very different from the Circe Homer wrote. IMDB The film has entirely erased Princess Nausicaa, who lives with her parents on the island of Scheria. In the poem, says Beard, Nausicaa is just coming to marriageable age and is thinking about getting a husband when Odysseus washes up on her island, naked. There are these “quasi-erotic encounters” between them, she says. “They’ve downgraded the sex ... and so you’ve got a rather different feel to the whole thing. For me, The Odyssey is wonderfully domestic, wonderfully ironic. Sex is always at the margins – who’s going to entrap Odysseus next, or who is Odysseus going to decide to go off with next? And that has gone.” The Odyssey isn’t the only Nolan film to largely do away with sex. From Memento to The Dark Knight, most of the British director’s movies omit any kind of extended sexual encounter, earning him something of a reputation for creating “sexless” titles. One of the few outliers is Oppenheimer (2023), which contains brief scenes of partial nudity. The editor of Classics at The London Review of Books, Beard has made ancient Rome and the Classics her speciality over five decades. She points to the fact Homer’s poem was considered so female that in the 19th century, Samuel Butler wrote a book called The Authoress of the Odyssey claiming that it had to have been written by a woman.



Mary Beard has made ancient Rome and the Classics her speciality over five decades. Louie Douvis In Nolan’s take, Calypso (Charlize Theron) is the main woman other than Odysseus’ wife Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, yet she appears in about 10 minutes of the three-hour film. Beard also argues that Nolan has introduced an entire theme that is absent from Homer’s original text, again perhaps inspired by our contemporary reality. “It is this sense we’re a civilisation on the brink of collapse, that there are threats coming to us ... Now, that is very much a contemporary American anxiety, a contemporary Western anxiety. In the original Odyssey, I don’t see a thing about civilisation coming to an end. Actually, it’s quite confident, [with] perhaps a misplaced confidence.” Anne Hathaway plays Penelope, wife of the long-lost Odysseus. Melinda Sue Gordon She is aware that the original poem is a lengthy beast and that Nolan had to make decisions about what would stay and what would go. “I’m not a pedant and these works are there for every age to do what they want with,” Beard says. “My job is to say maybe we’ve lost more than we’ve gained here. That’s all.



Related Article Literature The 3000-year-old poem Australians suddenly can’t get enough of “As the critiques have gone on and become rather more ferocious, I have become more sympathetic to him.” To Beard’s mind, The Odyssey is one of the most approachable works of ancient literature, “rich and complicated”. Recent interpretations include Caribbean writer Derek Walcott’s play of the same name and his poem Omeros, James Joyce’s novel Ulysses and the 2000 Coen Brothers film O Brother, Where Art Thou? The questions Homer asked are questions that we still ask, she says, so “there’s no surprise that The Odyssey has been so central in literature”. Regardless of her thoughts on his film, Beard does credit Nolan with inviting a whole new audience to discover this remarkable work, and for that she is grateful: “You’ve seen the film, now read the book.”



An evening with Mary Beard: Talking Classics tours Australia from November 20. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Of all the hotels I’ve stayed in around the world, this type is my favourite
World.content:
InspirationTravel tips Opinion Of all the hotels I’ve stayed in around the world, this type is my favourite Lee Tulloch Travel columnist August 11, 2026 — 5:00am

August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you asked me to name my favourite style of hotel, I would without hesitation say the Moroccan riad. A riad is a traditional Moorish house built around a central garden. In North Africa, particularly Morocco, it more often means a guesthouse in a heritage building where the rooms are arranged facing a shared courtyard. Some riads are quite simple, run by the family that has lived there for generations. Izza, Marrakesh’s central courtyard. The rooms can be small but even in the modest households, they open to courtyards covered in mosaic tiles, known as zellige, with a splashing fountain in the centre and surrounded by greenery, usually citrus trees planted in pots.



This style of inward-facing architecture that keeps families cool was perfected in the 12th century and little has changed. 



Apart from the astounding aesthetic beauty, there are many other things I love about staying in a Moroccan riad. Breakfasts are almost always included. Served with gallons of mint tea, they’re extravagant and dangerous for the waistline, especially msemen pancakes and baghrir crumpets, drizzled with honey. And I love the price. Staying in a riad can be surprisingly good value. Many will barely set you back $200 to $300, often less, in the centre of the city. Even more than this, I love the sense of place. The oldest houses are concentrated within the medina walls, which means guests are immersed in local culture as soon as they step outside the door.



Moroccans are extremely hospitable, so you’re not just invited into their house – you become part of their neighbourhood. But many riads fall into ruin because of the immense cost of labour-intensive repairs. The medinas of Marrakesh, Rabat, Essaouira and Fes have UNESCO World Heritage status. Increasingly, the houses in them are being bought and renovated by foreigners – it’s often only foreigners who have the money required to restore a heritage building. Riad Romeo, Marrakesh, owned by Italian fashion designer Romeo Gigli. Thankfully, many have been captivated by the magic of the medina. The restorations have sustained the skills of the traditional artisans, which might have been lost without private support.



Last year, I stayed at Riad Romeo, which is in one of the oldest parts of the Marrakesh medina. It’s owned by Italian fashion designer Romeo Gigli, who moved to Marrakesh when he retired from fashion more than 20 years ago. Gigli collaborated with local artisans on the traditional work such as the zellige tiling in the bathrooms and in the spectacular yellow-tiled waterfall in the courtyard, and on modern furnishings he designed himself. The result is a modern take on the riad that still retains many of the traditional features. Room Yves in Izza. The interiors are pink-toned and filled with vintage pieces. Izza and its art. Known as the “house of friends”, Izza was inspired by the bohemians of the 1970s who flocked to Marrakesh, such as Yves Saint Laurent, Talitha Getty and Marianne Faithfull, and the 14 rooms are named for each of them.



British tech entrepreneur Neil Hutchinson bought and restored eight interlinked riads, transforming them into one to create Izza and filling it with about €5 million ($8 million) worth of art from his collection. Izza is gorgeous, rambling across three courtyards and multiple rooftops, full of arresting art and contemporary furniture as well as magnificent zellige wherever the eye lands. Interiors at five-bedroom Riad Rosemary, Marrakech. Courtyard sanctuary in Riad Rosemary. Belgian artist Laurence Leenaert and her partner Ayoub Boualam opened Riad Rosemary the week of the 2023 Moroccan earthquake. The lovely five-bedroom riad is full of her bright ceramic plates and pots, which luckily mostly survived the upheaval.



Related Article Africa The unknown corner of North Africa that has been seen by billions Riad Botanica is owned by Angela and Mohamed Mallak (she’s from Melbourne; he’s from Morocco). It’s another small Marrakesh riad that has had a painstaking restoration and makeover. Traditional Moroccan mosaics, plasterwork and ornate cedar doors have been teamed with art deco wallpaper by Florence Broadhurst, an Australian contemporary twist. There are so many riads in Marrakesh, I could probably spend a year there and not stay in them all. Keep the mint tea warm for me. The writer was a guest of Riad Romeo and Izza.

World.title: Meta releases new AI model as Zuckerberg writes 6500-word essay on the future
World.content:
TechnologyAI Meta releases new AI model as Zuckerberg writes 6500-word essay on the future Vlad Savov August 11, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Meta Platforms introduced a new, downloadable AI model that can run on a personal computer, adding fuel to a US debate over whether the increasingly powerful technology should be freely available or kept under tighter control. Users will be able to download and customise the new Muse Glimmer, a distilled version of the company’s Muse Spark 1.2 model designed with a focus on efficiency to minimise system requirements, Meta said. “Rather than centralising superintelligence, we should distribute it widely and give every person the ability to direct it”: Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg. AP At 30 billion parameters, the Muse Glimmer is “small enough” to need only one graphics card to power its work, which will primarily involve agent-like AI tasks such as schedule management and file organisation, according to Meta. The release, along with a 6500-word essay penned by Meta chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg, challenge a vision of AI championed by startups like OpenAI and Anthropic, which largely favour keeping the technology under tight control. Google offers its Gemma family of open-weight models that can be run on local devices, while low-cost open models from Chinese companies including DeepSeek, Moonshot and Alibaba Group have intensified pressure on US rivals who charge for access.



The weights, or values that help the AI system make decisions, for Muse Glimmer will be available via the Hugging Face collaboration platform. Meta intends to make the weights for a version of the more powerful Muse Spark available as well. There is no fee for download, though users would bear their own computing costs. Related Article AI Moon landing: Why this Chinese AI model rattled global sharemarkets Shares of Meta were up about 1 per cent in New York trading on Monday. “Rather than centralising superintelligence, we should distribute it widely and give every person the ability to direct it,” Zuckerberg wrote in the essay. “This has the potential to begin a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential.”



Zuckerberg didn’t name specific companies but criticised rivals that are “focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions.” OpenAI and Anthropic have raised concerns about the safety of open models after a series of reported breaches that saw AI models escape testing environments. Zuckerberg said Meta is creating “personal superintelligence for everyone.” Zuckerberg’s missive puts Meta at centre stage in the intensifying debate in Washington and Silicon Valley over how to respond to a wave of open-weight AI models from Chinese startups like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 that pose a new challenge to the proprietary products from leading American labs. View post on X Some policymakers have considered imposing restrictions on open-weight models from China, and the prospect of government curbs has drawn objections from tech industry leaders, including Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang. They insist that open-weight models are good for the long-term development of AI and help bolster its security, and in his essay, Zuckerberg concurred. “I do not believe restricting access to foreign open-source models is an effective solution,” the Meta chief wrote. “Our goal should be for American open-source models to be the best globally.” Zuckerberg has spent years promoting the idea of open-weight technology, and the company previously released several open-weight AI models known as Llama, which received mixed reviews.



Trump administration officials have held back on any steps to rein in open systems, and last week told top US tech companies that open-weight models wouldn’t be subject to government testing for now under a new AI safety framework that was completed earlier this month. Under the program, companies would have 30 days to voluntarily submit cutting-edge models for safety reviews before their release. In his essay, Zuckerberg cautioned against relying on what he called a “rigid process and review timeline,” arguing instead for closer collaboration between the government and the private sector that speeds the release of American models to preserve the US advantage in AI. “This has the potential to begin a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential.” Mark Zuckerberg US technology firms are pouring money into AI development, with companies including Meta, Amazon.com, Alphabet and Microsoft committing more than $US2 trillion for expansion. The huge sums being spent have triggered investor concerns that the lavish spending will ever pay off. Meta began charging for developer access for its Muse Spark 1.1 model for the first time last month.



Meta is also developing plans for a cloud infrastructure business that will sell access to AI computing power and models, along the lines of Amazon Web Services, though the lack of detail on the plan from Zuckerberg has frustrated investors who worry about the company achieving a return on investment. Related Article Updated

AI Anthropic’s Claude AI hacked three real companies during testing The company said on Monday that it intends to set up a $US1 billion fund to invest in US communities where it owns and operates data centres. Major infrastructure projects proposed by companies like Meta and Google have been met with resistance in many locations across the US as detractors protest against data centres’ use of land, energy and water. World.title: FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaMental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence Grant McArthur August 11, 2026 — 5:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victoria’s flagship new youth mental health service is being led by a fly-in, fly-out boss from Queensland, as reports mount of violence, drug use and patient deaths in its first year of operation. The Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service has been beset by staff claims of deteriorating patient care and frustration with senior management – including chief executive Dr Leanne Geppert, who they say only attends the service for a handful of days a month from her interstate base. Dr Leanne Geppert has been reappointed as the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service’s CEO despite living in Queensland. At least six senior youth mental health clinicians, leading specialty programs at the service, have quit, the deaths of two patients last month have been referred to the coroner and WorkSafe is looking into complaints of ongoing security concerns. Earlier this month, four thugs forced their way into the reception area at the service’s Sunshine campus and assaulted two people and fled before police arrived.



News of the troubled program comes after The Age yesterday revealed a landmark report into Victoria’s progress following the mental health royal commission had been significantly altered to remove remarks critical of the state government’s progress. Queensland-based Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service CEO Dr Leanne Geppert’s LinkedIn post from Easter 2026. The youth service was billed as a major response to Victoria’s mental health royal commission when it opened in June 2025, operating as the state’s first dedicated public youth mental health service for people aged 12-25. Six workers at the service – including psychiatrists, psychologists and nurses – spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, to detail the senior medical staff exodus, a rise in violent incidents, widespread drug use in secure wards, and claims that the hospital’s management is more focused on its brand than patient care. One of their most significant concerns is so-called “absentee management”, led by Brisbane-based Geppert who was recently awarded a three-year contract extension.



“The chief executive lives in Queensland. We don’t see her often at all and, when we do, she is dealing with the board,” a senior clinician said. Geppert was initially appointed as interim chief executive to transition Orygen’s world-renowned clinical service from the Royal Melbourne Hospital’s management into a new standalone state government youth mental health service. A Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service spokesperson said Geppert was appointed based on “her deep expertise in youth mental health, system reform and clinical service leadership”, and recently reappointed due to her strong performance. But the government-funded health service refused to provide information about how frequently its chief executive is on site. “Dr Geppert maintains a regular presence across PYMHWS sites and meets with staff, consumers and stakeholders as part of her leadership responsibilities,” the spokesperson said.



Geppert has a strong background in mental health having previously been the chief of clinical services at Orygen in Brisbane, the Deputy Commissioner for the Queensland Family and Child Commission, and in her continuing role as an adjunct senior lecturer at Griffith University. But some of Victoria’s most experienced youth mental health experts say they have grave concerns about the flagging performance of the service. Orygen executive director Professor Pat McGorry has become so troubled by issues within his partner organisation that he last month presented Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt with a six-page briefing outlining his concerns. Patrick McGorry has raised his concerns about the youth mental health service with the Mental Health Minister. Luis Enrique Ascui As well as its Parkville hospital, the service also operates in Sunshine, Footscray and Werribee, where it is co-located and works in partnership with Orygen-run headspace services.



McGorry’s briefing, seen by The Age, claims the organisation is not delivering safe, high-quality or sustainable care, and has failed to spend its budget treating desperate young people due to a lack of staff. A former Australian of the Year for his pioneering work in youth mental health, McGorry said the “absentee model of management” may have contributed to a wider crisis at the service which undermined vital post-royal commission reforms. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress “There are serious concerns that clinical care is being affected and that an escalation in serious incidents involving PYMHWS clients is creating significant risk for PYMHWS patients and staff, for the young people and families attending co-located headspace services and for Orygen’s headspace staff,” McGorry said. “There are also concerns that clinical practice guidelines are no longer being consistently followed. Patients are being discharged earlier than guidelines mandate and fidelity to evidence-based treatment is declining.”



McGorry told this masthead he had not heard back from Stitt regarding the claims set out in his briefing, and that he remained highly concerned about the situation. A PYMHWS spokesperson said the service was committed to providing safe, high-quality care. “PYMHWS continues to perform strongly against the vast majority of measures used to assess our performance,” they said in a statement. “In its first year, PYMHWS has maintained a strong focus on recruitment and retention as the service has grown. Workforce availability continues to be a challenge across the broader system.” Australian Medical Association Victorian president Dr Simon Judkins said he was worried the once world-renowned service would not recover if it was not immediately turned around.



“We are concerned that an exemplar service is being ruined by poor management decisions,” Judkins said. “Huge concerns that if the senior, experienced clinicians continue to leave, this valuable service will not recover.” A nurse working in the service’s inpatient ward said they were distraught by the recent death of a patient with complex and long-term issues. After months as an inpatient, the young man was discharged to a hotel room and found dead six days later. “We did harm here. We were the cause of this harm, and that hurts,” the nurse said.



“We’ve been a health service for all of a year.” The service said it would be inappropriate to comment on “individuals, specific incidents or potential coronial matters”. Staff said the patient’s death came amid wider concerns at the levels of drugs being used on wards and the lack of integrated drug and alcohol counselling. “PYMHWS is not here as a health organisation, PYMHWS is here for the brand,” the nurse said.



“It is about keeping up this image. It is messed up – these are human beings.” Health and Community Services Union Victorian branch secretary, Paul Healey, said mental health staffing and bed shortages meant young consumers were falling through the cracks. “The Victorian state government must urgently intervene to fund staff, implement ratios and deliver on the royal commission in the way in which it was intended,” he said. A senior psychiatrist still working at the service said many of the managers and new clinicians had little or no expertise or interest in youth mental health and the service had abandoned its internationally recognised model that has achieved positive patient outcomes. “The whole point of the royal commission was that the mental health system was broken, and yet they are dedicated to making it [PYMHWS] look like every other mediocre service,” the senior psychiatrist said.



“There has been a complete takeover by bureaucrats whose sole focus is corporate structure and values, and activity targets with no real purpose, certainly not good patient outcomes. “There has been an exodus of expertise, including many senior leaders in the field. They have left in despair because their decades of painstaking work and progress is being destroyed.” PYMHWS told The Age its workforce had grown by 42 per cent in its first year, with five new people hired for every one who departed, while transitioning the 500-strong workforce from Royal Melbourne Hospital into the standalone youth service.



Another psychiatrist, working in a different area of the service, said care for complex patients was being displaced in favour of lower acuity patients that look better on a reporting spreadsheet. “It’s like Peter Mac saying: ‘We’re now going to treat ingrown toenails’,” the doctor said. The psychiatrist said well-documented and researched long-care options were being pushed aside. “That is being absolutely run into the ground by people that are either not competent enough to know what it involves, or are wilfully destroying it. “So we seem to be moving back to a model of episodic care, which is everything that we really kind of pushed against 30 years ago, knowing that it didn’t work.



“And management doesn’t listen. None of them have ever attended our clinical reviews, they don’t really know what we do.” WorkSafe confirmed it was now monitoring the service over the ongoing incidents. “WorkSafe is monitoring the workplace to ensure health and safety obligations are being met and health and safety risks are being adequately addressed,” a WorkSafe spokesperson said. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. World.title: Thomas Keneally told Matt Nable to keep writing, so he quit his job
World.content:
CultureBooksTake 7 Thomas Keneally told Matt Nable to keep writing, so he quit his job Kylie Northover August 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Nable is quite the Renaissance man, having begun his career as a professional NRL player for Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles and South Sydney Rabbitohs, before becoming a national amateur boxing champion. After retiring from sport in his 20s, he began writing a novel about the sporting world, and sought the advice of playwright and author Thomas Keneally, who mentored him. The Final Winter eventually became a screenplay for his debut film, in which he also starred – launching him as both writer and actor. These days he’s also a director and a bestselling author. With the recent release of his latest novel, Mire, Nable says if it wasn’t for Keneally, he wouldn’t be enjoying the multifaceted career he has today. “That conversation,” he says, “changed my life.” Renaissance man: Matt Nable’s career spans professional sports, acting, directing and writing. Sally Flegg Worst habit?

I have a few. But probably being a noisy eater. At least that’s what my wife and daughter tell me. It really annoys them. And an internal habit that drives me crazy is that I can fixate on something, and it plays on a loop in my head – really frustrating when you’re trying to move forward and be productive. Over the years, I have gotten better at shutting down that noise and letting go. But every now and then, it still bites me. Greatest fear?

Losing one of my children. Beyond that, I can’t see anything to be afraid of that matters. There’s fear around certain things that I would consider irrational fears; I don’t like spiders or snakes, sharks I have a healthy fear of, but none of those keep me up at night. Losing a child does. I think all parents feel that way. I used to fear death. That’s completely gone. I don’t quite know why that it is, but I’m not afraid of dying. I was a horribly affected Catholic boy, to a point I was in some constant manner of guilt. It was exhausting. I was going to hell for everything. When I turned, and I turned hard, I had no fear of where I’d go when I died. So maybe that’s how I got to where I am now.



Nable (right) with his brother Aaron, who died from MND in 2024. The line that has stayed with you? “The people that matter, are the people that believe you matter … and tomorrow is never promised.” My brother passed away with MND in March 2024. And when he was diagnosed, and because there is no cure, he had that quote tattooed on his arm. It was a stark reminder that we are all just here without any idea of what’s coming and how long we have left. I now have the same tattoo. In February last year I did a psilocybin retreat, which for me was profound – confronting but enlightening. One of the great understandings I got from the experience was the people who matter are the people who believe you matter. And that’s where my attention, my time and my love need to be directed. Biggest regret?



Not being more present when my kids were smaller. I’m envious of parents when I see them with their small kids. It just went so fast. I yearn for those moments now, I cherish the memories. I look at photos all the time … I was far too self-involved back then. If I could run into my younger self, I’d give him a good clip behind the ear, and tell him to pay attention to what’s going on right before him. Nable’s latest novel, Mire is out now. Tell us about your turning point I had written a manuscript and had given it to Thomas Keneally. He’s a mad Manly fan, and somehow remembered me when I’d played there. He read it, and told me that I should continue writing. I did. And 12 months later he read my next effort. It took a while for him to get back to me, but he called one day, and he said, “Son, this is what you should be doing, and I wouldn’t say that if I didn’t believe it because it would be immoral of me.” I literally quit the job I was doing a week later. If not for Tommy and what he’d said, I’m not doing any of this. Not writing, not acting … I don’t know where I’d be. The artwork or song you wish was yours?



I have great respect and a love of songwriters who are able to tell vivid stories in short pieces of language. John Mellencamp, Billy Joel – they have the ability to give enormous texture through words mixed with the music. You can taste and smell where they’re talking about, and you can feel the people in the centre of the composition. I’d love to be able to do that. I started playing guitar in 2002, and I really am not very good. I got to a level and just kind of stayed there. So, I tried to write a few songs – and it was just awful. I quickly packed that up and got back in my own lane. Related Article Take 7 ‘My opinion didn’t count’: Tina Arena discusses ill-fated marriage to Ralph Carr in new documentary If you could time travel, where would you choose to go? The future is kind of scary to me. I’m not technological, so I fear I’d be redundant somewhere in the not-too-distant future. Perhaps to when I was a young boy, with my family bouncing around army barracks. As I said, I lost my youngest brother in 2024. We were all together back then. They were much simpler times, and we were all so happy. I’ve written about those memories to some degree in every novel that’s been published. There are moments while writing that are of real joy, and sometimes sadness. And then [I’d go] to a time when all my children were younger. Mire (Hachette) by Matt Nable is out now.

World.title: ASX set to dip on RBA day, Wall Street drifts; Oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip on RBA day, Wall Street drifts; Oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty Stan Choe August 11, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is drifting near its all-time high, while oil prices rise on uncertainty about when the Strait of Hormuz could reopen and get the global flow of crude going again. The S&P 500 fell 0.1 per cent after flipping between small gains and losses, coming off its record set on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 133 points, or 0.3 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.4 per cent lower. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a steady session. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent at the open. The ASX slid 0.3 per cent on Monday. The Reserve Bank announces its interest rates decision at 2.30pm AEST, with money markets and economists in near-unanimous agreement that the central bank’s monetary policy board will hold the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent when it wraps up its latest two-day meeting. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.56¢. Reporting season is starting to heat up, with Southern Cross Media Group and Life360 among companies due up today.



Momentum is slowing for US stocks following a rally powered by soaring profits for big US companies. Reports are on track to show earnings per share for companies in the S&P 500 were 50 per cent higher in the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That would be the best growth since five years ago, when the economy was roaring out of the chasm created by COVID. Related Article Opinion

Retail How one David Jones supplier got paid when the others didn’t Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Berkshire Hathaway is one of the latest companies to deliver a stronger profit for the last quarter than analysts expected, and the company built by legendary investor Warren Buffett said over the weekend that it’s also invested some of its massive pile of cash into stocks under its new CEO, Greg Abel. Berkshire Hathaway has been famous for buying stocks at what it considers low prices, and criticism has been high that US stocks generally look too expensive. But when they report strong profits, it helps them look less pricey. Berkshire Hathaway’s stock rose 1.4 per cent, and its immense size made it one of the strongest forces pushing upward on the S&P 500 index.



MarineMax jumped 45.8 per cent after the retailer, marina operator and superyacht services provider said it agreed to sell itself for about $US1.5 billion ($2.1 billion) in cash to a portfolio company of Blackstone. Varex Imaging leaped 48.7 per cent after Teledyne Technologies said it would buy the maker of X-ray imaging components for $US18.90 per share in cash. Technology stocks were the biggest weights on the market. Nvidia fell 2.5 per cent and Apple fell 2 per cent. Intel fell 3.4 per cent after saying it may sell $US15 billion of its stock. Such a move would dilute the ownership stakes of existing investors, and Intel said it would likely use the cash for investments to take advantage of the huge spending underway on artificial-intelligence technology. In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 4.7 per cent to $US87.50. It had swung between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach an agreement that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Middle East again to deliver crude worldwide.



But hopes are turning toward caution again, and the price of Brent is back to where it was earlier this month, as well as in mid-July, mid-June and in the first week of the war in March. Higher oil prices push inflation upward, and the main event for Wall Street this week will likely be Wednesday’s update on how bad inflation was last month. Economists expect it to show inflation slowed to 3.4 per cent from 3.5 per cent in June. Related Article Opinion

Japan Why fears of a Japanese implosion have the world on edge Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist A slowdown would mean less pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they would also slow the economy by making it more expensive for US households and companies to borrow money. They would also undercut prices for stocks and other investments. A report on Friday showing unexpectedly weak hiring across the United States lowered Wall Street’s expectations for an upcoming hike to interest rates. But traders still see a 50 per cent chance the Fed will raise its main interest rate at its next meeting in September, according to data from CME Group.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.70 per cent from 4.65 per cent late Friday. That’s up from 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran, and it’s already sent rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe after rising in much of Asia. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 2.1 per cent for one of the world’s bigger moves.
