World.title: First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCity life First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square Megan Gorrey August 11, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The City of Sydney is forging ahead with plans to bulldoze seven buildings opposite Town Hall to create a $150 million civic square featuring native trees and water fountains, new designs reveal, despite a backlash over the project’s cost and scale. Lord Mayor Clover Moore’s council in February voted to accelerate demolition of the buildings, including Woolworths supermarket, to make way for the long-promised public plaza at the corner of George, Park and Pitt streets in the heart of the central business district in about six years. An artist’s impression of the proposed civic square opposite Town Hall in Sydney’s CBD. Choi Render The designs include a curved grove of native trees and water fountains to cool the square. Choi Render Moore said the designs for the square, prepared by Sydney design practice JPW and landscape architects ASPECT Studios and to be published today, would mitigate rising urban heat.



“The trees and the water element will create a cooling environment for people to meet and greet or come to celebrations we might hold there,” Moore said. “I’m really thrilled that it’s very Sydney. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Clover’s vision: Town Hall Square will be George Street on steroids Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “It’s another change that will be fantastic for the city, and I think when people see it they will fall in love with it.” Moore said the 4200-square-metre plaza would feature eucalypts, moving water, seating and circular paving patterns to provide an outdoor venue for large events and celebrations including markets, festivals, concerts and sporting event live-sites. The square will have an Aboriginal name. “We’ve reached a point where we’ve acquired the buildings, we’ve saved the money, we’re ready to go.”



JPW director Matthew Morel said the “uniquely Sydney” square would “provide generous, flexible civic space found in the world’s great cities”. ASPECT Studios global design director Sacha Coles said night lighting would boost safety, and the square would be “a stage for Sydney’s civic life”. The City of Sydney has been planning for more than 40 years to demolish the Woolworths block and six other buildings to create a new public domain. The tree canopy would be lit up at night to improve safety. Choi Render The council hopes the square will provide a live-site for sporting matches. Choi Render In February, Moore signalled her ambition to start demolition work for the square – which had previously been delayed for another decade – before the council term ends in 2028.



Between 1985 and 2019, the council acquired six of the seven properties required for the project, starting with the Woolworths building on the corner of George and Park streets. Negotiations are under way for the council to compulsorily acquire the final building, home to a Foot Locker shoe store, on George Street. Related Article Opinion

City life Sydneysiders must shape their new Town Hall Square before it shapes them Carlo Ratti Architect and engineer Councillors endorsed the proposed scope of works for the project, allowing it to proceed to the next stage of concept design, planning approvals and construction. When the development application is submitted next month, there will be an opportunity for public comment on the draft designs. The Central Sydney Planning Committee will decide the application. The square is due to be completed in 2031. Labor councillor Yvonne Weldon has opposed the project due to its steep cost, telling a council meeting earlier this year the project was putting the organisation under “serious financial stress”, and the public plaza would “come at the cost of other projects and programs”.



“I’m all about improving and expanding our public spaces, but to me, this just doesn’t stack up.” Business Sydney executive director Paul Nicolaou, a staunch critic, has also warned the project would weaken the city’s economic core when it needed more investment and jobs. The Woolworths building is among seven blocks that will be bulldozed for the square. Edwina Pickles “The proposal would require the demolition of an active commercial building at significant cost, followed by the further expense of constructing and maintaining a new civic plaza. At a time when governments and cities face competing infrastructure, transport, housing and safety priorities, it is difficult to justify such expenditure, particularly when the city already has substantial public open space,” Nicolaou has said. The council says it has allocated $150 million for design, demolition and construction. All costs for the square, including those associated with the termination of existing leases and funds to acquire the final property, have been factored into long-term financial plans.



Moore said the council would need to invest more than $200 million to upgrade the existing buildings to modern office standards so they could be rented – a spend she said would be “crazy”. Related Article Climate crisis Dark roofs, no trees and black roads: The Sydney suburbs designed to get even hotter “It was the same when we pedestrianised George Street – [critics said] it was too costly, it shouldn’t happen,” she said. “Private investment in George Street [since then] has been $8 billion; we anticipate this square will be an enhancement for people wanting to visit, work and invest.” Woolworths has said the Town Hall outlet is its most visited supermarket nationally, drawing 6.5 million customers a year.



Tourism and Transport Forum chief executive Margy Osmond said the council’s “once-in-a-generation” project would create a landmark, attracting investment and visitors and potentially changing “the way people experience this part of the city”. World.title: If space is the true measure of cruising luxury, this is a winner
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceShip reviews If space is the true measure of cruising luxury, this is a winner Kate Armstrong August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Silversea Silver Moon Built 2020

2020 The cruise Busan to Tokyo (seven days of a 14-day itinerary) via Kanazawa, Aomori and Hakodate

Busan to Tokyo (seven days of a 14-day itinerary) via Kanazawa, Aomori and Hakodate Passengers 596

596 Crew 411

411 Decks eight passenger decks

eight passenger decks Length 212.8 metres Silver Moon is one of Silversea’s Classic ships. The Ship Mirroring her sister ship Silver Muse, Silver Moon is one of Silversea’s eight Classic ships. An additional four in the fleet are Expedition ships. Owned since 2018 by the Royal Caribbean Group, the brand has maintained a loyal following, as reflected by the many repeat clients on this trip.



Boarding 



The spaces The Panorama Lounge serves morning tea and coffee and later morphs into a cocktail venue. Silver Moon’s true strength is its spaces. There are many, and these distinct and welcoming areas ensure there’s no pressure for room. It’s easy to find your patch. The Dolce Vita, the heart of the ship, is home to both reception and the shore excursion desk (I love its pale turquoise velvet accents). The elegant Panorama Lounge serves morning tea and coffee before morphing into a cocktail venue, while the Observation Library has books and games tables. True to its name, the cosy Arts Cafe serves up an arty theme along with a decent cappuccino, specialty teas and pastries. A pool deck, jogging track and fitness centre cater to the active. Evening restaurants range from the 220-seater Atlantide to the delightfully intimate 32-seat venue Kaiseki. The Venetian Lounge is an inviting entertainment venue. The stateroom A curtain divides the bed and the sitting room in the neutral-hued Veranda Suite.



Our Deluxe Veranda Suite is very comfortable. The palette is neutral and the layout is perfect. A curtain divides the bed from the lounge area where there’s a decent-sized sofa with cushions and a throw blanket, plus a coffee table and a generous-sized desk with adjacent shelving. Floor-to-ceiling glass windows let in plenty of sun; heavy curtains block out nocturnal lights. The verandah has deck chairs and a table. The bathroom’s full-length bathtub is a bonus, and perfect for winding down after the busy day on shore. A walk-in robe’s ample storage helps you keep things shipshape. The food S.A.L.T. Kitchen restaurant on Silver Moon. With eight restaurants, Silver Moon offers everything from French dishes at La Dame, to pizza at Spaccanapoli, to Asian fare and an omakase menu at Kaiseki. The quality between venues can vary, however. The “classic” restaurant, Atlantide, is the most reliable in terms of consistency, even though it’s the largest option. Our standout favourite, and to our surprise the least frequented, is S.A.L.T. Kitchen. During this cruise, it prepares superb Japanese and Asian fusion dishes. (S.A.L.T. is Silversea’s “Sea And Land Taste” program that offers locally inspired menus and land-based culinary excursions). For sweet lovers, the gelati, made on board, are consistently excellent. The S.A.L.T. Bar’s cocktail staff shake up the scene, with martinis to gimlets and any challenge thrown their way. Don’t miss the Silver Moon cocktail. Wellness



With a full program, I don’t have time to try the Zagara Spa, but it offers a hair salon, a thermal suite, massage and medi-spa treatments (including Botox and fillers), plus several seaweed-based therapies. For an extra fee you can access a compact outdoor relaxation space with a small hydrotherapy pool (the area is “private”, but shared with others who’ve upgraded). The well-equipped fitness centre has plenty of room, light and ocean vistas. Entertainment S.A.L.T. Lab is the venue for hands-on cooking classes. Here, it’s less about the “cruisical” and more about a variety of performances, held in the Venetian Lounge where club chairs are arranged around small tables, or you can sit in tiered banquettes. The program ranges from traditional South Korean music to the final evening’s Motown-style production. Themed dances, such as the 1970s-focused Boogie Fever, light up the Panorama Lounge. A jazz duo channel Ella Fitzgerald and other melodies at Silver Note, an intimate New York-style jazz bar that also serves cocktails, while pianists perform at various locations around the ship. The insightful presentations about each port by on-board lecturer Evelyn Evans are a hit. Daily classes range from bridge to origami, but my choice is the class at S.A.L.T. Lab, a fabulous hands-on cooking session, where I learn to whip up grated turnip miso soup and daikon leaf rice. The crew



Although all suites have an assigned butler in addition to a room attendant, we have no requirements beyond the regular suite service and generally, the crew are pleasant and respectful. Service standards fluctuate in the restaurants, especially at breakfast, where there’s both a buffet and hot dish menu in La Terrazza. In smaller venues, it’s another matter; our server in S.A.L.T. Kitchen, Kai, describes each dish so evocatively that his enthusiasm alone makes it worth dining there. The verdict Subtle elegance, fascinating port stops and informative talks. The details Silversea’s 14-day (12-night) Japan itinerary sails from Tokyo to Tokyo. Fares from $19,100 a person. See silversea.com



Related Article Cruises Port guide: Tokyo, Japan Our rating out of five ★★★★ Swell An easy-going ship experience with attractive suites, refined and uncrowded spaces, an excellent choice of dining options and entertainment and a good selection of shore excursions (these may cost extra depending on the fare type).



Not so swell Standards: not Silversea’s fault (they consistently stress the dress code in communications), but some passengers insist on wearing inappropriately casual clothing in formal settings. And, as a non-smoker, I don’t appreciate how the designated smokers’ lounge (Connoisseur’s Corner) is located so close to the delightful Panorama Lounge. The writer was a guest of Silversea.

World.title: What happened to all the sex in The Odyssey?
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCinema What happened to all the sex in The Odyssey? Kerrie O'Brien August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Christopher Nolan’s interpretation of The Odyssey – the film that’s drawn millions to cinemas around the world since its release in July – is missing some of the poem’s really interesting women, and its sexiness, according to Classicist Mary Beard. “It’s de-feminised it,” she says. “And turned it into a kind of battle scene.” The UK-based writer, podcaster and former professor of Classics at Cambridge University is concerned people will walk away from the movie thinking that what Homer wrote in around the eighth century BC was an aggressive, tough story. “Actually, The Odyssey is one of the least macho works of ancient Greek literature,” she says. Calypso, played by Charlize Theron, appears in Christopher Nolan’s version of The Odyssey. But where’s all the sex? Alamy Stock Photo “I feel pretty strongly that this is an Odyssey rewritten for contemporary 21st-century American, slightly masculinist culture.” For Beard, one of the key themes of Odysseus’ homecoming to his wife is the rival sexual encounters on the way. “So there is Calypso, who keeps him as a kind of sex toy for about seven years and that is featured in the movie. But also you have Circe, this enticing witch, who – at least in the poem of The Odyssey – turns his men into pigs,” she says. “Now, the point of Circe in the poem is that she too is keeping Odysseus there to be her lover. Now, she’s not doing that in Nolan[’s film]; she’s a rather wonderful character ... but she’s not the same.”



Mary Beard says Circe (played by Samantha Morton) is “a rather wonderful character”, but she’s very different from the Circe Homer wrote. IMDB The film has entirely erased Princess Nausicaa, who lives with her parents on the island of Scheria. In the poem, says Beard, Nausicaa is just coming to marriageable age and is thinking about getting a husband when Odysseus washes up on her island, naked. There are these “quasi-erotic encounters” between them, she says. “They’ve downgraded the sex ... and so you’ve got a rather different feel to the whole thing. For me, The Odyssey is wonderfully domestic, wonderfully ironic. Sex is always at the margins – who’s going to entrap Odysseus next, or who is Odysseus going to decide to go off with next? And that has gone.” The Odyssey isn’t the only Nolan film to largely do away with sex. From Memento to The Dark Knight, most of the British director’s movies omit any kind of extended sexual encounter, earning him something of a reputation for creating “sexless” titles. One of the few outliers is Oppenheimer (2023), which contains brief scenes of partial nudity. The editor of Classics at The London Review of Books, Beard has made ancient Rome and the Classics her speciality over five decades. She points to the fact Homer’s poem was considered so female that in the 19th century, Samuel Butler wrote a book called The Authoress of the Odyssey claiming that it had to have been written by a woman.



Mary Beard has made ancient Rome and the Classics her speciality over five decades. Louie Douvis In Nolan’s take, Calypso (Charlize Theron) is the main woman other than Odysseus’ wife Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, yet she appears in about 10 minutes of the three-hour film. Beard also argues that Nolan has introduced an entire theme that is absent from Homer’s original text, again perhaps inspired by our contemporary reality. “It is this sense we’re a civilisation on the brink of collapse, that there are threats coming to us ... Now, that is very much a contemporary American anxiety, a contemporary Western anxiety. In the original Odyssey, I don’t see a thing about civilisation coming to an end. Actually, it’s quite confident, [with] perhaps a misplaced confidence.” Anne Hathaway plays Penelope, wife of the long-lost Odysseus. Melinda Sue Gordon She is aware that the original poem is a lengthy beast and that Nolan had to make decisions about what would stay and what would go. “I’m not a pedant and these works are there for every age to do what they want with,” Beard says. “My job is to say maybe we’ve lost more than we’ve gained here. That’s all.



Related Article Literature The 3000-year-old poem Australians suddenly can’t get enough of “As the critiques have gone on and become rather more ferocious, I have become more sympathetic to him.” To Beard’s mind, The Odyssey is one of the most approachable works of ancient literature, “rich and complicated”. Recent interpretations include Caribbean writer Derek Walcott’s play of the same name and his poem Omeros, James Joyce’s novel Ulysses and the 2000 Coen Brothers film O Brother, Where Art Thou? The questions Homer asked are questions that we still ask, she says, so “there’s no surprise that The Odyssey has been so central in literature”. Regardless of her thoughts on his film, Beard does credit Nolan with inviting a whole new audience to discover this remarkable work, and for that she is grateful: “You’ve seen the film, now read the book.”



An evening with Mary Beard: Talking Classics tours Australia from November 20. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Of all the hotels I’ve stayed in around the world, this type is my favourite
World.content:
InspirationTravel tips Opinion Of all the hotels I’ve stayed in around the world, this type is my favourite Lee Tulloch Travel columnist August 11, 2026 — 5:00am

August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you asked me to name my favourite style of hotel, I would without hesitation say the Moroccan riad. A riad is a traditional Moorish house built around a central garden. In North Africa, particularly Morocco, it more often means a guesthouse in a heritage building where the rooms are arranged facing a shared courtyard. Some riads are quite simple, run by the family that has lived there for generations. Izza, Marrakesh’s central courtyard. The rooms can be small but even in the modest households, they open to courtyards covered in mosaic tiles, known as zellige, with a splashing fountain in the centre and surrounded by greenery, usually citrus trees planted in pots.



This style of inward-facing architecture that keeps families cool was perfected in the 12th century and little has changed. 



Apart from the astounding aesthetic beauty, there are many other things I love about staying in a Moroccan riad. Breakfasts are almost always included. Served with gallons of mint tea, they’re extravagant and dangerous for the waistline, especially msemen pancakes and baghrir crumpets, drizzled with honey. And I love the price. Staying in a riad can be surprisingly good value. Many will barely set you back $200 to $300, often less, in the centre of the city. Even more than this, I love the sense of place. The oldest houses are concentrated within the medina walls, which means guests are immersed in local culture as soon as they step outside the door.



Moroccans are extremely hospitable, so you’re not just invited into their house – you become part of their neighbourhood. But many riads fall into ruin because of the immense cost of labour-intensive repairs. The medinas of Marrakesh, Rabat, Essaouira and Fes have UNESCO World Heritage status. Increasingly, the houses in them are being bought and renovated by foreigners – it’s often only foreigners who have the money required to restore a heritage building. Riad Romeo, Marrakesh, owned by Italian fashion designer Romeo Gigli. Thankfully, many have been captivated by the magic of the medina. The restorations have sustained the skills of the traditional artisans, which might have been lost without private support.



Last year, I stayed at Riad Romeo, which is in one of the oldest parts of the Marrakesh medina. It’s owned by Italian fashion designer Romeo Gigli, who moved to Marrakesh when he retired from fashion more than 20 years ago. Gigli collaborated with local artisans on the traditional work such as the zellige tiling in the bathrooms and in the spectacular yellow-tiled waterfall in the courtyard, and on modern furnishings he designed himself. The result is a modern take on the riad that still retains many of the traditional features. Room Yves in Izza. The interiors are pink-toned and filled with vintage pieces. Izza and its art. Known as the “house of friends”, Izza was inspired by the bohemians of the 1970s who flocked to Marrakesh, such as Yves Saint Laurent, Talitha Getty and Marianne Faithfull, and the 14 rooms are named for each of them.



British tech entrepreneur Neil Hutchinson bought and restored eight interlinked riads, transforming them into one to create Izza and filling it with about €5 million ($8 million) worth of art from his collection. Izza is gorgeous, rambling across three courtyards and multiple rooftops, full of arresting art and contemporary furniture as well as magnificent zellige wherever the eye lands. Interiors at five-bedroom Riad Rosemary, Marrakech. Courtyard sanctuary in Riad Rosemary. Belgian artist Laurence Leenaert and her partner Ayoub Boualam opened Riad Rosemary the week of the 2023 Moroccan earthquake. The lovely five-bedroom riad is full of her bright ceramic plates and pots, which luckily mostly survived the upheaval.



Related Article Africa The unknown corner of North Africa that has been seen by billions Riad Botanica is owned by Angela and Mohamed Mallak (she’s from Melbourne; he’s from Morocco). It’s another small Marrakesh riad that has had a painstaking restoration and makeover. Traditional Moroccan mosaics, plasterwork and ornate cedar doors have been teamed with art deco wallpaper by Florence Broadhurst, an Australian contemporary twist. There are so many riads in Marrakesh, I could probably spend a year there and not stay in them all. Keep the mint tea warm for me. The writer was a guest of Riad Romeo and Izza.

World.title: Amalgamation to deliver 'more efficient' system, Simon Watts says
World.content:
Local Government Minister on amalgamation proposals Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The local government minister hopes amalgamating councils across the country will deliver a more efficient system.

Government set a three-month deadline in May for every council outside of Auckland to come up with an amalgamation plan or have one imposed on it, after the 2028 local elections.

Minister for Local Government Simon Watts told Morning Report the submissions were just the start.

"This is the first step in that local government simplification process," he said.

"We have signalled a Back Stop that we'll put in play post-election, and we'll use these proposals to help inform that, but I'm pretty impressed.

"This is going to form a more efficient local government system that's more fit for purpose, and we know the current model is too complex and too much duplication."

Watts said about 44 councils had submitted Head Start proposals, while less than 20 did not.

With only one amalgamation in the last 35 years, he was pleased with the number of submissions.

"I think we're pretty impressed with how many we've got through. We're going to work through them," he said.

"We've only had them for a day, but we're going to work through them in the coming weeks and look to take some decisions before Parliament rises on the 24th."

Simon Watts. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Watts said Head Start was "completely voluntary" and councils showed they were up for it with their proposals.

He said councils wanted a fast process, and that is what they got.

"We gave them that and as a result we've got some pretty comprehensive proposals on the table. We're going to work through those," Watts said.

"But I think it's pretty important to show that actually we've got councils and leadership out there that say we can do things more efficiently.

"We can get a clearer, more responsible model to operate under and that's going to flow through to better value for ratepayers as well."

Watts said 18 proposals on the table showed councils were ready to get on with the job.

There were going to be those that needed more time, he said.

"But we want to get working with those councils that are up for the change because we also want to make sure that's legislated by midway through next year, so it gives them plenty of runway before the '28 election.

"And that is going to be important from a capacity of system point of view, there's a lot of change happening. We need to make sure that we manage that change through over the next 18 months."

Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Deputy PM Seymour on amalgamation and unemployment First Up Download MP3 5m

Earlier, Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour said the government would make counter proposals for councils which had refused to submit their own.

Seymour told First Up that refusals by some councils wouldn't stop merges.

"If they don't make a proposal then we'll make a counter proposal as the government, because at the end of the day we have far too many councils," he said.

"While the people who work in the council office, and in some cases people who sit on the council, may not want to vote for an early Christmas, there's still a lot of people talking to us who are very frustrated with the service that they're getting from their councils.

"We have a duty to deliver a better solution to New Zealanders up and down the country."

Seymour said proposals needed to have community interest and a coordination of infrastructure.

He said there would be a few considerations they would have to work through, including physical, practical, human and political to form a viable network of local government.

World.title: Where have all the ATMs gone?
World.content:
If you have looked for somewhere to get cash out recently, you might have noticed a change - many bank-owned ATMs have vanished.

Sometimes they been replaced with non-bank options, which can cost $2.50 per withdrawal, and sometimes they have been removed completely.

The country's largest bank ANZ said it has reduced its ATM numbers by 85 in the past two years. In all but 10 cases, the contract for the site was given to another provider.

Westpac said its number had dropped by 54 over the same period.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

The Reserve Bank said the number of bank branches around the country was down by 40 percent and the number of bank-owned ATMs had dropped 32 percent over the past decade. Between 2012 and 2017, total ATM numbers fell by 14.7 percent per million people.

Consumer NZ said it was concerned.

"While cash use is declining, it is still used by many people. The Reserve Bank's latest cash-use data, from September 2025, found that 40.3 percent of people said they used cash for everyday things and only 2.5 percent said they never use cash."

New Zealand Banking Association chief executive Roger Beaumont said banks were responding to customer demand.

"The main reason there are fewer ATMs is that fewer customers are using them. Around 1.5 percent of all customer transactions are made at an ATM, and that's slowly reducing every year.

"In some cases, landlords making changes to tenancy agreements, or seismic risk, may lead to banks removing or relocating ATMs."

Claire Matthews - a banking expert at Massey University - said there was a cost associated with ATMs and a risk due to the cash being held. There had to be enough use being made of them to make them worthwhile for banks, she said.

"People use less cash and are more likely to get cash with eftpos transactions if they do want it, so there is less use of cash. I'm struggling to remember when I used an ATM."

University of Auckland senior lecturer in economics Chanelle Duley said the drop in ATM numbers was part of a broader "retreat" from physical banking infrastructure.

Fincap the financial mentor network said cash was important for many of the people mentors dealt with. Some people used cash to help them budget.

It said that it had heard from mentors in urban and rural areas that some people found it hard to access cash.

"In rural areas the cost of significant travel to access cash can compound financial hardship. In urban areas, we have heard concerns around hardship or exclusion for clients who have a disability and/or, limited time amongst their other obligations to queue or travel for the limited local available services which do not charge for cash withdrawal."

It is something that the Reserve Bank has its eye on.

It has been consulting on plans to propose minimum standards for cash services in New Zealand and will release its findings late next month.

Its proposal was to put a floor under the number and location of places where bank customers could withdraw, deposit or swap cash.

It wants 95 percent of people living in urban areas to have walking-distance access to a free cash point.

It said meeting the standard would cost banks about $100 million a year but that was only 1 percent of their combined annual profit.

A spokesperson said it was analysing the 6000 submissions it had received and was not in a position to comment further at this stage.

World.title: Police didn't know child victim's name in reopened abuse case, documents reveal
World.content:
A review into how police handled 40 child protection complaints has already triggered nine reports of suspected abuse or neglect. A series of documents obtained by RNZ reveal NZ Police did not know the name of a child victim whose case they had reopened, and that Oranga Tamariki was unaware of the major investigation until media began asking questions. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports.

Review of police triggers reports of suspected abuse or neglect Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Eleven days before Oranga Tamariki was told of a major police investigation that involved the re-opening of 40 child protection complaints, police sought their help to identify a child linked to one of the cases under review.

Five days later, on 30 June, Oranga Tamariki (OT) replied saying it would grant access to the information request but, because of high demand, expected to provide the information by December.

Police responded saying they were "taking another look at an older file we believe holds risk for both police and OT".

"It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can't elaborate on at this time."

Internal police emails reveal the request was urgent because investigators needed information that would help identify the victim including the names and details of children placed in a person's care.

Police warned that waiting until December for the information "is going to create significant problems in addressing this risk".

The documents do not reveal what action, if any, OT took in response. It was not until 6 July that the agency was formally told about what Police had dubbed Operation Hark.

More than 100 pages of emails released to RNZ under the Official Information Act reveal how Oranga Tamariki first learned of the investigation, its scramble to assess dozens of affected cases, and senior staff's concern the agency could be "a bit over reliant on police's view" in the Child Protection Protocol process.

RNZ can also reveal that nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the NZ Police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases.

Detective Inspector Kevan Verry. Screenshot

The information request

Operation Hark began after concerns were raised in May about Detective Inspector Kevan Verry's handling of a historical sexual abuse case in Northland that had sat for a couple of years with no investigation. The initial case sparked a further review where another 13 cases were identified as requiring re-investigation

Police also carried out a rapid review of about 1000 files which were under Verry's oversight, with a further 40 cases identified for re-investigation. A team of specialist child protection and adult sexual assault investigators had been pulled together to work on the re-opened cases.

On 25 June, police sent the information request to Oranga Tamariki. Five days later they got a response from OT saying they would grant their request.

"As we are currently receiving more requests than anticipated, we are experiencing delays in processing these."

OT said it would supply the information by 7 December.

A police staffer, whose name is redacted from the OIA, sent an email that went to Detective Superintendent Uraia Vakaruru and another staff member asking if they had any way of fast-tracking the request.

One of the recipients asked what the file related to and said they would follow up with their contact at OT.

The staffer replied with information about the case (this information is redacted in the OIA).

"I have attached the IR that I submitted to OT - I did request a lot of information from them but the most important part was the names and details of children placed in her care as that would help us identify the victim."

One of the staff then emailed a staff member at OT saying they were taking another look at an older file "which we believe holds risk for both police and OT".

"It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can't elaborate on at this time.

"What I can say is that this IR relates to [redacted] so there is obvious risk and additional scrutiny attached to this."

Police asked for the request to be "escalated in the priority queue".

"The estimated response time of December 2026 by OT is going to create significant problems in addressing the risk."

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan. supplied

The 'heads up'

On 6 July, OT chief social worker Nicolette Dickson sent an email to six staff including deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan and national commissioner North Alison Cronin advising them she had just been contacted by an assistant commissioner at NZ Police who was managing a "conduct issue" relating to one of their Child Protection Protocol (CPP) investigators.

"It appears that this information in quite significant detail has been leaked to media…" Dickson said.

An urgent meeting was being set up for OT and police staff that afternoon.

"One of the key issues for me is that the CPP process is a joint process and we will need to assure ourselves that we took appropriate steps for at least the 30 cases where gaps have been raised.

"We can be a bit over reliant on police's view in the CPP process so we will need to check we took appropriate steps from a child safety/wellbeing perspective."

Ronan later emailed Assistant Commissioner Tusha Penny asking to have a chat ahead of a meeting that was planned for later in the week as OT needed to do "some assessment work off the back of it".

Penny cc'd in Assistant Commissioner Corrie Parnell who was in charge of investigations and asked him to have someone forward details relating to each child protection case to OT.

Later that evening, a member of police's media team emailed OT's media team with a copy of a statement that would be sent to media about Operation Hark.

The statement included a line that said police were "working with Oranga Tamariki, IPCA and other agencies, as we progress this matter".

OT chief of staff Stephanie Short replied in an internal email querying the line about working with OT and asked whether that referred to the meeting that was scheduled to take place later that week or the initial call that Dickson received earlier that day.

"I'm also concerned from our minister's office perspective about what and when we knew about this issue when the police media response indicates we are working together."

On 7 July, an email was sent to a group of OT staff about the operation in Te Tai Tokerau relating to concerns about CPP work.

The staffer who sent the email - whose name is redacted - said they had told chief advisor Simon Harding that the group of staff would be happy to be part of any work OT undertakes to look at the cases that have been identified so far.

"I noted we will have been across lots of these and we have noted some cases where delays occurred or decisions to not take actions.

"I will let you know when I hear more, it is great to see police moving to address the concerns and responding publicly as a team we have seen how serious things have been up in TTT for some time."

That morning RNZ approached OT with questions about Operation Hark.

Ronan emailed police and said they were getting a few media requests and hoped to get the case details from police "as soon as possible".

A police staffer said they had two staff assigned to sorting the information and hoped to have it completed by the following day.

In a separate email exchange on 7 July, Harding emailed some staff about the list of cases that was coming on 8 July and said they would need a "structured spreadsheet or template" to use to inform the reviews.

He then listed a series of possible things to cover including did OT know, and what actions OT took.

"Possibly something about what the Police told us? (unsure about this one, I am getting at the potential issue we may find of Police telling us things are fine when there is insufficient information to take that at face value, or perhaps that was about prosecution and we used it as the reason to close without considering safety and wellbeing more broadly? This could instead be a consideration under other areas)."

Harding also suggested questions around safety.

"I.e. is there evidence to show we considered safety risks and (if needed) either addressed them or were satisfied they were addressed? Are you worried about child safety after taking a look??"

Nine reports of concern

Ronan told RNZ OT had completed a review of all cases identified by police as potentially impacted and which involved children, all of whom were under 18 at the time of reporting to police.

"We did not identify any cases requiring urgent intervention to keep children safe.

"However, we continue to work with police locally to consider each case, share information, and determine any further actions required."

Asked how many of the CPP cases required further action by OT, Ronan said the agency had worked with police on most of the cases identified thus far to determine what further response was appropriate. This included engaging with children and families.

"Nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases," he said.

A report of concern is a notification to Oranga Tamariki about suspected abuse, neglect, harm, or wellbeing concerns for a child or young person.

RNZ also approached police for comment on the OIA including why the victim's name was not known and why Oranga Tamariki was not informed of the investigation before 6 July.

In response, Detective Superintendent Keith Borrell said police had made specific enquiries with OT "during an early and sensitive stage of our investigations".

"During the initial assessment phase of Operation Hark we were working to understand the scale of the situation. We have shared more fulsome information once it was appropriate to do so with OT."

World.title: All Blacks suffer scare as Cam Roigard pulled from lineup
World.content:
Star halfback Cam Roigard won't be involved in the All Blacks game against the Sharks in Durban on Wednesday morning.

The No.9 was named on the bench for the second game of Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour.

However, he has since been withdrawn with concerns about a tight calf.

A team source said the move was precautionary to allow some time for it to settle down.

Cam Roigard won't play against the Sharks. Masanori Udagawa/Photosport

Kyle Preston was named to start against the Sharks in Durban Wednesday morning (5am NZ time), while Cortez Ratima, who started the opening game against the Stormers has been brought onto the bench.

Roigard started all three of the All Blacks Nations Championship tests last month but was left out of the side that won last Saturday's clash with the Stormers in Cape Town, their opening match of the tour of South Africa.

Roigard is the All Blacks first choice halfback and they will want to do everything they can to ensure he's fully fit for the first test against the Springboks on 23 August.

The All Blacks went through their captains run today in Durban ahead of the match against the Sharks and loose forward Luke Jacobson, who will skipper the side, said they were seeking an improved performance from what they produced against the Stormers.

"It's an awesome challenge, an awesome opportunity for us to really dial in on maybe some things that didn't go as well for us in the last game."

Luke Jacobson is tackled by a French player. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Jacobson said the All Blacks were preparing to take on another physical South African side.

"We know how the South African teams play, they know their game, they've got their mauls, their scrums. There's going to be up front battles, so we're going to have to be ready to play that."

World.title: Number of teens with no qualifications higher than reported
World.content:
Those leaving school with no qualifications higher than stated Morning Report Download MP3 11m

The number of teens leaving school with no qualification is much higher than officially reported at nearly one-in-five of last year's 70,786 leavers.

The figure has been under-reported because since 2004 the Education Ministry has counted students half-way to a level two or three NCEA certificate as if they had a qualification, even if they didn't.

Including those students took the number of school-leavers with no qualification equivalent to at least NCEA level one to 13,165 last year - 19 percent of the total number of leavers and well above the previously reported figure of 10,496 or 15 percent.

Figures provided by the ministry also showed the number of school-leavers with 30 or more credits but no qualifications grew by 150 percent from 1058 in 2019 to 2669 last year, a period in which the total number of school-leavers increased 19 percent.

Adjusting 2019's result to include leavers with 30 or more credits but no qualification took that year's percentage of students with no qualification to 13 percent.

The practice of counting 30 or more credits at levels two and three as equivalent to a lower level certificate in the school-leaver statistics was no secret - it was included in the definitions used for each level of achievement - but it was a surprise to principals spoken to by RNZ.

Papakura High School principal Simon Craggs said he had no idea about the methodology and he did not agree half a level two or three certificate was equivalent to a level one certificate.

"For getting level one, particularly up until recently, you needed to have 80 credits so it's actually a lot hader to get level one than it is to get level two or three currently in terms of the number of credits accumulated," he said.

Papakura High School principal Simon Craggs. RNZ / Luka Forman

But Craggs said completed achievement or unit standards carried some value, even if students did not have a full NCEA certificate.

"A prospective employer can look at the things that a student is able to do and that's one of the strengths of the NCEA system," he said.

"Something that we've been advocating strongly for in the new qualification is that there is a list of what students can do and it's more strengths-based rather than they just passed or failed."

Steve McCracken from the Post Primary Teachers' Association (PPTA)'s secondary principals council said counting qualifications in the way the ministry did for its statistics way would make a big difference to schools' results - but they were not allowed to do that and it would not be true.

"I don't think it would be accurate would it, it would be a little bit of falsification of information really," he said.

"It's not right and it's not accurate so it needs to be rectified."

McCracken said schools relied on the ministry's figures to benchmark their own performance so it was important they compared like with like.

He said changing the interpretation of the results made a big difference to the school leaver figures.

Chair of the PPTA's Secondary Principals' Council, Steve McCracken. Supplied / Whangaparāoa College

"That's a significant increase isn't it in terms of people leaving without any formal qualifications," he said.

The ministry's data and insights general manager Grant Pollard said the practice was historical.

"The decision on that methodology was made at the time to reflect the transition in school quals. So 2002, NCEA level one was phased in as the primary qualification for Year 11 students replacing School Cert," he said.

Asked if the ministry decided at the time that 30 or more credits at levels two or three represented as much learning as a lower-level certificate, Pollard said it was possible to infer that but he could not definitively say why the decision was made.

He said the ministry would consider if it needed to change the methodology given a new qualification would be introduced from 2028-2030.

"We do need to look at it going forward," he said.

World.title: Christopher Luxon's grip on leadership questioned again
World.content:
Political update with Craig McCulloch Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Christopher Luxon's grip on his leadership is again being questioned following a week of communication gaffes and a fresh report his MPs are unhappy.

The Prime Minister last week endured days of mishaps and missteps and started this week inadvertently talking about three taxes the National Party may introduce if back in government.

He and his deputy, Nicola Willis, had called a press conference on Sunday to put pressure on Labour to sign up to its Budget responsibility rules, yet by his Monday morning media round Luxon was instead explaining that a fuel excise tax, bed tax, and bank tax would be on the table under a future National-led government.

On Monday night the NZ Herald reported National MPs had spent the day on the phones with one confirming they had fielded "several" phone calls about a potential leadership change.

"There's going to be change in the top job. It's just a question of who is going to be it", the NZ Herald reported the MP to have said.

RNZ spoke to about ten MPs on Monday night and received a mixture of responses.

Some said they wouldn't comment, while another said they couldn't comment, and others denied there were any leadership murmurings or that they knew about them.

One MP said the direct quotes in the reporting suggested there must be some truth to it, and at least one MP said it was nonsense.

RNZ understands the caucus will have a meeting online on Tuesday night, as Parliament is in recess this week.

On Saturday it was put to Luxon whether the confidence vote he called on his leadership back in April had resulted in a caucus split of 27 votes to 22.

He responded, "I have the support of my caucus - I'm very confident in my leadership."

It was speculation about whether Luxon was up to the job and had the backing of his caucus to stay on as leader that prompted him to test his support with a vote.

At the time when Luxon said that had put the rumour to bed and he had his caucus behind him.

Just four months later MPs appear to be musing about the prospect of changing leaders again.

While some spoken to by RNZ on Monday night said they supported Luxon, it wasn't unanimous.

There has been agitating since late last year from some MPs concerned Luxon's lack of personal popularity was also dragging the party vote down, and some MPs would lose their seats in Parliament if he didn't improve.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll in July had National down 2.1 points to 28.7 percent, its fourth consecutive decline in the Reid Research series and its weakest result since Luxon became leader in November 2021.

While Luxon's confidence vote win looked to have given him some reprieve, his performance in recent weeks has done little to convince concerned MPs they'll be safe come November 7.

Last Monday Luxon apologised to leaders from the Rotorua Business Chamber after he criticised them for having a "parent-child mentality" and relying on government too much.

He also faced questions about his foreign minister Winston Peters, and why he wasn't doing anything to reprimand him after labelling his comments about another MP, "racist".

Luxon then had to justify his use of a New Zealand Defence Force plane flying him home from a National Party fundraising dinner, and on the same day unemployment hit a record 11-year high.

On Thursday he was using talkback radio to make a captain's call to hold a referendum on MMP, which blindsided his own caucus.

World.title: Uni students skipping meals and classes to keep on top of bills
World.content:
Student questioning whether to continue due to cost-of-living Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A Wellington student is doubting that pursuing a degree is a smart move as she skips meals because she can't afford to eat.

A student association survey of 1238 students at Te Herenga Waka - Victoria University Wellington found many were skipping meals and missing classes as they worked to pay rent and bills on top of their studies.

Thirty-three percent of the students who responded to the survey said they had skipped a meal in the previous week because they couldn't afford to eat.

Pyper-Alex Adams is in her third year at Victoria University - studying Psychological Sciences.

She said a part-time job and a casual position on top of her full-time studies helped keep her rent paid, but she often skimped on meals - especially when shifts were sparse.

"If I get offered shifts that's great but I don't have any shifts this week, I don't have any shifts next week. I've actually had to apply to the student hardship grant to help with my power bill this month because I don't know if I'm going to be able to pay it without any shifts from my second job," Adams said.

She said she was starting to question whether a tertiary qualification was really a smart move.

"It makes me just want to drop out of university. I am barely able to afford rent. We're cold all the time because we're only using the heat pump during free power. I'm skipping meals.

"I'm going to university to try and get a degree. To maybe have a job someday - if I can get one in this country - but I'm seeing people my age that are doing so much better without the degree - which is the thing that we're all told in high school to do, right?" Adams said.

300 level student Pyper-Alex Adams. RNZ / Bill Hickman

Third-year maths and statistics student Cam Dickson was trying to be creative to find his way around the high cost of living.

"You know people talk about chicken and rice? We're not doing chicken and rice, we're doing beans and rice. I'm moving away from fresh fruit and vegetables because they're not super accessible right now. Going heavy on the carbs - on the cans - on the box stuff," Dickson said.

Dickson is one of the nearly 38 percent of students surveyed who said they had missed classes because they couldn't afford public transport costs.

"I don't have public transport in the wiggle room. I've got no way to own a car, to pay for the fuel. I'm very constrained to where my feet can get me and sometimes that's not university," Dickson said.

At the lower entrance to Victoria University, a billboard advertising open days asked whether people were 'Ready to experience Wellington like a Victoria University student?'.

Cam Dickson said many students' experience of the slogan might be different to what the advertisers imagined.

"It means to be cold a lot of the time. Sometimes it means to be hungry. Sometimes it means to be damp. Sometimes it means to just kind of struggle to get by and I wouldn't really recommend anyone that experience," Dickson said.

At the lower entrance to Victoria University, a billboard advertising open days asked whether people were 'Ready to experience Wellington like a Victoria University student?'. RNZ / Bill Hickman

The situation appeared to become more acute for students in their later stages of study.

Seventy-eight percent of third year students said they had considered heading overseas for better job opportunities - eight percent higher than respondents from across the entire survey population.

President of the Victoria University Students Association and Masters student, Aidan Donoghue, said the intense competition for work was changing how students approached their degrees.

"It's so competitive that you must be a straight A student. You must have X amount of internships. You must have all these extra curricular activities at this point just to put your name out there," Donoghue said

He had a message for people who saw today's student poverty as the same rite of passage experienced by previous generations.

"Students aren't just complaining. It's just as expensive as it was then but twenty years of inflation on top. Plus stagnant wage growth, plus competitive working environment. All the bad things of university that you have experienced have gotten worse over decades of compounding interest," Donoghue said.

World.title: Former championship winning team cut from A-Leagues
World.content:
Western United has had its A-Leagues participation agreement terminated, effectively ending any flicker of hope of the troubled club making a return.

United has essentially been an A-Leagues club in name only for more than a year amid varied financial woes, which included not paying players and staff.

The club was placed into hibernation by the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) in September 2025, with A-League Men and Women players having to scramble to continue their careers elsewhere.

Ownership West Melbourne Group avoided a wind-up order from the Australian Tax Office in January by settling a $15.5 million tax debt.

Football Australia declined to reinstate the Tarneit-based club's licence in May and United again won't participate in either the ALM or ALW.

West Melbourne Group have another wind-up hearing in the Federal Court on Tuesday and on Monday the APL officially terminated their participation agreement in the A-League competitions.

Western United won the A-League Men's grand final in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"Since the club was placed into conditional hibernation in September 2025, the APL has been in close consultation with Western United as they've worked through financial, governance and legal matters to try and rebuild the club," APL chair Stephen Conroy said in a statement.

"The APL board has since taken the decision to terminate Western United's club participation agreement.

"The club was in breach of a number of its obligations under that agreement, including its obligation to comply with the Football Australia National Club Licensing Regulations.

"It's been a difficult period for everyone connected to Western United — and we want to acknowledge the management, staff, players and especially the fans — who have given so much to the club and will no doubt be hurt by this news."

Sadness after Western United licence removal Western United fans have expressed their disappointment and sadness after the team was stripped of its A-League licence late last week.

AAP understands United still owes some of its former players and staff money.

United was granted a licence in 2018, off the back of grand promises to build its own stadium, entered the A-League Men ahead of the 2019-20 season and won the ALM championship in 2021-22.

A women's team followed in 2022-23 and reached the grand final in their first season.

United has consistently been defiant and adamant it will return to the A-Leagues.

When put into hibernation, the club claimed it wasn't a "step back".

Western United finally opened their small Ironbark Fields ground in 2024. It saw just one season of A-League football. (Getty Images: MB Media/Santanu Banik)

After the tax debt was paid in January, the club declared its ambition to seal a "strong return to the A-Leagues".

Despite the latest development, the club on Monday broadcast plans to return in a year's time under new ownership.

"Over recent months, we have worked closely with the APL on a pathway that gives the club the best opportunity to survive, rebuild and return to the A-League under new ownership," United said in a statement on Monday.

"This creates an opportunity for new custodians, new investment and a fresh start.

"The objective must now be to preserve Western United's identity in Melbourne's west and work towards a return to the A-League for the 2027-28 season.

"This should not be the end of Western United. It should be the reset that allows the club to rebuild and return stronger."

AAP

World.title: Injury could rule Socceroos defender out of Asian Cup
World.content:
Socceroos defender Cameron Burgess's Asian Cup hopes appear in jeopardy following a possible Achilles injury while playing for Swansea City.

The towering central defender played every minute of the gruelling English Championship campaign last season.

That made for 4,140 minutes, plus stoppage time, across all 46 league matches.

But there are fears Burgess's season is over after he limped off late in Swansea's 1-0 League Cup loss to Birmingham City.

In the 87th minute he challenged for a header, landed awkwardly and grabbed at his right lower leg, prompting his Birmingham opponents to check on him.

The 30-year-old, who has 29 Socceroos caps, headed to hospital for scans.

Cameron Burgess played against Türkiye and the USA for the Socceroos at the World Cup. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

"It doesn't look good, but I prefer to wait for the assessment we will do," Swansea head coach Vítor Matos said.

"It could be related to the Achilles, but let's see."

If Burgess has ruptured his Achilles, he faces a significant stint on the sidelines, ending his Asian Cup hopes.

Losing Burgess ahead of tournament, to be held in Saudi Arabia early next year, is a significant blow to Australia's defensive stocks.

Burgess lost his starting spot to teen sensation Lucas Herrington during the World Cup, with coach Tony Popovic preferring a back three involving the teenager, Harry Souttar and Alessandro Circati.

But as a left-footer, Burgess is always a valuable part of Popovic's squad.

Souttar spent more than a year on the sidelines after his own Achilles tear, while wing-back Lewis Miller is on the comeback trail from the same injury, which ruled him out of World Cup contention.

Star wing-back Jordan Bos is sidelined until about October after having surgery on the left knee injured in Australia's round-of-32 loss to Egypt.

The Socceroos are next in action for friendlies against Brazil in Townsville on September 25 and Brisbane four days later.

AAP

World.title: Head aims to maintain opening spot ahead of busy 12 months
World.content:
Travis Head can envisage himself continuing to open the batting for Australia at the end of next year's Ashes.

The positive mindset of the back-to-back Allan Border Medal winner is no surprise.

Head was a revelation in home conditions in last year's Ashes series with three centuries after moving up from the middle order.

Ahead of the opening Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, the 32-year-old was asked if his order switch was short-term or whether it could work across the 20 or more Tests Australia will play in the next 12 months.

There was a sense that Head's move up the order against England was intended to counter their ultra-aggressive "Bazball".

It worked so well that the term "Travball" was coined.

Prior to the home Ashes, his stints as an opener had been short-lived.

Travis Head scored three centuries as an opener in the last Ashes series. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Head was unstoppable on home tracks in the Ashes series, but he will face a variety of surfaces in Australia, South Africa, England and India in the next 12 months.

He says he is not worried about playing in different conditions.

"I feel like I have been adaptable in the places that I have played," Head said.

"In India and England I have opened the batting, which is a slightly different to Australia.

"Everything is going to be different, but what I have been able to do over my career is problem solve the best that I can and work through challenges — whether they are green wickets or flat wickets.

"It will look different in every Test match or every series. I am trying to be as calm and consistent as I can."

Whether Head stays an opener will depend largely on how he performs and also on the displays of the middle order.

Tweaks may be made but right now Head plans to be opening in the final Test of next year's away Ashes series.

"I think it will work," he said.

"If I have done it for [another] 20 Tests and I am sitting there in a few years and I have opened the batting the whole time … I would have done an OK job and been consistent, contributed and had a good partnership with Jake [Weatherald].

"It is a new challenge coming here and a new challenge in South Africa in a month's time and I am looking forward to the challenge."

International cricket coach Joe Gatting has posted videos of how Head plans for a variety of scenarios and surfaces and he is expected to continue to find the best approach in all conditions.

"We have a lot of footage and we couldn't be more resourced in that space. I'll continue to do that," Head said.

AAP

World.title: Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal
World.content:
Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's "please explain" as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Also on Monday, Geelong captain Patrick Dangerfield said the club had "buggered up", but strongly defended Hocking.

Pressure has been mounting on Geelong and the AFL since it emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who had a history of concussion.

Drummond apologises AFL chair Craig Drummond issues a statement apologising for his part in the Jake Kolodjashnij concussion contract saga.

"We acknowledge this has been a challenging time for Jake, our club and Geelong supporters," Cats president Grant McCabe said in a statement on Monday.

"The board has met this morning to discuss our response to the AFL's letter. That will be submitted by end of day Tuesday, 11 August.

"This will provide the club with the chance to detail the actions it took in navigating this complex matter. We welcome this opportunity.

"The club remains committed to providing our players with the highest standard of care and support."

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

On the weekend Hocking defended the club in a radio interview and argued there was not a lot they would do differently.

"As a leader it's really important to take ownership and just lead through this. It's not easy to do, but I wouldn't change too much — we are a really good football club," he said.

"I know there are people out there who say culturally we are maybe not as strong as we have been, but we do so much right and occasionally there might be one or two per cent we don't get right.

"In this case that will be proven, I would suggest, that will be proven with the 'please explain'. We don't get everything right."

Drummond also released a statement in which he apologised over the deal. He added he would not be involved in the AFL's assessment and deliberation of the Kolodjashnij situation.

On Monday, Dangerfield told Fox Footy that Hocking was one of the most "placid" people he had met and gave him his full support.

"He's a man of the highest integrity … we're lucky to have him," Dangerfield said.

But he acknowledged mistakes had been made.

"Clearly there were some parts that we buggered up as a club. We can be better," he said.

AAP

World.title: WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul
World.content:
DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky has been ejected after being called for a Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever.

Minutes after the eviction on Saturday (local time), Carrington posted on social media the words "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever.

Cunningham, who is white, was shooting a fast-break lay-up in the first quarter when Carrington, who is black, came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in.

Cunningham said she thought the foul in the 90–86 Indiana win was "absolutely" intentional.

"Clearly I think it was unnecessary," Cunningham said.

"I've never really spoken to her and I have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent-up stuff."

DiJonai Carrington had little to complain about, most suggested. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

Fever coach Stephanie White had a different view of the play.

"It was a hard foul," White said.

"I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did, but it did happen, and I thought it was the right call."

Cunningham got up immediately, charged toward Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.

"I popped up," Cunningham said.

"I'm not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that's why she did it, because she wants attention."

Sophie Cunningham had to be held back after popping up after the foul. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Melissa Tamez)

The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was wind-up, impact and follow-through on the foul.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he had not seen a replay of the play, but that seeing it live, he thought Carrington was making a play on the ball and that he did not believe it warranted a Flagrant 2 foul.

"I haven't looked at that play since, so I really don't know if it was justified or not," he said.

"But, that's what I thought in the moment."

Marsh was then asked about Carrington's social media post.

"I have to get back to you on that because I'm just now hearing about that," he said.

"So yeah, we'll handle that."

But Cunningham had plenty to say about the post.

"I think the league is taking care of that," she said.

"This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card."

In the third quarter, Fever star Caitlin Clark was assessed a technical foul after she made contact with a referee when she was forced out of bounds.

WNBA champs rubbish claims of Clark jealousy The outsized spotlight on Caitlin Clark has prompted some to suggest others in the WNBA are jealous of her, but two champions of the league say that is nonsense.

The technical was Clark's eighth of the season, triggering a one-game suspension for Indiana's next game if not rescinded by the league.

"She said I ran into her," Clark said in a post-game television interview.

"I've already watched it on the tape, so we'll let the league decide. But it wasn't intentional or anything, so I'm hoping it's getting rescinded,"

A few hours after the game, Clark got her way. The WNBA rescinded the technical foul.

Cunningham has frequently come to Clark's defence after physical play by opponents and has become one of the higher-profile players in the league this season.

AP

World.title: Brazilian footballer falls in tunnel after scoring disallowed goal
World.content:
Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão was rushing to meet a sea of his supporters, ball in hand and jumping with joy, before he fell down a dark tunnel.

The Corbita defender had just put his club 2-0 up against Chapecoense in the first half of a game in the Brazilian Serie A.

But just as he found his footing again and dusted himself off from the fall, the referee halted the game.

On review, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) found the 29-year-old's goal was offside.

Jacy managed to continue playing into the first few minutes of the second half before being substituted with an injury.

The incident was not the first time a footballer had fallen foul of the tunnel at the Estádio Major Antônio Couto Pereira.

Loading...

Almost a decade earlier, Cameroonian forward Diederrick Joel Tagueu-Tadjo ran to the same end of the pitch, jumping over the same advertising hoardings before falling into the now-infamous Corbita tunnel.

But unlike Jacy, his goal was not ruled out, and he managed to finish the game against São Paulo.

But according to Brazilian journalist Leonardo Mendes Jr, there was a striking similarity to the two incidents.

"There's one detail that makes it even more unbelievable," he posted on social media.

World.title: Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers
World.content:
Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

The signing of the Penrith Panthers flyer, who has represented NSW in State of Origin and Samoa in Test matches, was announced by the Chiefs on Monday.

To'o has signed a three-year deal to join the Chiefs, with 2027 to be his final year with the Panthers.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"Brian is an exceptional rugby league player, but this signing is about much more than football," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

"The PNG Chiefs will be a club proudly built in Papua New Guinea but with a strong Pacific identity.

"Across our region, family, culture, community and rugby league are deeply connected, and Brian represents those values every time he takes the field.

"He is fiercely proud of his Samoan heritage, incredibly close to his family and understands what it means to represent something bigger than yourself.

"That is exactly the kind of person we want wearing the Chiefs jersey."

To'o has been a key component of the Penrith Panthers dynasty, which won four consecutive premierships from 2021–2024, were grand finalists in 2020 and made last year's preliminary final.

The Panthers are on top of the NRL ladder in 2026, seeking a fifth title in six years.

To'o has played 151 matches for the Panthers since making his debut in 2019, scoring 99 tries to date.

He has played 17 Origins for the Blues, and 11 Tests for Samoa.

"Brian is an exceptional player, but he's an even better person. He's a great teammate, a devoted family man and someone who brings so much energy and positivity to our club every day," Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said.

"He's been a huge part of what we've built here and we're looking forward to sharing one more season with him before he begins his next chapter."

The Chiefs have now signed six players to its maiden roster, but have already secured key talent.

Former Penrith five-eighth Jarome Luai, who won four premierships with To'o, was the club's marquee signing earlier this year.

Alex Johnston, the all-time leading try scorer in Australian premiership rugby league, was a key outside back signed along with NSW Origin representative Zac Lomax.

Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson and Englishman Matty Lees have also been signed.

World.title: Yeo learns fate on pec in seismic moment for Panthers
World.content:
Penrith's premiership charge has received a massive boost, with Isaah Yeo a chance to play again this year after avoiding surgery on his pectoral injury.

Yeo had been at risk of missing the rest of the NRL season after he left the field in Friday's loss to the Warriors, in what shaped as a major blow for the Panthers.

But Penrith medical staff confirmed on Monday the club's co-captain would not go under the knife following scans, and could begin rehabilitation in a bid to play again in 2026.

The news will also likely come as a relief to Australia coach Kevin Walters, with Yeo expected to again lead the Kangaroos at the World Cup if he avoids later surgery.

Former Panther Apisai Koroisau missed just one week with a pectoral injury early this year, as opposed to the 10 weeks usually out if surgery is required.

Penrith has made a habit of having players play through injury to be part of premiership wins throughout their dynasty.

Almost half of their squad were walking wounded through the first title of their four-peat in 2021, which the club compared to climbing Mount Everest.

Halves Jarome Luai and Nathan Cleary both played through persistent shoulder issues in 2023 and 2024 respectively, with both requiring surgery afterwards.

Had Yeo been sidelined, it would have been a monumental blow to the first-placed Panthers, given the role he plays in both attack and defence at lock.

Ex-Panther Spencer Leniu described Yeo as the "heartbeat" of Penrith's team over the weekend, declaring his injury would be a "massive loss" for the club.

Penrith faces Leniu's Sydney Roosters in a blockbuster top-of-the-table clash on Thursday night, which Yeo would not be expected to play in.

AAP

Bluesky has added a new feature that lets you hide reposts from a specific person in your feeds. The tool might be helpful if you want to stop seeing reposts from that one person who clogs up your feed with reposts of things you don’t care about. If you follow me, I may be that person, I’m sorry. I try not to be.

You can hide reposts from individual users by going to their profile, clicking the three dots button, and selecting the option to “Hide reposts in feeds.” (X offers a similar toggle.)

Bluesky also says that it’s launching a beta feature that will automatically add post numbers to threads.
